abstract: It has remained unknown whether one can in principle carry out reliable digital computations with networks of biologically realistic models for neurons. This article presents rigorous constructions for simulating in real-time arbitrary given boolean circuits and fi(cid:173) nite automata with arbitrarily high reliability by networks of noisy spiking neurons. In addition we show that with the help of "shunting inhibition" even networks of very unreliable spiking neurons can simulate in real-time any McCulloch-Pitts neuron (or "threshold gate"), and therefore any multilayer perceptron (or "threshold circuit") in a reliable manner. These constructions provide a possible explana(cid:173) tion for the fact that biological neural systems can carry out quite complex computations within 100 msec. It turns out that the assumption that these constructions require about the shape of the EPSP's and the behaviour of the noise are surprisingly weak.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether networks of biologically realistic, noisy spiking neurons can perform reliable digital computation in principle. The challenge is that individual elements may behave unreliably, while digital operations require dependable outcomes. The authors address the question through rigorous constructions of networks that simulate established computational systems.

They show how to simulate arbitrary Boolean circuits and finite automata in real time with arbitrarily high reliability. With shunting inhibition, they also construct reliable simulations of threshold gates from very unreliable spiking neurons. Because threshold gates can form multilayer threshold networks, the result extends to that class of neural computation.

The constructions require only weak assumptions about excitatory postsynaptic potential shapes and noise behavior, according to the abstract. Their significance is an existence result: dependable, fast computation is compatible with noisy spiking components under those assumptions. The authors propose this as a possible explanation for complex biological computations occurring within 100 milliseconds, connecting formal computational capability with the speed of neural processing.
summary.tldr: Rigorous constructions show that noisy spiking-neuron networks can reliably simulate digital circuits and finite automata in real time.

title: On the Computational Power of Noisy Spiking Neurons

abstract: There is currently considerable interest in developing general non(cid:173) linear density models based on latent, or hidden, variables. Such models have the ability to discover the presence of a relatively small number of underlying 'causes' which, acting in combination, give rise to the apparent complexity of the observed data set. Unfortu(cid:173) nately, to train such models generally requires large computational effort. In this paper we introduce a novel latent variable algorithm which retains the general non-linear capabilities of previous models but which uses a training procedure based on the EM algorithm. We demonstrate the performance of the model on a toy problem and on data from flow diagnostics for a multi-phase oil pipeline.

paragraphs: The paper develops a nonlinear probability model built around latent variables: quantities that are not directly observed but help explain the data. The motivation is that a relatively small set of underlying factors can combine to produce observations that appear much more complicated. Learning such a representation can expose structure behind that complexity.

The obstacle addressed is the computational effort generally required to train nonlinear latent-variable models. The authors introduce a new algorithm that preserves the general nonlinear capabilities of earlier models while organizing training around expectation-maximization, or EM. The proposed change therefore concerns how a flexible hidden-variable model can be fitted to observations.

The authors demonstrate the model on a toy problem and on measurements used for flow diagnostics in a multiphase oil pipeline. These applications connect the modeling idea to both a simple example and an applied data problem. The contribution is an EM-based training approach for nonlinear density modeling, with demonstrations showing its use in uncovering a compact hidden description of observed data.
summary.tldr: A new latent-variable density model retains nonlinear flexibility while using EM-based training.

title: EM Optimization of Latent-Variable Density Models

abstract: The Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm is an iterative procedure for maximum likelihood parameter estimation from data sets with missing or hidden variables [2]. It has been applied to system identification in linear stochastic state-space models, where the state variables are hidden from the observer and both the state and the parameters of the model have to be estimated simultaneously [9]. We present a generalization of the EM algorithm for parameter estimation in nonlinear dynamical systems. The "expectation" step makes use of Extended Kalman Smoothing to estimate the state, while the "maximization" step re-estimates the parameters using these uncertain state estimates. In general, the nonlinear maximization step is difficult because it requires integrating out the uncertainty in the states. However, if Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) approximators are used to model the nonlinearities, the integrals become tractable and the maximization step can be solved via systems of linear equations.

paragraphs: This paper extends expectation-maximization to learning nonlinear dynamical systems whose internal states cannot be observed directly. The learning problem has two connected unknowns: the sequence of hidden states and the parameters governing the system. EM addresses them iteratively, using the current model to estimate hidden states and then using those estimates to revise the model.

The expectation step uses extended Kalman smoothing to estimate the hidden states. The maximization step updates the parameters while accounting for uncertainty in those state estimates. This uncertainty is central to the computational difficulty: nonlinear parameter updates generally require integrating over possible states, rather than simply treating an estimated trajectory as known.

The authors show that choosing Gaussian radial basis functions to represent the nonlinear relationships makes the required integrals tractable. With that representation, the maximization step reduces to solving systems of linear equations. The contribution is therefore a combination of approximate state inference and a carefully chosen nonlinear model that makes uncertainty-aware parameter learning computationally manageable.
summary.tldr: An EM method combines extended Kalman smoothing with Gaussian radial basis functions to make nonlinear dynamical-system parameter updates tractable.

title: Learning Nonlinear Dynamical Systems Using an EM Algorithm

abstract: We present a novel method for approximate inference in Bayesian mod- els and regularized risk functionals. It is based on the propagation of mean and variance derived from the Laplace approximation of condi- tional probabilities in factorizing distributions, much akin to Minka’s Expectation Propagation. In the jointly normal case, it coincides with the latter and belief propagation, whereas in the general case, it provides an optimization strategy containing Support Vector chunking, the Bayes Committee Machine, and Gaussian Process chunking as special cases.
originalAbstract: We present a novel method for approximate inference in Bayesian mod- els and regularized risk functionals. It is based on the propagation of mean and variance derived from the Laplace approximation of condi- tional probabilities in factorizing distributions, much akin to Minka’s Expectation Propagation. In the jointly normal case, it coincides with the latter and belief propagation, whereas in the general case, it provides an optimization strategy containing Support Vector chunking, the Bayes Committee Machine, and Gaussian Process chunking as special cases.

paragraphs: Laplace Propagation is a method for approximate inference in Bayesian models and for working with regularized risk objectives. It operates on distributions that can be expressed through factors. The method uses Laplace approximations of conditional probabilities to derive means and variances, then propagates those quantities through the factorized representation.

Its relationship to expectation propagation helps place the proposal within existing inference methods. In the special case of a jointly normal distribution, Laplace Propagation agrees with both expectation propagation and belief propagation. This equivalence identifies a setting in which the different procedures produce the same method, while leaving room for different behavior beyond that setting.

For more general distributions, the authors present the method as an optimization strategy encompassing several established procedures. Support Vector chunking, the Bayes Committee Machine, and Gaussian Process chunking appear as special cases. The contribution is thus both a proposed approximate inference procedure and a common framework linking methods through the propagation of locally derived means and variances.
summary.tldr: Laplace Propagation passes locally approximated means and variances, unifying several inference and optimization methods as special cases.

title: Laplace Propagation

abstract: Several unsupervised learning algorithms based on an eigendecompo- sition provide either an embedding or a clustering only for given train- ing points, with no straightforward extension for out-of-sample examples short of recomputing eigenvectors. This paper provides a uniﬁed frame- work for extending Local Linear Embedding (LLE), Isomap, Laplacian Eigenmaps, Multi-Dimensional Scaling (for dimensionality reduction) as well as for Spectral Clustering. This framework is based on seeing these algorithms as learning eigenfunctions of a data-dependent kernel. Numerical experiments show that the generalizations performed have a level of error comparable to the variability of the embedding algorithms due to the choice of training data.

This paper provides a uniﬁed frame- work for extending Local Linear Embedding (LLE), Isomap, Laplacian Eigenmaps, Multi-Dimensional Scaling (for dimensionality reduction) as well as for Spectral Clustering. Numerical experiments show that the generalizations performed have a level of error comparable to the variability of the embedding algorithms due to the choice of training data.

paragraphs: Several methods that use eigendecomposition produce an embedding or clustering only for the points supplied during training. Extending the result to a new point is not straightforward and can otherwise require recomputing eigenvectors. This paper addresses that gap for LLE, Isomap, multidimensional scaling, Laplacian Eigenmaps, and spectral clustering.

The authors provide one framework by interpreting these algorithms as learning eigenfunctions of a kernel that depends on the data. This view turns the spectral result into something that can be evaluated beyond the original training points. It connects methods for dimensionality reduction and clustering through a common account of how their learned structures extend.

Numerical experiments compare extension error with the variability caused by choosing different training data. The reported errors are comparable to that existing variability. This places the approximation in context: applying the learned structure to new examples introduces errors on a scale similar to changes already observed when the underlying embedding algorithms are trained on different data selections.
summary.tldr: A kernel-eigenfunction framework extends several spectral embedding and clustering methods to new points without recomputing their eigenvectors.

title: Out-of-Sample Extensions for LLE, Isomap, MDS, Eigenmaps, and Spectral Clustering

abstract: Existing source location and recovery algorithms used in magnetoen- cephalographic imaging generally assume that the source activity at dif- ferent brain locations is independent or that the correlation structure is known. However, electrophysiological recordings of local ﬁeld poten- tials show strong correlations in aggregate activity over signiﬁcant dis- tances. Indeed, it seems very likely that stimulus-evoked activity would follow strongly correlated time-courses in different brain areas. Here, we present, and validate through simulations, a new approach to source reconstruction in which the correlation between sources is modelled and estimated explicitly by variational Bayesian methods, facilitating accu- rate recovery of source locations and the time-courses of their activation.

However, electrophysiological recordings of local ﬁeld poten- tials show strong correlations in aggregate activity over signiﬁcant dis- tances. Indeed, it seems very likely that stimulus-evoked activity would follow strongly correlated time-courses in different brain areas. Here, we present, and validate through simulations, a new approach to source reconstruction in which the correlation between sources is modelled and estimated explicitly by variational Bayesian methods, facilitating accu- rate recovery of source locations and the time-courses of their activation.

paragraphs: Reconstructing brain activity from magnetoencephalographic measurements requires estimating where sources are located and how their activity changes over time. Existing methods generally assume either independent source activity or a correlation structure supplied in advance. This paper addresses the case where sources may be correlated and those relationships are unknown.

The motivation comes from electrophysiological recordings showing strong correlations in aggregate activity across substantial distances. The authors also consider it likely that stimulus-evoked activity in different brain areas follows correlated time courses. Their approach explicitly models correlations between sources and estimates them using variational Bayesian methods as part of reconstruction.

Simulation results validate the approach and support accurate recovery of source locations and activation time courses. Estimating correlation within the model matters because shared activity is then a feature to infer, rather than something excluded by independence or assumed known beforehand. The stated evidence supports this reconstruction strategy in simulations, including its ability to accommodate relationships among active sources.
summary.tldr: A variational Bayesian MEG method estimates unknown source correlations alongside locations and activation time courses.

title: Reconstructing MEG Sources with Unknown Correlations

abstract: We introduce a game-theoretic model for network formation inspired by earlier stochastic models that mix localized and long-distance connectivity. In this model, players may purchase edges at distance d at a cost of d , and wish to minimize the sum of their edge purchases and their average distance to other players. In this model, we show there is a striking "small world" threshold phenomenon: in two dimensions, if < 2 then every Nash equilibrium results in a network of constant diameter (independent of network size), and if > 2 then every Nash equilibrium results in a network whose diameter grows as a root of the network size, and thus is unbounded. We contrast our results with those of Kleinberg [8] in a stochastic model, and empirically investigate the "navigability" of equilibrium networks. Our theoretical results all generalize to higher dimensions.

In this model, we show there is a striking "small world" threshold phenomenon: in two dimensions, if < 2 then every Nash equilibrium results in a network of constant diameter (independent of network size), and if > 2 then every Nash equilibrium results in a network whose diameter grows as a root of the network size, and thus is unbounded. We contrast our results with those of Kleinberg [8] in a stochastic model, and empirically investigate the "navigability" of equilibrium networks. Our theoretical results all generalize to higher dimensions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how networks form when participants choose which connections to buy. Each player balances spending on edges against the average network distance to everyone else. The model connects individual economic decisions with a global question: when will the resulting network keep even its most distant participants close together?

The authors establish a sharp threshold for equilibrium networks in two dimensions. Below the threshold value of two for the model's distance-cost parameter, every Nash equilibrium has a diameter bounded independently of network size. Above two, every equilibrium has a diameter that grows as a root of network size. The supplied abstract has missing mathematical symbols, so it does not fully specify the cost formula.

The distinction is between networks whose maximum separation stays bounded as they expand and networks whose maximum separation keeps increasing. The theoretical results extend to higher dimensions. The authors also compare their findings with an earlier stochastic model and empirically examine navigability, asking how equilibrium network structure relates to the ability to find routes.
summary.tldr: A network formation game exhibits a threshold separating equilibria with size-independent diameter from equilibria whose diameter grows with network size.

title: A Small World Threshold for Economic Network Formation

abstract: We consider the scenario where training and test data are drawn from different distributions, commonly referred to as sample selection bias. Most algorithms for this setting try to ﬁrst recover sampling distributions and then make appro- priate corrections based on the distribution estimate. We present a nonparametric method which directly produces resampling weights without distribution estima- tion. Our method works by matching distributions between training and testing sets in feature space. Experimental results demonstrate that our method works well in practice.
originalAbstract: We consider the scenario where training and test data are drawn from different distributions, commonly referred to as sample selection bias. We present a nonparametric method which directly produces resampling weights without distribution estima- tion. Our method works by matching distributions between training and testing sets in feature space. Experimental results demonstrate that our method works well in practice.

paragraphs: This paper considers sample selection bias, where training data and test data come from different distributions. The training sample therefore represents a different mix of inputs from the one encountered at test time. Correcting that mismatch requires deciding how the training observations should contribute when learning for the test distribution.

The proposed nonparametric method directly computes resampling weights. It does so by matching the training and test distributions in feature space, using unlabeled data to inform the correction. This differs from approaches that first estimate the sampling distributions and then derive weights from those estimates. Here, the desired correction is obtained without that intermediate distribution-estimation step.

The authors report experimental evidence that the method works well in practice. The main methodological contribution is the direct route from a distribution mismatch to weights that adjust the training sample's representation. Feature-space matching supplies the criterion for those weights, connecting information about the test inputs to the treatment of training examples without requiring labels for the test data.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric method corrects sample selection bias by directly learning resampling weights through feature-space distribution matching.

title: Correcting Sample Selection Bias by Unlabeled Data

abstract: In kernel-based regression learning, optimizing each kernel individually is useful when the data density, curvature of regression surfaces (or decision boundaries) or magnitude of output noise (i.e., heteroscedasticity) varies spatially. Unfortunately, it presents a complex computational problem as the danger of overfitting is high and the individual optimization of every kernel in a learning system may be overly expensive due to the introduction of too many open learning parameters. Previous work has suggested gradient descent techniques or complex statistical hypothesis methods for local kernel shaping, typically requiring some amount of manual tuning of meta parameters. In this paper, we focus on nonparametric regression and introduce a Bayesian formulation that, with the help of variational approximations, results in an EM-like algorithm for simultaneous estimation of regression and kernel parameters. The algorithm is computationally efficient (suitable for large data sets), requires no sampling, automatically rejects outliers and has only one prior to be specified. It can be used for nonparametric regression with local polynomials or as a novel method to achieve nonstationary regression with Gaussian Processes. Our methods are particularly useful for learning control, where reliable estimation of local tangent planes is essential for adaptive controllers and reinforcement learning. We evaluate our methods on several synthetic data sets and on an actual robot which learns a task-level control law.

paragraphs: Kernel regression can benefit from adapting individual kernels when data density, surface curvature, or output noise varies across the input space. However, giving every kernel adjustable parameters creates both computational expense and a risk of overfitting. The paper addresses this tension through a Bayesian formulation of local kernel shaping.

Variational approximations yield an algorithm resembling expectation maximization that estimates regression and kernel parameters together. The authors describe it as computationally efficient for large datasets, requiring no sampling and only one specified prior. It also automatically rejects outliers. The framework applies to regression with local polynomials and provides a way to construct nonstationary Gaussian process regression.

The control motivation is that adaptive controllers and reinforcement learning need reliable estimates of local tangent planes: approximations to how a learned response changes nearby. Spatially adaptive kernels are intended to support those estimates. The authors evaluate the methods on synthetic datasets and on a real robot learning a task-level control law, connecting the regression formulation to an actual control application.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian algorithm jointly adapts regression models and local kernels, supporting efficient, outlier-resistant estimation for learning control.

title: Bayesian Kernel Shaping for Learning Control

abstract: A fundamental objective in reinforcement learning is the maintenance of a proper balance between exploration and exploitation. This problem becomes more challenging when the agent can only partially observe the states of its environment. In this paper we propose a dual-policy method for jointly learning the agent behavior and the balance between exploration exploitation, in partially observable environments. The method subsumes traditional exploration, in which the agent takes actions to gather information about the environment, and active learning, in which the agent queries an oracle for optimal actions (with an associated cost for employing the oracle). The form of the employed exploration is dictated by the specific problem. Theoretical guarantees are provided concerning the optimality of the balancing of exploration and exploitation. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated by experimental results on benchmark problems.

In this paper we propose a dual-policy method for jointly learning the agent behavior and the balance between exploration exploitation, in partially observable environments. The method subsumes traditional exploration, in which the agent takes actions to gather information about the environment, and active learning, in which the agent queries an oracle for optimal actions (with an associated cost for employing the oracle). The form of the employed exploration is dictated by the specific problem. Theoretical guarantees are provided concerning the optimality of the balancing of exploration and exploitation. paragraphs: The paper addresses the choice between gathering information and using existing knowledge to obtain reward. This balance becomes harder when an agent cannot fully observe its environment’s state. The authors propose a dual-policy method that jointly learns the agent’s behavior and how to balance exploration with exploitation in these partially observable environments.

The framework accommodates two forms of information gathering. An agent can take exploratory actions that reveal more about its environment, or it can ask an oracle for optimal actions while paying an associated cost. Which form of exploration is used depends on the problem. Bringing both into one method connects ordinary exploration with active learning.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees concerning the optimality of the exploration–exploitation balance and demonstrates effectiveness on benchmark problems. Its contribution is to make the balancing decision part of what the agent learns. This explicitly incorporates the value of acquiring information, including situations where useful guidance is available but costly.
summary.tldr: A dual-policy method learns behavior and the exploration–exploitation balance, including exploration through costly oracle queries.

title: Learning to Explore and Exploit in POMDPs

abstract: Despite the recent trend of increasingly large datasets for object detection, there still exist many classes with few training examples. To overcome this lack of train- ing data for certain classes, we propose a novel way of augmenting the training data for each class by borrowing and transforming examples from other classes. Our model learns which training instances from other classes to borrow and how to transform the borrowed examples so that they become more similar to instances from the target class. Our experimental results demonstrate that our new object detector, with borrowed and transformed examples, improves upon the current state-of-the-art detector on the challenging SUN09 object detection dataset.

To overcome this lack of train- ing data for certain classes, we propose a novel way of augmenting the training data for each class by borrowing and transforming examples from other classes. Our model learns which training instances from other classes to borrow and how to transform the borrowed examples so that they become more similar to instances from the target class. Our experimental results demonstrate that our new object detector, with borrowed and transformed examples, improves upon the current state-of-the-art detector on the challenging SUN09 object detection dataset.

paragraphs: Large object-detection datasets can still contain classes with very few training examples. The paper addresses this uneven supply of data by allowing a target class to use examples from other classes. The goal is to expand the training material available for a class whose own examples are insufficient, drawing on information already present elsewhere in the dataset.

The model learns both which outside examples to borrow and how to transform them to resemble examples of the target class more closely. Selection and transformation are therefore both part of the learning problem. This makes the contribution more specific than simply pooling data across classes: the borrowed instances are chosen and adapted for the class receiving them.

Experiments on the SUN09 object-detection dataset show that the resulting detector improves on the state-of-the-art detector used in the comparison. The findings support cross-class example borrowing as a way to strengthen object detection when some classes are poorly represented. The reported benefit comes from training with examples that are both borrowed and transformed.
summary.tldr: Learning which examples to borrow from other classes and how to transform them improves object detection on SUN09.

title: Transfer Learning by Borrowing Examples for Multiclass Object Detection

abstract: Motivated by large-scale multimedia applications we propose to learn mappings from high-dimensional data to binary codes that preserve semantic similarity. Binary codes are well suited to large-scale applications as they are storage efficient and permit exact sub-linear kNN search. The framework is applicable to broad families of mappings, and uses a flexible form of triplet ranking loss. We overcome discontinuous optimization of the discrete mappings by minimizing a piecewise-smooth upper bound on empirical loss, inspired by latent structural SVMs. We develop a new loss-augmented inference algorithm that is quadratic in the code length. We show strong retrieval performance on CIFAR-10 and MNIST, with promising classification results using no more than kNN on the binary codes.

Binary codes are well suited to large-scale applications as they are storage efficient and permit exact sub-linear kNN search. The framework is applicable to broad families of mappings, and uses a flexible form of triplet ranking loss. We overcome discontinuous optimization of the discrete mappings by minimizing a piecewise-smooth upper bound on empirical loss, inspired by latent structural SVMs. We develop a new loss-augmented inference algorithm that is quadratic in the code length. paragraphs: The paper learns mappings from high-dimensional data to binary codes while preserving semantic similarity. This is motivated by large multimedia collections, where compact storage and efficient retrieval are important. Binary representations offer storage efficiency and permit exact sublinear nearest-neighbor search, making the quality of their learned similarity structure central to their usefulness.

The framework supports broad families of mappings and trains them with a flexible triplet-ranking loss. Because discrete mappings create a discontinuous optimization problem, the authors minimize a piecewise-smooth upper bound on the empirical loss. The construction draws on latent structural SVMs and includes a new loss-augmented inference algorithm with cost quadratic in code length.

The authors report strong retrieval results on CIFAR-10 and MNIST. They also obtain promising classification results by applying only nearest-neighbor classification to the binary codes. Together, these results indicate that the learned codes retain useful semantic relationships for both retrieval and prediction, while the optimization method provides a way to train mappings despite their discrete outputs.
summary.tldr: A tractable upper-bound objective learns compact binary codes that preserve semantic similarity and perform well in retrieval.

title: Hamming Distance Metric Learning

abstract: The classification of high-dimensional data defined on graphs is particularly difficult when the graph geometry is unknown. We introduce a Haar scattering transform on graphs, which computes invariant signal descriptors. It is implemented with a deep cascade of additions, subtractions and absolute values, which iteratively compute orthogonal Haar wavelet transforms. Multiscale neighborhoods of unknown graphs are estimated by minimizing an average total variation, with a pair matching algorithm of polynomial complexity. Supervised classification with dimension reduction is tested on data bases of scrambled images, and for signals sampled on unknown irregular grids on a sphere.
originalAbstract: The classification of high-dimensional data defined on graphs is particularly difficult when the graph geometry is unknown. We introduce a Haar scattering transform on graphs, which computes invariant signal descriptors. It is implemented with a deep cascade of additions, subtractions and absolute values, which iteratively compute orthogonal Haar wavelet transforms. Multiscale neighborhoods of unknown graphs are estimated by minimizing an average total variation, with a pair matching algorithm of polynomial complexity. Supervised classification with dimension reduction is tested on data bases of scrambled images, and for signals sampled on unknown irregular grids on a sphere.

paragraphs: Classifying high-dimensional signals on graphs is especially challenging when the underlying graph geometry is unknown. This paper introduces a Haar scattering transform that computes invariant signal descriptors in that setting. The approach combines a deep computational structure with a procedure for estimating the multiscale neighborhoods needed to organize the signals.

The transform uses repeated additions, subtractions, and absolute values to build a cascade of orthogonal Haar wavelet transforms. To estimate neighborhoods when the graph is unknown, the authors minimize an average total-variation objective. They use a pair-matching algorithm with polynomial complexity, providing a computational procedure for constructing structure at multiple scales.

The resulting representations are evaluated through supervised classification with dimension reduction. Tests use scrambled-image databases and signals sampled on unknown irregular grids on a sphere. These settings directly exercise the problem of unavailable geometry. The abstract reports the evaluation settings without claiming a particular performance advantage. The contribution is a representation-building method that couples inferred graph neighborhoods with a deep cascade of simple operations for subsequent classification.
summary.tldr: Haar scattering builds invariant graph-signal descriptors through simple deep cascades while estimating unknown multiscale neighborhoods with polynomial-time pair matching.

title: Unsupervised Deep Haar Scattering on Graphs

abstract: We revisit from a statistical learning perspective the classical decision-theoretic problem of weighted expert voting. In particular, we examine the consistency (both asymptotic and finitary) of the optimal Nitzan-Paroush weighted majority and related rules. In the case of known expert competence levels, we give sharp error estimates for the optimal rule. When the competence levels are unknown, they must be empirically estimated. We provide frequentist and Bayesian analyses for this situation. Some of our proof techniques are non-standard and may be of independent interest. The bounds we derive are nearly optimal, and several challenging open problems are posed. Experimental results are provided to illustrate the theory.
originalAbstract: We revisit from a statistical learning perspective the classical decision-theoretic problem of weighted expert voting. In particular, we examine the consistency (both asymptotic and finitary) of the optimal Nitzan-Paroush weighted majority and related rules. In the case of known expert competence levels, we give sharp error estimates for the optimal rule. When the competence levels are unknown, they must be empirically estimated. We provide frequentist and Bayesian analyses for this situation. Some of our proof techniques are non-standard and may be of independent interest. The bounds we derive are nearly optimal, and several challenging open problems are posed. Experimental results are provided to illustrate the theory.

paragraphs: Weighted expert voting combines judgments while allowing different experts to carry different influence. This paper examines the statistical reliability of the optimal Nitzan-Paroush weighted-majority rule and related voting rules. It studies both asymptotic consistency and finite-setting guarantees, connecting the behavior of voting procedures with explicit estimates of their errors.

A key distinction is whether expert competence is already known. When competence levels are available, the authors give sharp error estimates for the optimal voting rule. When those levels are unknown, they must first be estimated from observations. The paper analyzes this additional estimation problem through both frequentist and Bayesian approaches.

That separation matters because choosing voting weights with known competence and learning those weights from data are different statistical tasks. The paper provides nearly optimal bounds and uses experiments to illustrate its theoretical findings. It also introduces proof techniques that the authors suggest may have wider interest. The contribution is a statistical account of when weighted voting is reliable, including the uncertainty introduced by estimating expert competence.
summary.tldr: The paper derives nearly optimal reliability bounds for weighted expert voting with either known or empirically estimated competence levels.

title: Consistency of weighted majority votes

abstract: Given a multi-armed bandit problem it may be desirable to achieve a smaller-than-usual worst-case regret for some special actions. I show that the price for such unbalanced worst-case regret guarantees is rather high. Specifically, if an algorithm enjoys a worst-case regret of B with respect to some action, then there must exist another action for which the worst-case regret is at least Ω(nK/B), where n is the horizon and K the number of actions. I also give upper bounds in both the stochastic and adversarial settings showing that this result cannot be improved. For the stochastic case the pareto regret frontier is characterised exactly up to constant factors.

I show that the price for such unbalanced worst-case regret guarantees is rather high. Specifically, if an algorithm enjoys a worst-case regret of B with respect to some action, then there must exist another action for which the worst-case regret is at least Ω(nK/B), where n is the horizon and K the number of actions. paragraphs: A bandit algorithm may be designed to give especially strong worst-case protection relative to a preferred action. This paper asks what that preference costs elsewhere. It studies regret guarantees separately for different comparison actions, exposing tradeoffs that are hidden when performance is summarized by a single balanced guarantee.

The central lower bound says that if worst-case regret relative to one action is B, some other action must have worst-case regret at least on the order of nK/B. Here n is the horizon and K is the number of actions. Thus, making the guarantee unusually small for one action forces a larger worst-case guarantee for another.

The author also provides upper bounds in stochastic and adversarial settings showing that the lower-bound result cannot be improved. In the stochastic setting, the achievable Pareto frontier is characterized up to constant factors. This identifies the attainable balance among action-specific guarantees and quantifies the price of favoring particular actions, rather than merely showing that some price exists.
summary.tldr: Giving one bandit action unusually low worst-case regret necessarily worsens another action’s guarantee, with tight tradeoffs established.

title: The Pareto Regret Frontier for Bandits

abstract: We consider moment matching techniques for estimation in Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). By drawing explicit links between LDA and discrete versions of independent component analysis (ICA), we first derive a new set of cumulant-based tensors, with an improved sample complexity. Moreover, we reuse standard ICA techniques such as joint diagonalization of tensors to improve over existing methods based on the tensor power method. In an extensive set of experiments on both synthetic and real datasets, we show that our new combination of tensors and orthogonal joint diagonalization techniques outperforms existing moment matching methods.

Moreover, we reuse standard ICA techniques such as joint diagonalization of tensors to improve over existing methods based on the tensor power method. In an extensive set of experiments on both synthetic and real datasets, we show that our new combination of tensors and orthogonal joint diagonalization techniques outperforms existing moment matching methods.

paragraphs: This paper revisits estimation in Latent Dirichlet Allocation through moment matching, an approach that learns model structure from statistical summaries of observations. The authors draw explicit connections between LDA and discrete forms of independent component analysis. Those connections supply both new statistical quantities to estimate and different computational tools for using them.

The first contribution is a new collection of tensors based on cumulants, with improved sample complexity. The second imports joint diagonalization techniques from independent component analysis to improve on approaches using the tensor power method. These address separate parts of estimation: which statistical summaries are constructed and how those summaries are processed to recover the model.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets evaluate the combination of the new tensors with orthogonal joint diagonalization. The authors report that this combination outperforms existing moment-matching methods. The significance is that a connection between two modeling traditions leads to practical changes in the estimation pipeline, supported by both a sample-complexity improvement and empirical comparisons of the resulting method.
summary.tldr: Connections between LDA and discrete independent component analysis yield improved statistical tensors and more effective moment-matching estimation.

title: Rethinking LDA: Moment Matching for Discrete ICA

abstract: We consider the problem of learning Bayesian networks optimally, when subject to background knowledge in the form of ancestral constraints. Our approach is based on a recently proposed framework for optimal structure learning based on non-decomposable scores, which is general enough to accommodate ancestral constraints. The proposed framework exploits oracles for learning structures using decomposable scores, which cannot accommodate ancestral constraints since they are non-decomposable. We show how to empower these oracles by passing them decomposable constraints that they can handle, which are inferred from ancestral constraints that they cannot handle. Empirically, we demonstrate that our approach can be orders-of-magnitude more efficient than alternative frameworks, such as those based on integer linear programming.

The proposed framework exploits oracles for learning structures using decomposable scores, which cannot accommodate ancestral constraints since they are non-decomposable. We show how to empower these oracles by passing them decomposable constraints that they can handle, which are inferred from ancestral constraints that they cannot handle. Empirically, we demonstrate that our approach can be orders-of-magnitude more efficient than alternative frameworks, such as those based on integer linear programming.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn an optimal Bayesian-network structure while respecting background knowledge about ancestry. An ancestral constraint concerns whether one variable lies upstream of another through the network. Such requirements involve relationships across the structure, making them difficult to handle with learning tools that operate through decomposable scores.

The proposed approach uses a framework for optimal structure learning with non-decomposable scores. Within it, the authors exploit existing structure-learning oracles that accept decomposable scores and constraints. The key step is to infer decomposable constraints from the ancestral requirements and pass those usable constraints to the oracles. This lets locally organized tools contribute to solving a problem with global structural restrictions.

The empirical results show that this approach can be orders of magnitude more efficient than alternatives such as integer-linear-programming frameworks. The improvement is an observed possibility, not a universal runtime guarantee. Its practical significance is that background knowledge about ancestry can be incorporated while retaining the objective of optimal structure learning.
summary.tldr: The method turns implications of ancestral constraints into constraints existing Bayesian-network learning tools can use efficiently.

title: Learning Bayesian networks with ancestral constraints

abstract: Recent work has extended the theoretical analysis of boosting algorithms to multiclass problems and to online settings. However, the multiclass extension is in the batch setting and the online extensions only consider binary classification. We fill this gap in the literature by defining, and justifying, a weak learning condition for online multiclass boosting. This condition leads to an optimal boosting algorithm that requires the minimal number of weak learners to achieve a certain accuracy. Additionally, we propose an adaptive algorithm which is near optimal and enjoys an excellent performance on real data due to its adaptive property.
originalAbstract: Recent work has extended the theoretical analysis of boosting algorithms to multiclass problems and to online settings. However, the multiclass extension is in the batch setting and the online extensions only consider binary classification. We fill this gap in the literature by defining, and justifying, a weak learning condition for online multiclass boosting. This condition leads to an optimal boosting algorithm that requires the minimal number of weak learners to achieve a certain accuracy. Additionally, we propose an adaptive algorithm which is near optimal and enjoys an excellent performance on real data due to its adaptive property.

paragraphs: Boosting combines weak learners into a stronger predictor. The theoretical work described in this paper had addressed multiclass classification in batch learning and online learning for binary classification, leaving their intersection unresolved. The authors develop a framework for boosting when learning is online and predictions can belong to more than two classes.

Their starting point is a weak-learning condition suited to this combined setting. Defining and justifying that condition establishes what the component learners must provide for the boosting analysis to work. It leads to an optimal algorithm in a specific sense: the algorithm needs the minimum number of weak learners to reach a given accuracy.

The paper also proposes an adaptive algorithm that is near optimal and performs strongly on real data. The abstract attributes its practical performance to adaptivity. Together, the algorithms connect a theoretical requirement on weak learners to both an optimal learner-count result and an adaptive alternative, giving the online multiclass setting its own boosting foundations.
summary.tldr: A weak-learning condition for online multiclass boosting supports an optimal learner-count algorithm and a near-optimal adaptive alternative.

title: Online multiclass boosting

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods such as the Deep Q-Network (DQN) have achieved state-of-the-art results in a variety of challenging, high-dimensional domains. This success is mainly attributed to the power of deep neural networks to learn rich domain representations for approximating the value function or policy. Batch reinforcement learning methods with linear representations, on the other hand, are more stable and require less hyper parameter tuning. Yet, substantial feature engineering is necessary to achieve good results. In this work we propose a hybrid approach -- the Least Squares Deep Q-Network (LS-DQN), which combines rich feature representations learned by a DRL algorithm with the stability of a linear least squares method. We do this by periodically re-training the last hidden layer of a DRL network with a batch least squares update. Key to our approach is a Bayesian regularization term for the least squares update, which prevents over-fitting to the more recent data. We tested LS-DQN on five Atari games and demonstrate significant improvement over vanilla DQN and Double-DQN. We also investigated the reasons for the superior performance of our method. Interestingly, we found that the performance improvement can be attributed to the large batch size used by the LS method when optimizing the last layer.

Key to our approach is a Bayesian regularization term for the least squares update, which prevents over-fitting to the more recent data. We tested LS-DQN on five Atari games and demonstrate significant improvement over vanilla DQN and Double-DQN. We also investigated the reasons for the superior performance of our method. Interestingly, we found that the performance improvement can be attributed to the large batch size used by the LS method when optimizing the last layer.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can learn useful representations from high-dimensional inputs, while batch methods with linear representations offer stability and require less hyperparameter tuning. This paper combines those strengths in Least Squares Deep Q-Network, or LS-DQN. The goal is to retain learned features while using a linear least-squares method for part of the update.

The method periodically retrains the network's last hidden layer using a batch least-squares update. A Bayesian regularization term prevents this update from overfitting to more recent data. This makes the shallow retraining step part of a hybrid learning procedure, with deep representation learning and batch estimation contributing different capabilities.

Experiments on five Atari games show significant improvements over vanilla DQN and Double-DQN. The authors also investigate why the method improves performance and attribute the gain to the large batch size used when optimizing the last layer. That finding is central to interpreting the result: the evidence highlights how much data informs the shallow update, alongside the proposed least-squares formulation.
summary.tldr: LS-DQN combines deep features with regularized least-squares updates, with reported gains attributed to large batches for last-layer optimization.

title: Shallow Updates for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Many image-to-image translation problems are ambiguous, as a single input image may correspond to multiple possible outputs. In this work, we aim to model a distribution of possible outputs in a conditional generative modeling setting. The ambiguity of the mapping is distilled in a low-dimensional latent vector, which can be randomly sampled at test time. A generator learns to map the given input, combined with this latent code, to the output. We explicitly encourage the connection between output and the latent code to be invertible. This helps prevent a many-to-one mapping from the latent code to the output during training, also known as the problem of mode collapse, and produces more diverse results. We explore several variants of this approach by employing different training objectives, network architectures, and methods of injecting the latent code. Our proposed method encourages bijective consistency between the latent encoding and output modes. We present a systematic comparison of our method and other variants on both perceptual realism and diversity.

The ambiguity of the mapping is distilled in a low-dimensional latent vector, which can be randomly sampled at test time. A generator learns to map the given input, combined with this latent code, to the output. We explicitly encourage the connection between output and the latent code to be invertible. This helps prevent a many-to-one mapping from the latent code to the output during training, also known as the problem of mode collapse, and produces more diverse results. Our proposed method encourages bijective consistency between the latent encoding and output modes. We present a systematic comparison of our method and other variants on both perceptual realism and diversity.

paragraphs: Image-to-image translation can be ambiguous: one input may have several valid outputs. This paper models that range of possibilities using a low-dimensional latent vector alongside the input image. At test time, sampling different latent codes lets the generator produce different outputs for the same input, expressing uncertainty in the mapping.

The key training idea is to encourage an invertible connection between the latent code and the generated output. If many codes produce the same result, the model loses the diversity those codes are supposed to represent. Encouraging consistency in both directions helps prevent this many-to-one behavior, a form of mode collapse, and leads to more diverse results.

The authors investigate variants that change training objectives, network architectures, and how the latent code enters the generator. They systematically compare perceptual realism and output diversity. Considering both properties matters because the task requires plausible alternatives as well as variation. The proposed method encourages a one-to-one relationship between latent encodings and output modes, rather than treating a noise input alone as sufficient to preserve diversity.
summary.tldr: Encouraging an invertible relationship between latent codes and outputs helps image translation generate diverse results for the same input.

title: Toward Multimodal Image-to-Image Translation

abstract: Ordinal regression seeks class label predictions when the penalty incurred for mistakes increases according to an ordering over the labels. The absolute error is a canonical example. Many existing methods for this task reduce to binary classification problems and employ surrogate losses, such as the hinge loss. We instead derive uniquely defined surrogate ordinal regression loss functions by seeking the predictor that is robust to the worst-case approximations of training data labels, subject to matching certain provided training data statistics. We demonstrate the advantages of our approach over other surrogate losses based on hinge loss approximations using UCI ordinal prediction tasks.
originalAbstract: Ordinal regression seeks class label predictions when the penalty incurred for mistakes increases according to an ordering over the labels. The absolute error is a canonical example. Many existing methods for this task reduce to binary classification problems and employ surrogate losses, such as the hinge loss. We instead derive uniquely defined surrogate ordinal regression loss functions by seeking the predictor that is robust to the worst-case approximations of training data labels, subject to matching certain provided training data statistics. We demonstrate the advantages of our approach over other surrogate losses based on hinge loss approximations using UCI ordinal prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Ordinal regression predicts labels that have a meaningful order, so mistakes can carry different penalties depending on how far a prediction lies from the correct label. Absolute error is one familiar way to express this distinction. The paper asks how to construct a training loss that respects this ordered prediction problem.

Many existing approaches divide the task into binary classification problems and use substitute objectives such as hinge losses. The authors instead derive losses from a robustness requirement. They seek a predictor that performs well against the worst allowed approximation of the training labels, while requiring those approximations to match specified statistics of the training data.

This construction produces uniquely defined surrogate losses for ordinal regression. Its significance is that the substitute training objective follows from an explicit adversarial formulation tied to the available statistics. Experiments on UCI ordinal prediction tasks demonstrate advantages over other surrogate losses built from hinge approximations. Those findings support the proposed formulation on the evaluated tasks, rather than establishing universal superiority for every ordered-label problem.
summary.tldr: The paper derives ordinal regression losses from robustness to worst-case label approximations that preserve specified training statistics.

title: Adversarial Surrogate Losses for Ordinal Regression

abstract: This paper considers online convex optimization (OCO) with stochastic constraints, which generalizes Zinkevich's OCO over a known simple fixed set by introducing multiple stochastic functional constraints that are i.i.d. generated at each round and are disclosed to the decision maker only after the decision is made. This formulation arises naturally when decisions are restricted by stochastic environments or deterministic environments with noisy observations. It also includes many important problems as special case, such as OCO with long term constraints, stochastic constrained convex optimization, and deterministic constrained convex optimization. To solve this problem, this paper proposes a new algorithm that achieves $O(\sqrt{T})$ expected regret and constraint violations and $O(\sqrt{T}\log(T))$ high probability regret and constraint violations. Experiments on a real-world data center scheduling problem further verify the performance of the new algorithm.
originalAbstract: This paper considers online convex optimization (OCO) with stochastic constraints, which generalizes Zinkevich's OCO over a known simple fixed set by introducing multiple stochastic functional constraints that are i.i.d. generated at each round and are disclosed to the decision maker only after the decision is made. This formulation arises naturally when decisions are restricted by stochastic environments or deterministic environments with noisy observations. It also includes many important problems as special case, such as OCO with long term constraints, stochastic constrained convex optimization, and deterministic constrained convex optimization. To solve this problem, this paper proposes a new algorithm that achieves $O(\sqrt{T})$ expected regret and constraint violations and $O(\sqrt{T}\log(T))$ high probability regret and constraint violations. Experiments on a real-world data center scheduling problem further verify the performance of the new algorithm.

paragraphs: Online decisions sometimes face restrictions that are uncertain when an action is chosen. This paper extends online convex optimization to multiple stochastic functional constraints that are independently and identically generated at each round. The decision maker learns the realized constraints only after acting, so the method must manage uncertainty about feasibility as well as prediction or optimization loss.

The proposed algorithm has expected regret and constraint violations bounded by O(sqrt(T)), where T is the number of rounds. It also provides high-probability bounds of O(sqrt(T) log(T)) for both quantities. These sublinear bounds describe how cumulative performance shortfalls and violations grow over time; they do not require every individual decision to satisfy every realized constraint.

The formulation includes long-term constrained online optimization and both stochastic and deterministic constrained convex optimization as special cases. Experiments on real-world data center scheduling further support the algorithm's performance. The contribution is a unified treatment of decision quality and constraint control when restrictions become observable only after decisions have been made.
summary.tldr: An online optimization algorithm controls regret and constraint violations when i.i.d. stochastic constraints are revealed only after each decision.

title: Online Convex Optimization with Stochastic Constraints

abstract: We consider a team of reinforcement learning agents that concurrently operate in a common environment, and we develop an approach to efficient coordinated exploration that is suitable for problems of practical scale. Our approach builds on the seed sampling concept introduced in Dimakopoulou and Van Roy (2018) and on a randomized value function learning algorithm from Osband et al. (2016). We demonstrate that, for simple tabular contexts, the approach is competitive with those previously proposed in Dimakopoulou and Van Roy (2018) and with a higher-dimensional problem and a neural network value function representation, the approach learns quickly with far fewer agents than alternative exploration schemes.
originalAbstract: We consider a team of reinforcement learning agents that concurrently operate in a common environment, and we develop an approach to efficient coordinated exploration that is suitable for problems of practical scale. Our approach builds on the seed sampling concept introduced in Dimakopoulou and Van Roy (2018) and on a randomized value function learning algorithm from Osband et al. (2016). We demonstrate that, for simple tabular contexts, the approach is competitive with those previously proposed in Dimakopoulou and Van Roy (2018) and with a higher-dimensional problem and a neural network value function representation, the approach learns quickly with far fewer agents than alternative exploration schemes.

paragraphs: This paper considers a team of reinforcement learning agents operating concurrently in a common environment. It develops an approach to coordinated exploration intended to work at practical scales. The objective is to make the team's exploration effective when several agents are learning at once, including settings that require a richer representation than a table.

The approach combines seed sampling with a randomized value-function learning algorithm. These are the two foundations of the proposed exploration method. The study evaluates the combination in both simple tabular settings and a higher-dimensional problem using a neural network to represent the value function, directly examining its use across different levels of representation complexity.

In the tabular experiments, the method is competitive with earlier approaches considered by the authors. In the higher-dimensional setting, it learns quickly using far fewer agents than alternative exploration schemes. That finding supports the practical aim of effective exploration without needing a large concurrent team in the tested problem. The abstract presents this scaling benefit as an experimental result.
summary.tldr: Combining seed sampling with randomized value learning enables effective coordinated exploration, using fewer agents in a tested higher-dimensional problem.

title: Scalable Coordinated Exploration in Concurrent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Coordinate descent methods minimize a cost function by updating a single decision variable (corresponding to one coordinate) at a time. Ideally, we would update the decision variable that yields the largest marginal decrease in the cost function. However, finding this coordinate would require checking all of them, which is not computationally practical. Therefore, we propose a new adaptive method for coordinate descent. First, we define a lower bound on the decrease of the cost function when a coordinate is updated and, instead of calculating this lower bound for all coordinates, we use a multi-armed bandit algorithm to learn which coordinates result in the largest marginal decrease and simultaneously perform coordinate descent. We show that our approach improves the convergence of the coordinate methods both theoretically and experimentally.
originalAbstract: Coordinate descent methods minimize a cost function by updating a single decision variable (corresponding to one coordinate) at a time. Ideally, we would update the decision variable that yields the largest marginal decrease in the cost function. However, finding this coordinate would require checking all of them, which is not computationally practical. Therefore, we propose a new adaptive method for coordinate descent. First, we define a lower bound on the decrease of the cost function when a coordinate is updated and, instead of calculating this lower bound for all coordinates, we use a multi-armed bandit algorithm to learn which coordinates result in the largest marginal decrease and simultaneously perform coordinate descent. We show that our approach improves the convergence of the coordinate methods both theoretically and experimentally.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent improves an objective by changing one variable at a time. Its efficiency therefore depends partly on which variable it chooses next. Ideally, each step would select the coordinate offering the largest improvement, but checking every candidate can make the selection process itself too expensive.

This paper introduces an adaptive selection method based on a multi-armed bandit algorithm. The authors first derive a lower bound on the objective decrease from updating a coordinate. Rather than evaluating that bound for every coordinate at every step, the algorithm learns which coordinates tend to offer larger decreases while simultaneously carrying out the optimization.

The approach makes coordinate selection a learning problem within the larger optimization process. Information gathered during updates guides later choices, addressing the cost of repeatedly searching all variables. The authors establish improvements in convergence through both theoretical analysis and experiments. The contribution is thus a way to make more informed coordinate choices without paying the full cost of exhaustive comparison at each step.
summary.tldr: Bandit-guided coordinate descent learns which variables offer larger improvements, improving convergence without exhaustively checking every coordinate.

title: Coordinate Descent with Bandit Sampling

abstract: Multi-layered distributed representation is believed to be the key ingredient of deep neural networks especially in cognitive tasks like computer vision. While non-differentiable models such as gradient boosting decision trees (GBDTs) are still the dominant methods for modeling discrete or tabular data, they are hard to incorporate with such representation learning ability. In this work, we propose the multi-layered GBDT forest (mGBDTs), with an explicit emphasis on exploring the ability to learn hierarchical distributed representations by stacking several layers of regression GBDTs as its building block. The model can be jointly trained by a variant of target propagation across layers, without the need to derive backpropagation nor differentiability. Experiments confirmed the effectiveness of the model in terms of performance and representation learning ability.
originalAbstract: Multi-layered distributed representation is believed to be the key ingredient of deep neural networks especially in cognitive tasks like computer vision. While non-differentiable models such as gradient boosting decision trees (GBDTs) are still the dominant methods for modeling discrete or tabular data, they are hard to incorporate with such representation learning ability. In this work, we propose the multi-layered GBDT forest (mGBDTs), with an explicit emphasis on exploring the ability to learn hierarchical distributed representations by stacking several layers of regression GBDTs as its building block. The model can be jointly trained by a variant of target propagation across layers, without the need to derive backpropagation nor differentiability. Experiments confirmed the effectiveness of the model in terms of performance and representation learning ability.

paragraphs: Deep neural networks learn representations through multiple layers, while gradient boosting decision trees are widely used for discrete and tabular data. This paper explores whether layered representation learning can also be built from boosted trees. The proposed model stacks several layers of regression GBDTs into a multi-layered forest.

The goal is to learn hierarchical distributed representations, with the stacked tree layers serving as the representation-building components. Training these layers jointly poses a challenge because the model does not rely on differentiable building blocks. The authors address this using a variant of target propagation across layers, avoiding the need to derive backpropagation for the tree architecture.

Experiments support the model’s effectiveness in both predictive performance and representation learning. The contribution broadens the architectural possibilities for boosted trees: they can participate in a jointly trained hierarchy rather than only serving as a single prediction stage. The findings provide empirical support for this construction, connecting the familiar strengths of tree models with an explicit attempt to learn representations across multiple layers.
summary.tldr: Stacked gradient boosting trees learn hierarchical representations through target propagation without requiring differentiable layers.

title: Multi-Layered Gradient Boosting Decision Trees

abstract: Deep neural networks often work well when they are over-parameterized and trained with a massive amount of noise and regularization, such as weight decay and dropout. Although dropout is widely used as a regularization technique for fully connected layers, it is often less effective for convolutional layers. This lack of success of dropout for convolutional layers is perhaps due to the fact that activation units in convolutional layers are spatially correlated so information can still flow through convolutional networks despite dropout. Thus a structured form of dropout is needed to regularize convolutional networks. In this paper, we introduce DropBlock, a form of structured dropout, where units in a contiguous region of a feature map are dropped together. We found that applying DropbBlock in skip connections in addition to the convolution layers increases the accuracy. Also, gradually increasing number of dropped units during training leads to better accuracy and more robust to hyperparameter choices. Extensive experiments show that DropBlock works better than dropout in regularizing convolutional networks. On ImageNet classification, ResNet-50 architecture with DropBlock achieves $78.13\%$ accuracy, which is more than $1.6\%$ improvement on the baseline. On COCO detection, DropBlock improves Average Precision of RetinaNet from $36.8\%$ to $38.4\%$.

We found that applying DropbBlock in skip connections in addition to the convolution layers increases the accuracy. Also, gradually increasing number of dropped units during training leads to better accuracy and more robust to hyperparameter choices. paragraphs: DropBlock is a regularization method designed for convolutional neural networks. Ordinary dropout removes individual activations during training, but nearby convolutional activations are spatially correlated. The authors suggest that this correlation may let information continue flowing despite individual removals, helping explain why dropout is often less effective in convolutional layers than in fully connected layers.

DropBlock instead removes activations together within a contiguous region of a feature map. This makes the disruption spatially structured. The authors find that applying it to skip connections as well as convolutional layers increases accuracy. They also find that gradually increasing the number of removed units during training improves accuracy and makes results less sensitive to hyperparameter choices.

Experiments show better convolutional-network regularization than dropout in the tested settings. On ImageNet, ResNet-50 with DropBlock reaches 78.13% accuracy, improving the baseline by more than 1.6 percentage points. On COCO object detection, RetinaNet’s Average Precision rises from 36.8% to 38.4%. These results demonstrate benefits for both image classification and detection.
summary.tldr: DropBlock removes contiguous activation regions during training and improves convolutional-network performance on image classification and object detection.

title: DropBlock: A regularization method for convolutional networks

abstract: Teaching is critical to human society: it is with teaching that prospective students are educated and human civilization can be inherited and advanced. A good teacher not only provides his/her students with qualified teaching materials (e.g., textbooks), but also sets up appropriate learning objectives (e.g., course projects and exams) considering different situations of a student. When it comes to artificial intelligence, treating machine learning models as students, the loss functions that are optimized act as perfect counterparts of the learning objective set by the teacher. In this work, we explore the possibility of imitating human teaching behaviors by dynamically and automatically outputting appropriate loss functions to train machine learning models. Different from typical learning settings in which the loss function of a machine learning model is predefined and fixed, in our framework, the loss function of a machine learning model (we call it student) is defined by another machine learning model (we call it teacher). The ultimate goal of teacher model is cultivating the student to have better performance measured on development dataset. Towards that end, similar to human teaching, the teacher, a parametric model, dynamically outputs different loss functions that will be used and optimized by its student model at different training stages. We develop an efficient learning method for the teacher model that makes gradient based optimization possible, exempt of the ineffective solutions such as policy optimization. We name our method as ``learning to teach with dynamic loss functions'' (L2T-DLF for short). Extensive experiments on real world tasks including image classification and neural machine translation demonstrate that our method significantly improves the quality of various student models.

Here, a second model acts as a teacher by producing loss functions for a student model at different training stages. The teacher’s goal is to improve the student’s performance on a development dataset.

This setup makes the learning objective itself an output of a trainable system. The teacher is a parametric model whose choices shape what the student optimizes over time. The authors develop an efficient way to train the teacher with gradient-based optimization, avoiding the policy-optimization approach described as ineffective for this purpose.

The resulting method, L2T-DLF, is evaluated on real-world tasks including image classification and neural machine translation. Extensive experiments show significant improvements in the quality of various student models. These findings support dynamically learned loss functions as a useful way to guide training, with success measured by the student’s development performance rather than simply by its progress on a fixed training objective.
summary.tldr: A trainable teacher dynamically supplies student loss functions, improving tested image-classification and translation models through gradient-based teacher learning.

title: Learning to Teach with Dynamic Loss Functions

abstract: This paper studies the problem of sparse regression where the goal is to learn a sparse vector that best optimizes a given objective function. Under the assumption that the objective function satisfies restricted strong convexity (RSC), we analyze orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP), a greedy algorithm that is used heavily in applications, and obtain support recovery result as well as a tight generalization error bound for OMP. Furthermore, we obtain lower bounds for OMP, showing that both our results on support recovery and generalization error are tight up to logarithmic factors. To the best of our knowledge, these support recovery and generalization bounds are the first such matching upper and lower bounds (up to logarithmic factors) for {\em any} sparse regression algorithm under the RSC assumption.

paragraphs: Sparse regression seeks a model with relatively few nonzero coefficients. This paper analyzes orthogonal matching pursuit, a widely used greedy algorithm, with attention to both identifying the relevant variables and predicting beyond the observed data. Recovering the support means identifying which entries of the sparse vector are nonzero.

The analysis assumes that the objective satisfies restricted strong convexity. Under that condition, the authors obtain a support recovery result and a generalization error bound. These address related but distinct questions: whether the algorithm can locate the sparse model's active components, and how well its learned predictor can generalize.

The authors also derive lower bounds for orthogonal matching pursuit that match their upper bounds up to logarithmic factors. This indicates that the guarantees are close to the algorithm's limits in the analyzed setting, rather than merely being loose sufficient estimates. They describe these as the first such matching support recovery and generalization bounds for a sparse regression algorithm under restricted strong convexity, to the best of their knowledge.
summary.tldr: Under restricted strong convexity, orthogonal matching pursuit has support recovery and generalization bounds that match lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.

title: Support Recovery for Orthogonal Matching Pursuit: Upper and Lower bounds

abstract: Summarizing high-dimensional data using a small number of parameters is a ubiquitous first step in the analysis of neuronal population activity. Recently developed methods use "targeted" approaches that work by identifying multiple, distinct low-dimensional subspaces of activity that capture the population response to individual experimental task variables, such as the value of a presented stimulus or the behavior of the animal. These methods have gained attention because they decompose total neural activity into what are ostensibly different parts of a neuronal computation. However, existing targeted methods have been developed outside of the confines of probabilistic modeling, making some aspects of the procedures ad hoc, or limited in flexibility or interpretability. Here we propose a new model-based method for targeted dimensionality reduction based on a probabilistic generative model of the population response data. The low-dimensional structure of our model is expressed as a low-rank factorization of a linear regression model. We perform efficient inference using a combination of expectation maximization and direct maximization of the marginal likelihood. We also develop an efficient method for estimating the dimensionality of each subspace. We show that our approach outperforms alternative methods in both mean squared error of the parameter estimates, and in identifying the correct dimensionality of encoding using simulated data. We also show that our method provides more accurate inference of low-dimensional subspaces of activity than a competing algorithm, demixed PCA.
