paragraphs: Neuronal population recordings contain many dimensions of activity. Targeted dimensionality reduction summarizes them using separate low-dimensional subspaces associated with experimental variables, such as a stimulus or an animal’s behavior. This paper gives that decomposition a probabilistic foundation, addressing ad hoc choices and limits in the flexibility or interpretation of earlier methods.

The proposed generative model represents low-dimensional structure through a low-rank factorization of linear regression. Inference combines Expectation Maximization with direct maximization of the marginal likelihood. The authors also develop an efficient procedure for estimating the dimension of each subspace, so the method addresses both the structure of a response and how many dimensions describe it.

On simulated data, the approach outperforms alternatives in parameter-estimation mean squared error and in recovering the correct encoding dimensionality. The paper also reports more accurate inference of activity subspaces than demixed PCA. These findings support using an explicit probabilistic model to separate task-related patterns of neural activity and estimate their complexity, rather than choosing the low-dimensional summary solely through a less structured procedure.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic low-rank regression model more accurately estimates task-related neural subspaces and their dimensions in the reported comparisons.

title: Model-based targeted dimensionality reduction for neuronal population data

abstract: We combine Recurrent Neural Networks with Tensor Product Representations to learn combinatorial representations of sequential data. This improves symbolic interpretation and systematic generalisation. Our architecture is trained end-to-end through gradient descent on a variety of simple natural language reasoning tasks, significantly outperforming the latest state-of-the-art models in single-task and all-tasks settings. We also augment a subset of the data such that training and test data exhibit large systematic differences and show that our approach generalises better than the previous state-of-the-art.

This improves symbolic interpretation and systematic generalisation. Our architecture is trained end-to-end through gradient descent on a variety of simple natural language reasoning tasks, significantly outperforming the latest state-of-the-art models in single-task and all-tasks settings. We also augment a subset of the data such that training and test data exhibit large systematic differences and show that our approach generalises better than the previous state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Learning from sequences requires a representation of how their parts fit together. This paper combines recurrent neural networks with tensor product representations to learn such combinatorial structure. The aim is to make the resulting representations easier to interpret symbolically and better able to generalize systematically when the arrangement of familiar information changes.

The architecture is trained end to end with gradient descent on several simple natural-language reasoning tasks. The authors evaluate it both when learning an individual task and when learning all tasks together. In both settings, they report substantial improvements over the latest state-of-the-art models used for comparison.

The paper also modifies a subset of the data so that training and test examples differ in large, systematic ways. The proposed approach generalizes better than the previous state of the art under this evaluation. That result supports the purpose of the representation design: learned combinations can help reasoning extend across structured differences between training and testing. The evidence concerns the simple reasoning tasks and altered data studied in the paper.
summary.tldr: Combining recurrent networks with tensor product representations improves simple language reasoning and generalization across systematic data differences.

title: Learning to Reason with Third Order Tensor Products

abstract: We present group equivariant capsule networks, a framework to introduce guaranteed equivariance and invariance properties to the capsule network idea. Our work can be divided into two contributions. First, we present a generic routing by agreement algorithm defined on elements of a group and prove that equivariance of output pose vectors, as well as invariance of output activations, hold under certain conditions. Second, we connect the resulting equivariant capsule networks with work from the field of group convolutional networks. Through this connection, we provide intuitions of how both methods relate and are able to combine the strengths of both approaches in one deep neural network architecture. The resulting framework allows sparse evaluation of the group convolution operator, provides control over specific equivariance and invariance properties, and can use routing by agreement instead of pooling operations. In addition, it is able to provide interpretable and equivariant representation vectors as output capsules, which disentangle evidence of object existence from its pose.

paragraphs: Capsule representations can distinguish evidence that an object exists from information about its pose. This paper develops a framework that gives such representations controlled responses to transformations. Equivariance means pose vectors change consistently with a transformation, while invariance means the corresponding activation values remain unchanged.

The first contribution is a general routing-by-agreement algorithm defined over group elements. Under specified conditions, the authors prove equivariance of output poses and invariance of output activations. The conditions matter: the guarantees apply to the construction when those requirements hold. Routing provides a way to combine capsule information while preserving these transformation properties.

The second contribution connects this construction with group convolutional networks and combines the two approaches within one architecture. The framework supports sparse evaluation of group convolutions and can use routing instead of pooling. Its output capsules provide interpretable representation vectors that separate object-presence evidence from pose, while giving control over the particular invariance and equivariance properties built into the network.
summary.tldr: Group-based capsule routing provides conditional transformation guarantees and connects capsule representations with group convolutional networks.

title: Group Equivariant Capsule Networks

abstract: In the last year, new models and methods for pretraining and transfer learning have driven striking performance improvements across a range of language understanding tasks. The GLUE benchmark, introduced a little over one year ago, offers a single-number metric that summarizes progress on a diverse set of such tasks, but performance on the benchmark has recently surpassed the level of non-expert humans, suggesting limited headroom for further research. In this paper we present SuperGLUE, a new benchmark styled after GLUE with a new set of more difficult language understanding tasks, a software toolkit, and a public leaderboard. SuperGLUE is available at https://super.gluebenchmark.com.

SuperGLUE is available at https://super.gluebenchmark.com.

paragraphs: SuperGLUE responds to rapid improvements in language understanding driven by pretraining and transfer learning. Its predecessor, GLUE, summarized performance across diverse tasks in a single score. The authors report that model performance had surpassed non-expert human performance on that benchmark, suggesting that it offered limited remaining room to distinguish further progress.

The paper introduces a new benchmark modeled after GLUE but built around more difficult language-understanding tasks. Its purpose is to provide a more demanding shared evaluation for general-purpose systems. The motivating human comparison concerns performance on GLUE; it serves as evidence about that benchmark's remaining headroom, rather than establishing that language understanding as a whole has been solved.

The contribution includes the task collection, a software toolkit, and a public leaderboard. Together, these provide an evaluation target and supporting infrastructure for comparing systems. The paper's central response to strong existing benchmark performance is to raise the difficulty of the shared test, giving subsequent research a more challenging setting in which to measure improvements across tasks.
summary.tldr: SuperGLUE introduces harder language-understanding tasks, a toolkit, and a leaderboard as GLUE offers diminishing headroom.

title: SuperGLUE: A Stickier Benchmark for General-Purpose Language Understanding Systems

abstract: Iterative learning to infer approaches have become popular solvers for inverse problems. However, their memory requirements during training grow linearly with model depth, limiting in practice model expressiveness. In this work, we propose an iterative inverse model with constant memory that relies on invertible networks to avoid storing intermediate activations. As a result, the proposed approach allows us to train models with 400 layers on 3D volumes in an MRI image reconstruction task. In experiments on a public data set, we demonstrate that these deeper, and thus more expressive, networks perform state-of-the-art image reconstruction.

As a result, the proposed approach allows us to train models with 400 layers on 3D volumes in an MRI image reconstruction task. In experiments on a public data set, we demonstrate that these deeper, and thus more expressive, networks perform state-of-the-art image reconstruction.

paragraphs: Learned iterative solvers can reconstruct images from indirect measurements, but training memory usually grows with network depth. That limits how many iterative layers can be used, especially for three-dimensional data. This paper targets the memory constraint in learning-based inverse-problem solvers.

The proposed iterative inverse model uses invertible networks so that intermediate activations do not all have to be stored during training. The authors describe a constant-memory approach with respect to depth, allowing substantially deeper reconstruction models within the available memory.

In an MRI reconstruction application, they train 400-layer models on three-dimensional volumes. Experiments on a public dataset achieve state-of-the-art reconstruction performance. The abstract attributes the opportunity to greater model depth and expressiveness, but does not provide numerical image-quality results or a runtime comparison. The demonstrated benefit is specific to the evaluated reconstruction setting and memory-saving architecture.
summary.tldr: Invertible networks enable deep iterative MRI reconstruction without storing every layer’s activations.

title: Invert to Learn to Invert

abstract: Designing effective architectures is one of the key factors behind the success of deep neural networks. Existing deep architectures are either manually designed or automatically searched by some Neural Architecture Search (NAS) methods. However, even a well-searched architecture may still contain many non-significant or redundant modules or operations (e.g., convolution or pooling), which may not only incur substantial memory consumption and computation cost but also deteriorate the performance. Thus, it is necessary to optimize the operations inside an architecture to improve the performance without introducing extra computation cost. Unfortunately, such a constrained optimization problem is NP-hard. To make the problem feasible, we cast the optimization problem into a Markov decision process (MDP) and seek to learn a Neural Architecture Transformer (NAT) to replace the redundant operations with the more computationally efficient ones (e.g., skip connection or directly removing the connection). Based on MDP, we learn NAT by exploiting reinforcement learning to obtain the optimization policies w.r.t. different architectures. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed strategies, we apply NAT on both hand-crafted architectures and NAS based architectures. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets, i.e., CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, demonstrate that the transformed architecture by NAT significantly outperforms both its original form and those architectures optimized by existing methods.

paragraphs: Even carefully designed or automatically searched neural networks can contain redundant operations. These operations consume memory and computation and may also hurt predictive performance. This paper studies how to improve an existing architecture’s operations while respecting a constraint against additional computation, a problem the authors describe as NP-hard.

To make the task manageable, they formulate architecture modification as a Markov decision process. A Neural Architecture Transformer, or NAT, learns modification policies through reinforcement learning. Its changes replace redundant operations with more computationally efficient alternatives, such as skip connections, or remove connections. The learned policy therefore acts on an existing architecture to improve its design.

The authors apply NAT to both manually constructed networks and architectures produced by neural architecture search. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet show that the transformed architectures significantly outperform their original versions and architectures optimized by existing methods. These findings indicate that architecture search or manual design can leave useful opportunities for subsequent optimization, and that a learned transformation policy can exploit those opportunities in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: NAT uses reinforcement learning to replace redundant network operations with efficient alternatives and improve existing architectures.

title: NAT: Neural Architecture Transformer for Accurate and Compact Architectures

abstract: What makes a paper independently reproducible? Debates on reproducibility center around intuition or assumptions but lack empirical results. Our field focuses on releasing code, which is important, but is not sufficient for determining reproducibility. We take the first step toward a quantifiable answer by manually attempting to implement 255 papers published from 1984 until 2017, recording features of each paper, and performing statistical analysis of the results. For each paper, we did not look at the authors code, if released, in order to prevent bias toward discrepancies between code and paper.
originalAbstract: What makes a paper independently reproducible? Debates on reproducibility center around intuition or assumptions but lack empirical results. Our field focuses on releasing code, which is important, but is not sufficient for determining reproducibility. We take the first step toward a quantifiable answer by manually attempting to implement 255 papers published from 1984 until 2017, recording features of each paper, and performing statistical analysis of the results. For each paper, we did not look at the authors code, if released, in order to prevent bias toward discrepancies between code and paper.

paragraphs: The paper investigates what makes machine learning research independently reproducible. Its starting point is that discussions often rely on intuition about good research practices rather than measurements of actual reproduction attempts. Releasing code matters, but the authors argue that code availability alone does not determine whether a paper can be independently reproduced.

To gather empirical evidence, they manually attempted to implement 255 papers published between 1984 and 2017. They recorded features of each paper and statistically analyzed the outcomes. This design connects characteristics of research reports with the practical experience of trying to implement their methods.

A defining choice was to avoid consulting the original authors' code, even when it was available. That kept implementation attempts from being guided by discrepancies between the paper and its accompanying software. The contribution described here is an empirical basis for studying independent reproducibility: it makes implementation attempts and paper characteristics the objects of measurement, rather than treating released code as a complete answer.
summary.tldr: Independent implementation attempts on 255 papers provide an empirical basis for studying what makes machine learning research reproducible.

title: A Step Toward Quantifying Independently Reproducible Machine Learning Research

abstract: Graph structured data are abundant in the real world. Among different graph types, directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) are of particular interest to machine learning researchers, as many machine learning models are realized as computations on DAGs, including neural networks and Bayesian networks. In this paper, we study deep generative models for DAGs, and propose a novel DAG variational autoencoder (D-VAE). To encode DAGs into the latent space, we leverage graph neural networks. We propose an asynchronous message passing scheme that allows encoding the computations on DAGs, rather than using existing simultaneous message passing schemes to encode local graph structures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed DVAE through two tasks: neural architecture search and Bayesian network structure learning. Experiments show that our model not only generates novel and valid DAGs, but also produces a smooth latent space that facilitates searching for DAGs with better performance through Bayesian optimization.

paragraphs: Directed acyclic graphs represent computations in models such as neural networks and Bayesian networks. This paper develops D-VAE, a variational autoencoder for generating such graphs. Its purpose is to represent DAGs in a latent space that supports both producing valid new structures and searching for structures with better performance.

The encoder uses a graph neural network with asynchronous message passing. This scheme is designed to encode the computations performed on a DAG, whereas the simultaneous message-passing approaches discussed in the abstract encode local graph structure. The distinction matters because a graph used as a computational model carries information about how computation flows through it.

The authors evaluate D-VAE on neural architecture search and Bayesian network structure learning. Their experiments show that it generates novel, valid DAGs and learns a smooth latent space that facilitates Bayesian optimization. The reported benefit is a representation in which searching for better graphs can be carried out through latent-space optimization, alongside a generative model that can produce the graph structures.
summary.tldr: D-VAE encodes computations on directed acyclic graphs into a smooth latent space that supports generating and optimizing graph structures.

title: D-VAE: A Variational Autoencoder for Directed Acyclic Graphs

abstract: We consider the problem of aggregating models learned from sequestered, possibly heterogeneous datasets. Exploiting tools from Bayesian nonparametrics, we develop a general meta-modeling framework that learns shared global latent structures by identifying correspondences among local model parameterizations. Our proposed framework is model-independent and is applicable to a wide range of model types. After verifying our approach on simulated data, we demonstrate its utility in aggregating Gaussian topic models, hierarchical Dirichlet process based hidden Markov models, and sparse Gaussian processes with applications spanning text summarization, motion capture analysis, and temperature forecasting.

Exploiting tools from Bayesian nonparametrics, we develop a general meta-modeling framework that learns shared global latent structures by identifying correspondences among local model parameterizations. Our proposed framework is model-independent and is applicable to a wide range of model types. After verifying our approach on simulated data, we demonstrate its utility in aggregating Gaussian topic models, hierarchical Dirichlet process based hidden Markov models, and sparse Gaussian processes with applications spanning text summarization, motion capture analysis, and temperature forecasting.

paragraphs: Models trained on separate datasets may contain related underlying structures even when the datasets differ. This paper studies how to aggregate such models when their training data remain sequestered. The task is to identify what their learned parameterizations have in common and use those correspondences to construct shared global structure.

The proposed framework uses Bayesian nonparametric tools to perform this matching. It operates as a meta-model over local model parameterizations, learning correspondences between them rather than starting from a pooled dataset. The authors describe the approach as model-independent and applicable to a wide range of model types, making parameter matching the common organizing principle.

After verification on simulated data, the paper demonstrates aggregation of Gaussian topic models, hierarchical Dirichlet process hidden Markov models, and sparse Gaussian processes. The associated applications include text summarization, motion-capture analysis, and temperature forecasting. This variety illustrates the framework's intended breadth: shared latent structure can be sought across independently learned models in several distinct statistical settings.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric framework aggregates separately trained models by matching their parameters to learn shared latent structure.

title: Statistical Model Aggregation via Parameter Matching

abstract: Accurate estimation of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty is crucial to build safe and reliable systems. Traditional approaches, such as dropout and ensemble methods, estimate uncertainty by sampling probability predictions from different submodels, which leads to slow uncertainty estimation at inference time. Recent works address this drawback by directly predicting parameters of prior distributions over the probability predictions with a neural network. While this approach has demonstrated accurate uncertainty estimation, it requires defining arbitrary target parameters for in-distribution data and makes the unrealistic assumption that out-of-distribution (OOD) data is known at training time. In this work we propose the Posterior Network (PostNet), which uses Normalizing Flows to predict an individual closed-form posterior distribution over predicted probabilites for any input sample. The posterior distributions learned by PostNet accurately reflect uncertainty for in- and out-of-distribution data -- without requiring access to OOD data at training time. PostNet achieves state-of-the art results in OOD detection and in uncertainty calibration under dataset shifts.

Recent works address this drawback by directly predicting parameters of prior distributions over the probability predictions with a neural network. While this approach has demonstrated accurate uncertainty estimation, it requires defining arbitrary target parameters for in-distribution data and makes the unrealistic assumption that out-of-distribution (OOD) data is known at training time. paragraphs: Reliable prediction requires representing uncertainty, including uncertainty associated with the data and with what the model has learned. Sampling predictions from dropout variants or ensembles can make inference slow. Another approach predicts distributions over class probabilities directly, but prior methods described here require arbitrary target parameters and access to out-of-distribution examples during training.

Posterior Network, or PostNet, uses normalizing flows to produce a closed-form posterior distribution over predicted probabilities for each input. This represents uncertainty about the probability prediction itself. Crucially, the method learns without requiring out-of-distribution training samples, addressing a dependency that is difficult to satisfy when future unfamiliar inputs are unknown.

The paper reports that the learned posterior distributions accurately reflect uncertainty for both familiar and out-of-distribution inputs. It also reports state-of-the-art results in detecting out-of-distribution examples and calibrating uncertainty under dataset shifts. The central contribution is an input-specific posterior construction that supports uncertainty estimation without supplying examples of the unfamiliar data it will later need to recognize.
summary.tldr: PostNet uses normalizing flows to estimate predictive uncertainty without out-of-distribution training data, achieving strong detection and calibration results.

title: Posterior Network: Uncertainty Estimation without OOD Samples via Density-Based Pseudo-Counts

abstract: Recently, we have witnessed great progress in the field of medical imaging classification by adopting deep neural networks. However, the recent advanced models still require accessing sufficiently large and representative datasets for training, which is often unfeasible in clinically realistic environments. When trained on limited datasets, the deep neural network is lack of generalization capability, as the trained deep neural network on data within a certain distribution (e.g. the data captured by a certain device vendor or patient population) may not be able to generalize to the data with another distribution. In this paper, we introduce a simple but effective approach to improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in the field of medical imaging classification. Motivated by the observation that the domain variability of the medical images is to some extent compact, we propose to learn a representative feature space through variational encoding with a novel linear-dependency regularization term to capture the shareable information among medical data collected from different domains. As a result, the trained neural network is expected to equip with better generalization capability to the ``unseen" medical data. Experimental results on two challenging medical imaging classification tasks indicate that our method can achieve better cross-domain generalization capability compared with state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Medical image classifiers may learn from a limited collection of devices or patient populations and then encounter different data in use. A network trained on one distribution may generalize poorly to another, especially when large, representative training collections are unavailable. This paper aims to improve that cross-domain generalization by changing the features the network learns.

The approach is motivated by the observation that variation among medical imaging domains is compact to some extent. It combines variational encoding with a linear-dependency regularization term to learn a representative feature space. The regularizer encourages the representation to capture information that can be shared across domains, with the expectation that this information will also help on previously unseen medical data.

Experiments on two challenging medical image classification tasks indicate better cross-domain generalization than leading baselines. The findings support the proposed representation-learning approach in those tasks. The central idea is to use relationships among training domains to shape the feature space, improving the chance that learned information remains useful when the data distribution changes.
summary.tldr: Variational encoding with linear-dependency regularization improves reported cross-domain medical image classification by encouraging features shared across training domains.

title: Domain Generalization for Medical Imaging Classification with Linear-Dependency Regularization

abstract: In this work we consider partially observable environments with sparse rewards. We present a self-supervised representation learning method for image-based observations, which arranges embeddings respecting temporal distance of observations. This representation is empirically robust to stochasticity and suitable for novelty detection from the error of a predictive forward model. We consider episodic and life-long uncertainties to guide the exploration. We propose to estimate the missing information about the environment with the world model, which operates in the learned latent space. As a motivation of the method, we analyse the exploration problem in a tabular Partially Observable Labyrinth. We demonstrate the method on image-based hard exploration environments from the Atari benchmark and report significant improvement with respect to prior work. The source code of the method and all the experiments is available at https://github.com/htdt/lwm.
originalAbstract: In this work we consider partially observable environments with sparse rewards. We present a self-supervised representation learning method for image-based observations, which arranges embeddings respecting temporal distance of observations. This representation is empirically robust to stochasticity and suitable for novelty detection from the error of a predictive forward model. We consider episodic and life-long uncertainties to guide the exploration. We propose to estimate the missing information about the environment with the world model, which operates in the learned latent space. As a motivation of the method, we analyse the exploration problem in a tabular Partially Observable Labyrinth. We demonstrate the method on image-based hard exploration environments from the Atari benchmark and report significant improvement with respect to prior work. The source code of the method and all the experiments is available at https://github.com/htdt/lwm.

paragraphs: Exploration is difficult when rewards are sparse and an agent sees only part of its environment. This paper addresses that setting using image observations and a learned world model. The central goal is to estimate what information about the environment is still missing and use that estimate to guide further exploration.

The method first learns representations without external labels, arranging image embeddings according to the temporal distance between observations. The authors find this representation empirically robust to stochasticity and suitable for detecting novelty through a forward model’s prediction errors. The world model operates in this latent representation, while exploration considers uncertainty within an episode and across the agent’s longer experience.

A tabular partially observable labyrinth provides an analysis motivating the approach. The authors then demonstrate it on Atari environments with difficult image-based exploration and report significant improvement over prior work. The findings connect representation learning to exploration: the learned space supports prediction-error signals that can help an agent seek information when external rewards provide little direction.
summary.tldr: A world model in a temporally organized latent space guides exploration through uncertainty and novelty, improving results on hard Atari exploration tasks.

title: Latent World Models For Intrinsically Motivated Exploration

abstract: BERT adopts masked language modeling (MLM) for pre-training and is one of the most successful pre-training models. Since BERT neglects dependency among predicted tokens, XLNet introduces permuted language modeling (PLM) for pre-training to address this problem. However, XLNet does not leverage the full position information of a sentence and thus suffers from position discrepancy between pre-training and fine-tuning. In this paper, we propose MPNet, a novel pre-training method that inherits the advantages of BERT and XLNet and avoids their limitations. MPNet leverages the dependency among predicted tokens through permuted language modeling (vs. MLM in BERT), and takes auxiliary position information as input to make the model see a full sentence and thus reducing the position discrepancy (vs. PLM in XLNet). We pre-train MPNet on a large-scale dataset (over 160GB text corpora) and fine-tune on a variety of down-streaming tasks (GLUE, SQuAD, etc). Experimental results show that MPNet outperforms MLM and PLM by a large margin, and achieves better results on these tasks compared with previous state-of-the-art pre-trained methods (e.g., BERT, XLNet, RoBERTa) under the same model setting. We attach the code in the supplemental materials.

The paper combines ideas from both approaches.

MPNet uses permuted language modeling to account for relationships among predicted tokens. It also supplies auxiliary positional information so that the model has access to the full sentence’s position structure. These two components address different aspects of the training objective: how target predictions depend on one another, and what positional context is available while making them.

The authors pretrain on more than 160 GB of text and fine-tune on tasks including GLUE and SQuAD. Their experiments report large gains over masked and permuted language modeling, as well as better results than BERT, XLNet, and RoBERTa under the same model setting. The findings support the combined objective within those controlled model comparisons.
summary.tldr: MPNet combines dependencies among predicted tokens with full positional information to improve language understanding in the reported comparisons.

title: MPNet: Masked and Permuted Pre-training for Language Understanding

abstract: Machine learning has proved its ability to produce accurate models -- but the deployment of these models outside the machine learning community has been hindered by the difficulties of interpreting these models. This paper proposes an algorithm that produces a continuous global interpretation of any given continuous black-box function. Our algorithm employs a variation of projection pursuit in which the ridge functions are chosen to be Meijer G-functions, rather than the usual polynomial splines. Because Meijer G-functions are differentiable in their parameters, we can "tune" the parameters of the representation by gradient descent; as a consequence, our algorithm is efficient. Using five familiar data sets from the UCI repository and two familiar machine learning algorithms, we demonstrate that our algorithm produces global interpretations that are both faithful (highly accurate) and parsimonious (involve a small number of terms). Our interpretations permit easy understanding of the relative importance of features and feature interactions. Our interpretation algorithm represents a leap forward from the previous state of the art.

paragraphs: An accurate model can still be difficult to use when people cannot understand how its predictions depend on its inputs. This paper proposes an algorithm that produces a continuous, global interpretation of a given continuous black-box function. The aim is an interpretable representation of the function’s behavior as a whole, including the relative importance of features and their interactions.

The algorithm adapts projection pursuit, using Meijer G-functions as its ridge functions in place of the polynomial splines usually used. These functions are differentiable with respect to their parameters. That allows gradient descent to tune the representation, providing the basis for the authors’ claim that the procedure is efficient.

Experiments use five UCI datasets and two machine learning algorithms. The resulting interpretations are reported to be both faithful to the black boxes and parsimonious, using few terms. These findings support the possibility of capturing complicated predictive behavior in a compact continuous representation. The combination matters because an explanation needs both accuracy and manageable complexity to make feature contributions and interactions understandable.
summary.tldr: A projection-pursuit method using trainable Meijer G-functions produces compact, accurate global interpretations of continuous black-box models in the reported experiments.

title: Learning outside the Black-Box: The pursuit of interpretable models

abstract: While previous distribution shift detection approaches can identify if a shift has occurred, these approaches cannot localize which specific features have caused a distribution shift---a critical step in diagnosing or fixing any underlying issue. For example, in military sensor networks, users will want to detect when one or more of the sensors has been compromised, and critically, they will want to know which specific sensors might be compromised. Thus, we first define a formalization of this problem as multiple conditional distribution hypothesis tests and propose both non-parametric and parametric statistical tests. For both efficiency and flexibility, we then propose to use a test statistic based on the density model score function (i.e. gradient with respect to the input)---which can easily compute test statistics for all dimensions in a single forward and backward pass. Any density model could be used for computing the necessary statistics including deep density models such as normalizing flows or autoregressive models. We additionally develop methods for identifying when and where a shift occurs in multivariate time-series data and show results for multiple scenarios using realistic attack models on both simulated and real-world data.

paragraphs: Detecting that a dataset has changed does not necessarily reveal which features are responsible. That distinction matters when a response requires locating a specific problem, such as identifying potentially compromised sensors. This paper turns feature-level localization into a statistical problem, rather than stopping at a single alarm for the entire dataset.

The authors formulate localization through multiple hypothesis tests on conditional distributions. These tests examine features in relation to the other observed variables. They propose both parametric and non-parametric approaches, then introduce an efficient statistic based on a density model’s score function: its gradient with respect to the input. Statistics for every dimension can be computed in one forward and backward pass.

The framework permits different density models, including normalizing flows and autoregressive models, making the choice of statistical representation flexible. The authors also develop methods for identifying both when and where changes occur in multivariate time series. Results cover realistic attack scenarios using simulated and real-world data. The contribution is a route from detecting an overall distribution change to localizing the features and times associated with it.
summary.tldr: Conditional distribution tests localize shifted features, with density-model gradients enabling efficient statistics across all dimensions.

title: Feature Shift Detection: Localizing Which Features Have Shifted via Conditional Distribution Tests

abstract: Recently, there is a growing interest in the study of median-based algorithms for distributed non-convex optimization. Two prominent examples include signSGD with majority vote, an effective approach for communication reduction via 1-bit compression on the local gradients, and medianSGD, an algorithm recently proposed to ensure robustness against Byzantine workers. The convergence analyses for these algorithms critically rely on the assumption that all the distributed data are drawn iid from the same distribution. However, in applications such as Federated Learning, the data across different nodes or machines can be inherently heterogeneous, which violates such an iid assumption. This work analyzes signSGD and medianSGD in distributed settings with heterogeneous data. We show that these algorithms are non-convergent whenever there is some disparity between the expected median and mean over the local gradients. To overcome this gap, we provide a novel gradient correction mechanism that perturbs the local gradients with noise, which we show can provably close the gap between mean and median of the gradients. The proposed methods largely preserve nice properties of these median-based algorithms, such as the low per-iteration communication complexity of signSGD, and further enjoy global convergence to stationary solutions. Our perturbation technique can be of independent interest when one wishes to estimate mean through a median estimator.

paragraphs: Median-based distributed optimization offers useful properties: signSGD with majority voting reduces communication through one-bit gradient compression, while medianSGD was proposed for robustness against Byzantine workers. Their convergence analyses, however, rely heavily on workers receiving independent data from the same distribution. Federated settings often violate that assumption because users have different data.

This paper analyzes what happens under such heterogeneity. It identifies a mismatch between the expected median and mean of local gradients as a source of non-convergence. The distinction matters because aggregating workers through a median need not produce the direction represented by their mean when their data distributions differ.

The proposed correction perturbs local gradients with noise. The authors prove that this mechanism can close the mean–median gap and establish convergence to stationary solutions for the resulting methods. The correction largely retains desirable properties such as signSGD’s low communication cost per iteration. Beyond distributed training, the technique may also help when a median estimator is used to estimate a mean.
summary.tldr: Noise-based gradient correction closes a mean–median mismatch that can prevent median-based distributed training from converging on heterogeneous data.

title: Distributed Training with Heterogeneous Data: Bridging Median- and Mean-Based Algorithms

abstract: Episodic training is a core ingredient of few-shot learning to train models on tasks with limited labelled data. Despite its success, episodic training remains largely understudied, prompting us to ask the question: what is the best way to sample episodes? In this paper, we first propose a method to approximate episode sampling distributions based on their difficulty. Building on this method, we perform an extensive analysis and find that sampling uniformly over episode difficulty outperforms other sampling schemes, including curriculum and easy-/hard-mining. As the proposed sampling method is algorithm agnostic, we can leverage these insights to improve few-shot learning accuracies across many episodic training algorithms. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method across popular few-shot learning datasets, algorithms, network architectures, and protocols.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning commonly trains models through episodes, each representing a small task with limited labeled data. The choice of which episodes to present can shape what the model learns. This paper studies that sampling decision directly, asking how training should distribute its attention across tasks of different difficulty.

The authors first develop a method for approximating episode-sampling distributions in terms of difficulty. They then use it to compare sampling strategies. Their analysis finds that sampling uniformly over difficulty performs better than alternatives including curricula and schemes that emphasize easy or hard episodes. The relevant balance is across difficulty levels, so the method explicitly considers how challenging sampled tasks are.

Because the sampling approach is independent of a particular episodic learning algorithm, it can be used across different few-shot methods. Evaluations cover popular datasets, learning algorithms, network architectures, and protocols, demonstrating improved accuracy across the studied settings. The findings identify episode selection as a useful training choice in its own right and support balanced coverage of difficulty over the compared alternatives.
summary.tldr: Sampling training episodes uniformly across difficulty improves few-shot learning over the compared curriculum and easy- or hard-focused strategies.

title: Uniform Sampling over Episode Difficulty

abstract: We present Cross-lingual Open-Retrieval Answer Generation (CORA), the first unified many-to-many question answering (QA) model that can answer questions across many languages, even for ones without language-specific annotated data or knowledge sources.We introduce a new dense passage retrieval algorithm that is trained to retrieve documents across languages for a question.Combined with a multilingual autoregressive generation model, CORA answers directly in the target language without any translation or in-language retrieval modules as used in prior work. We propose an iterative training method that automatically extends annotated data available only in high-resource languages to low-resource ones. Our results show that CORA substantially outperforms the previous state of the art on multilingual open QA benchmarks across 26 languages, 9 of which are unseen during training. Our analyses show the significance of cross-lingual retrieval and generation in many languages, particularly under low-resource settings.

paragraphs: Multilingual question answering is difficult when a language lacks annotated examples or its own knowledge sources. CORA addresses this with a unified model that can retrieve information across languages and answer in the requested language. This allows a question's useful evidence to come from sources beyond those written in that same language.

The system pairs a new cross-lingual dense passage retriever with a multilingual autoregressive answer generator. It produces answers directly in the target language without separate translation or in-language retrieval modules. An iterative training procedure also extends annotations available in high-resource languages to low-resource languages automatically, helping broaden the model's training coverage.

On multilingual open question-answering benchmarks covering 26 languages, CORA substantially improves on the previous state of the art. Nine evaluated languages were unseen during training. The authors' analyses emphasize the contribution of both cross-lingual retrieval and multilingual generation, especially in low-resource settings. The results support sharing access to knowledge and answer-generation capabilities across languages within one system, including cases without language-specific training annotations.
summary.tldr: CORA combines cross-lingual retrieval and multilingual generation to answer questions across 26 evaluated languages, including nine unseen during training.

title: One Question Answering Model for Many Languages with Cross-lingual Dense Passage Retrieval

abstract: Safe reinforcement learning is a promising path toward applying reinforcement learning algorithms to real-world problems, where suboptimal behaviors may lead to actual negative consequences. In this work, we focus on the setting where unsafe states can be avoided by planning ahead a short time into the future. In this setting, a model-based agent with a sufficiently accurate model can avoid unsafe states.We devise a model-based algorithm that heavily penalizes unsafe trajectories, and derive guarantees that our algorithm can avoid unsafe states under certain assumptions. Experiments demonstrate that our algorithm can achieve competitive rewards with fewer safety violations in several continuous control tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies safe reinforcement learning in environments where a short look ahead can reveal how to avoid unsafe states. This assumption defines the setting: near-future planning must be sufficient to steer away from danger. Within that setting, an agent with a sufficiently accurate model of the environment can use predicted consequences to support safer decisions.

The proposed model-based algorithm assigns heavy penalties to unsafe predicted trajectories. Planning therefore evaluates potential behavior with an explicit cost for entering dangerous states. The authors derive guarantees that the algorithm can avoid unsafe states under certain assumptions. These are conditional guarantees, tied to the setting and the requirements of the analysis rather than an unconditional promise of safe behavior.

Experiments on several continuous-control tasks show competitive rewards with fewer safety violations. This combination matters because safety is evaluated alongside the agent's ability to accomplish its task. The empirical result supports the practical value of short-horizon model-based planning in the tested environments, while the theory explains why accurate prediction can provide safety benefits when nearby hazards are avoidable.
summary.tldr: Penalizing unsafe predicted trajectories improves safety in tested control tasks, with conditional guarantees when short-horizon planning can avoid danger.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning by Imagining the Near Future

abstract: Most existing policy learning solutions require the learning agents to receive high-quality supervision signals, e.g., rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) or high-quality expert demonstrations in behavioral cloning (BC). These quality supervisions are either infeasible or prohibitively expensive to obtain in practice. We aim for a unified framework that leverages the available cheap weak supervisions to perform policy learning efficiently. To handle this problem, we treat the weak supervision'' as imperfect information coming from a peer agent, and evaluate the learning agent's policy based on a correlated agreement'' with the peer agent's policy (instead of simple agreements). Our approach explicitly punishes a policy for overfitting to the weak supervision. In addition to theoretical guarantees, extensive evaluations on tasks including RL with noisy reward, BC with weak demonstrations, and standard policy co-training (RL + BC) show that our method leads to substantial performance improvements, especially when the complexity or the noise of the learning environments is high.

paragraphs: Policy learning often depends on reliable rewards or high-quality expert demonstrations, both of which can be costly or unavailable. This paper develops a unified approach for learning from cheaper, imperfect supervision across reinforcement learning and behavioral cloning.

The method interprets weak supervision as information supplied by a peer agent. It evaluates the learner through correlated agreement with the peer's policy, rather than simple agreement. This changes the objective used to decide whether following the peer is useful.

The approach explicitly penalizes policies that overfit the weak supervision. That matters because imperfect guidance can contain noise as well as helpful information. The framework aims to use the available signal while discouraging a policy from fitting its imperfections too closely.

Alongside theoretical guarantees, the paper reports extensive evaluations with noisy rewards, weak demonstrations, and combined reinforcement-learning and behavioral-cloning training. Performance improves substantially in those experiments, especially as environmental complexity or noise increases. The findings support correlated agreement as a common learning principle across several forms of weak policy supervision.
summary.tldr: Evaluating correlated agreement with an imperfect peer enables policy learning from weak supervision while penalizing overfitting to that guidance.

title: Policy Learning Using Weak Supervision

abstract: There has been enormous progress in the last few years in designing neural networks that respect the fundamental symmetries and coordinate freedoms of physical law. Some of these frameworks make use of irreducible representations, some make use of high-order tensor objects, and some apply symmetry-enforcing constraints. Different physical laws obey different combinations of fundamental symmetries, but a large fraction (possibly all) of classical physics is equivariant to translation, rotation, reflection (parity), boost (relativity), and permutations. Here we show that it is simple to parameterize universally approximating polynomial functions that are equivariant under these symmetries, or under the Euclidean, Lorentz, and Poincaré groups, at any dimensionality $d$. The key observation is that nonlinear O($d$)-equivariant (and related-group-equivariant) functions can be universally expressed in terms of a lightweight collection of scalars---scalar products and scalar contractions of the scalar, vector, and tensor inputs. We complement our theory with numerical examples that show that the scalar-based method is simple, efficient, and scalable.

paragraphs: Physical predictions should transform consistently when coordinates change or equivalent inputs are reordered. This property, equivariance, motivates machine-learning architectures that respect physical symmetries. The paper studies how to construct broadly expressive functions with these properties using a relatively lightweight set of mathematical ingredients.

The key observation is that scalar products and scalar contractions of scalar, vector, and tensor inputs can support universal expressions for the equivariant functions considered. The authors show how to parameterize universally approximating polynomial functions respecting the stated symmetries, including those associated with Euclidean, Lorentz, and Poincaré groups, in any dimension. This gives a scalar-based route to functions whose outputs obey the required transformation rules.

The framework addresses symmetries such as translation, rotation, reflection, boosts, and permutations, which are relevant across much of classical physics. Numerical examples complement the theory and demonstrate simplicity, efficiency, and scalability. The result matters because it connects strong expressiveness guarantees with a comparatively economical construction, offering a way to build physical symmetry into models without making high-order representations the central computational ingredient.
summary.tldr: Scalar products and contractions provide a simple, universally expressive foundation for functions that respect important physical symmetries.

title: Scalars are universal: Equivariant machine learning, structured like classical physics

abstract: One common task in many data sciences applications is to answer questions about the effect of new interventions, like: `what would happen to $Y$ if we make $X$ equal to $x$ while observing covariates $Z=z$?'. Formally, this is known as conditional effect identification, where the goal is to determine whether a post-interventional distribution is computable from the combination of an observational distribution and assumptions about the underlying domain represented by a causal diagram. A plethora of methods was developed for solving this problem, including the celebrated do-calculus [Pearl, 1995]. In practice, these results are not always applicable since they require a fully specified causal diagram as input, which is usually not available. In this paper, we assume as the input of the task a less informative structure known as a partial ancestral graph (PAG), which represents a Markov equivalence class of causal diagrams, learnable from observational data. We make the following contributions under this relaxed setting. First, we introduce a new causal calculus, which subsumes the current state-of-the-art, PAG-calculus. Second, we develop an algorithm for conditional effect identification given a PAG and prove it to be both sound and complete. In words, failure of the algorithm to identify a certain effect implies that this effect is not identifiable by any method. Third, we prove the proposed calculus to be complete for the same task.

paragraphs: The paper asks when observational data and causal assumptions can determine the effect of an intervention while conditioning on observed covariates. Many established identification methods require a fully specified causal diagram. In practice, the available information may instead support several diagrams that cannot be distinguished through their observational relationships.

The authors work with a partial ancestral graph, or PAG, which represents such a Markov equivalence class of causal diagrams and is learnable from observational data. They introduce a causal calculus that subsumes the existing PAG-calculus and develop an algorithm for identifying conditional effects directly from this less informative structure. This makes uncertainty about the causal diagram part of the identification task.

The algorithm is proved sound and complete, and the calculus is also complete for the same problem. Soundness supports the validity of identified effects; completeness means that failure is decisive within the supplied information and assumptions. If the algorithm cannot identify an effect from the PAG and observational distribution, another method cannot identify it from that same information either.
summary.tldr: A sound and complete algorithm determines which conditional causal effects are identifiable when only a class of compatible causal diagrams is known.

title: Causal Identification under Markov equivalence: Calculus, Algorithm, and Completeness

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have received extensive research attention for their promising performance in graph machine learning. Despite their extraordinary predictive accuracy, existing approaches, such as GCN and GPRGNN, are not robust in the face of homophily changes on test graphs, rendering these models vulnerable to graph structural attacks and with limited capacity in generalizing to graphs of varied homophily levels. Although many methods have been proposed to improve the robustness of GNN models, most of these techniques are restricted to the spatial domain and employ complicated defense mechanisms, such as learning new graph structures or calculating edge attentions. In this paper, we study the problem of designing simple and robust GNN models in the spectral domain. We propose EvenNet, a spectral GNN corresponding to an even-polynomial graph filter. Based on our theoretical analysis in both spatial and spectral domains, we demonstrate that EvenNet outperforms full-order models in generalizing across homophilic and heterophilic graphs, implying that ignoring odd-hop neighbors improves the robustness of GNNs. We conduct experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of EvenNet. Notably, EvenNet outperforms existing defense models against structural attacks without introducing additional computational costs and maintains competitiveness in traditional node classification tasks on homophilic and heterophilic graphs.

Despite their extraordinary predictive accuracy, existing approaches, such as GCN and GPRGNN, are not robust in the face of homophily changes on test graphs, rendering these models vulnerable to graph structural attacks and with limited capacity in generalizing to graphs of varied homophily levels. Although many methods have been proposed to improve the robustness of GNN models, most of these techniques are restricted to the spatial domain and employ complicated defense mechanisms, such as learning new graph structures or calculating edge attentions. In this paper, we study the problem of designing simple and robust GNN models in the spectral domain. We propose EvenNet, a spectral GNN corresponding to an even-polynomial graph filter. Based on our theoretical analysis in both spatial and spectral domains, we demonstrate that EvenNet outperforms full-order models in generalizing across homophilic and heterophilic graphs, implying that ignoring odd-hop neighbors improves the robustness of GNNs. We conduct experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of EvenNet. Notably, EvenNet outperforms existing defense models against structural attacks without introducing additional computational costs and maintains competitiveness in traditional node classification tasks on homophilic and heterophilic graphs.

paragraphs: EvenNet addresses graph neural networks whose performance deteriorates when the tendency of connected nodes to share labels changes between training and testing. This tendency is called homophily; heterophilic graphs instead connect dissimilar nodes more often. Sensitivity to these changes can limit transfer between graphs and leave models vulnerable to attacks that alter graph structure.

The proposed model uses an even-polynomial graph filter in the spectral domain. Its defining restriction omits odd-hop neighbor contributions. The authors analyze the design in both spatial and spectral terms and show advantages over full-order models when generalizing across homophilic and heterophilic graphs. This provides theoretical support for using a restricted filter to improve robustness.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the approach. EvenNet outperforms existing defense models against structural attacks without adding computational costs, while remaining competitive on conventional node classification tasks across both graph types. The findings make a case for addressing this robustness problem through the model's filter structure, offering a simple design alongside defenses that learn new graph structures or calculate edge attention.
summary.tldr: EvenNet restricts graph filtering to even-order terms to improve robustness to homophily changes and structural attacks.

title: EvenNet: Ignoring Odd-Hop Neighbors Improves Robustness of Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Implicit neural 3D representation has achieved impressive results in surface or scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis, which typically uses the coordinate-based multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) to learn a continuous scene representation. However, existing approaches, such as Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) and its variants, usually require dense input views (i.e. 50-150) to obtain decent results. To relive the over-dependence on massive calibrated images and enrich the coordinate-based feature representation, we explore injecting the prior information into the coordinate-based network and introduce a novel coordinate-based model, CoCo-INR, for implicit neural 3D representation. The cores of our method are two attention modules: codebook attention and coordinate attention. The former extracts the useful prototypes containing rich geometry and appearance information from the prior codebook, and the latter propagates such prior information into each coordinate and enriches its feature representation for a scene or object surface. With the help of the prior information, our method can render 3D views with more photo-realistic appearance and geometries than the current methods using fewer calibrated images available. Experiments on various scene reconstruction datasets, including DTU and BlendedMVS, and the full 3D head reconstruction dataset, H3DS, demonstrate the robustness under fewer input views and fine detail-preserving capability of our proposed method.

CoCo-INR addresses this dependence by enriching coordinate features with prior information about geometry and appearance.

Coordinate attention then distributes this information to individual coordinates. This gives the representation additional information for describing a particular scene or object surface when fewer input views are available.

Experiments cover scene reconstruction on DTU and BlendedMVS as well as full head reconstruction on H3DS. The authors report more photorealistic appearance and geometry than current comparison methods with fewer calibrated images, together with robustness to reduced view counts and preservation of fine detail. The findings support using prior information to strengthen coordinate-based reconstruction when observations are relatively sparse.
summary.tldr: CoCo-INR injects codebook information into coordinate features to improve 3D reconstruction from fewer calibrated views.

title: Coordinates Are NOT Lonely - Codebook Prior Helps Implicit Neural 3D representations

abstract: We study the problem of policy optimization (PO) with linear temporal logic (LTL) constraints. The language of LTL allows flexible description of tasks that may be unnatural to encode as a scalar cost function. We consider LTL-constrained PO as a systematic framework, decoupling task specification from policy selection, and an alternative to the standard of cost shaping. With access to a generative model, we develop a model-based approach that enjoys a sample complexity analysis for guaranteeing both task satisfaction and cost optimality (through a reduction to a reachability problem). Empirically, our algorithm can achieve strong performance even in low sample regimes.

paragraphs: Some tasks are awkward to express as a single numerical cost. This paper studies policy optimization with constraints written in linear temporal logic, a language for describing task requirements over time. The framework separates specifying what a policy must accomplish from choosing a policy that performs well according to its cost.

The authors develop a model-based approach that assumes access to a generative model. They reduce the constrained optimization problem to a reachability problem, making it possible to analyze how many samples are needed. Their sample complexity analysis addresses both satisfying the task and achieving cost optimality, rather than evaluating cost alone.

Empirical results show that the algorithm can perform strongly even when samples are limited. The approach matters because it offers a systematic alternative to encoding every task requirement through cost shaping. Its guarantees belong to the stated setting with generative-model access, while the experiments provide evidence that this formal treatment of task requirements can also work well in low-sample regimes.
summary.tldr: Temporal-logic constraints separate task requirements from policy costs, enabling sample guarantees through a reachability-based approach.

title: Policy Optimization with Linear Temporal Logic Constraints

abstract: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is an established approach for uncertainty quantification and propagation in scientific applications. A key challenge in applying MCMC to scientific domains is computation: the target density of interest is often a function of expensive computations, such as a high-fidelity physical simulation, an intractable integral, or a slowly-converging iterative algorithm. Thus, using an MCMC algorithms with an expensive target density becomes impractical, as these expensive computations need to be evaluated at each iteration of the algorithm. In practice, these computations often approximated via a cheaper, low-fidelity computation, leading to bias in the resulting target density. Multi-fidelity MCMC algorithms combine models of varying fidelities in order to obtain an approximate target density with lower computational cost. In this paper, we describe a class of asymptotically exact multi-fidelity MCMC algorithms for the setting where a sequence of models of increasing fidelity can be computed that approximates the expensive target density of interest. We take a pseudo-marginal MCMC approach for multi-fidelity inference that utilizes a cheaper, randomized-fidelity unbiased estimator of the target fidelity constructed via random truncation of a telescoping series of the low-fidelity sequence of models. Finally, we discuss and evaluate the proposed multi-fidelity MCMC approach on several applications, including log-Gaussian Cox process modeling, Bayesian ODE system identification, PDE-constrained optimization, and Gaussian process parameter inference.

paragraphs: Scientific uncertainty estimation often requires sampling from a density whose evaluation involves an expensive simulation, integral, or iterative calculation. Repeating that work at every Markov chain Monte Carlo step can be impractical. Cheaper approximations save computation but can bias the density being sampled.

The paper develops asymptotically exact multi-fidelity algorithms for settings with an available sequence of increasingly accurate models approximating the target density. It constructs a cheaper unbiased estimator by randomly truncating a telescoping series built from that sequence. A pseudo-marginal MCMC method then uses this randomized-fidelity estimator for inference.

The key distinction is between approximating individual computations and changing the eventual sampling target. The proposed construction supports asymptotic exactness while using models of varying fidelity; it does not claim finite-run exactness. The authors discuss and evaluate applications to log-Gaussian Cox processes, Bayesian identification of ordinary differential equation systems, optimization constrained by partial differential equations, and Gaussian process parameter inference. These examples span several sources of expensive density evaluations.
summary.tldr: Randomized combinations of increasingly accurate models enable asymptotically exact MCMC with cheaper unbiased density estimates.

title: Multi-fidelity Monte Carlo: a pseudo-marginal approach

abstract: In this paper, we demonstrate that information retrieval can be accomplished with a single Transformer, in which all information about the corpus is encoded in the parameters of the model. To this end, we introduce the Differentiable Search Index (DSI), a new paradigm that learns a text-to-text model that maps string queries directly to relevant docids; in other words, a DSI model answers queries directly using only its parameters, dramatically simplifying the whole retrieval process. We study variations in how documents and their identifiers are represented, variations in training procedures, and the interplay between models and corpus sizes. Experiments demonstrate that given appropriate design choices, DSI significantly outperforms strong baselines such as dual encoder models. Moreover, DSI demonstrates strong generalization capabilities, outperforming a BM25 baseline in a zero-shot setup.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a single transformer can perform information retrieval by storing corpus information in its learned parameters. Its Differentiable Search Index, or DSI, treats retrieval as a text-to-text prediction problem: given a query string, the model directly produces identifiers of relevant documents.

The approach makes the model's parameters serve as the search index. Answering a query therefore means predicting document identifiers using the model itself. The authors study how this depends on the representation of documents and identifiers, the training procedure, and the relationship between model size and corpus size. Those choices are central to evaluating the proposed retrieval paradigm.

With appropriate design choices, experiments show DSI significantly outperforming strong baselines, including dual encoders. The model also exceeds a BM25 baseline in a zero-shot setup, which the authors present as evidence of generalization. The findings demonstrate that direct identifier generation can be effective in the studied settings, while preserving the qualification that performance depends on how the differentiable index is designed and trained.
summary.tldr: A Differentiable Search Index stores corpus information in transformer parameters and directly predicts relevant document identifiers from queries.

title: Transformer Memory as a Differentiable Search Index

abstract: We propose a new representation for encoding 3D shapes as neural fields. The representation is designed to be compatible with the transformer architecture and to benefit both shape reconstruction and shape generation. Existing works on neural fields are grid-based representations with latents being defined on a regular grid. In contrast, we define latents on irregular grids which facilitates our representation to be sparse and adaptive. In the context of shape reconstruction from point clouds, our shape representation built on irregular grids improves upon grid-based methods in terms of reconstruction accuracy. For shape generation, our representation promotes high-quality shape generation using auto-regressive probabilistic models. We show different applications that improve over the current state of the art. First, we show results of probabilistic shape reconstruction from a single higher resolution image. Second, we train a probabilistic model conditioned on very low resolution images. Third, we apply our model to category-conditioned generation. All probabilistic experiments confirm that we are able to generate detailed and high quality shapes to yield the new state of the art in generative 3D shape modeling.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a way to represent 3D shapes that supports both reconstructing existing objects and generating new ones. It encodes shapes as neural fields, with learned latent information attached to locations in space. The central change is to place those locations on an irregular grid, allowing the representation to be sparse and adaptive instead of following a fixed regular layout.

The representation is designed to work with transformers. For reconstruction, it uses point clouds as input and achieves better reconstruction accuracy than the grid-based methods considered. For generation, it works with autoregressive probabilistic models, which build a shape representation through a sequence of predictions. This connects the same underlying representation to both recovering geometry and modeling possible shapes.

The authors demonstrate probabilistic reconstruction from a single higher-resolution image, generation conditioned on very low-resolution images, and generation conditioned on object category. Across the reported probabilistic experiments, they obtain detailed, high-quality shapes and report improvements over the state of the art. The findings support irregular latent placement as a useful design choice for generative 3D modeling.
summary.tldr: Irregular latent grids provide a sparse, adaptive shape representation that improves reported 3D reconstruction and generation results.

title: 3DILG: Irregular Latent Grids for 3D Generative Modeling

abstract: A common approach to solving prediction tasks on large networks, such as node classification or link prediction, begin by learning a Euclidean embedding of the nodes of the network, from which traditional machine learning methods can then be applied. This includes methods such as DeepWalk and node2vec, which learn embeddings by optimizing stochastic losses formed over subsamples of the graph at each iteration of stochastic gradient descent. In this paper, we study the effects of adding an $\ell_2$ penalty of the embedding vectors to the training loss of these types of methods. We prove that, under some exchangeability assumptions on the graph, this asymptotically leads to learning a graphon with a nuclear-norm-type penalty, and give guarantees for the asymptotic distribution of the learned embedding vectors. In particular, the exact form of the penalty depends on the choice of subsampling method used as part of stochastic gradient descent. We also illustrate empirically that concatenating node covariates to $\ell_2$ regularized node2vec embeddings leads to comparable, when not superior, performance to methods which incorporate node covariates and the network structure in a non-linear manner..

paragraphs: Network embedding methods assign each node a vector so that standard learning methods can use network information for tasks such as node classification and link prediction. This paper studies what happens when methods such as DeepWalk and node2vec also penalize the squared sizes of those vectors. The question is what this familiar regularization choice means for the network structure being learned.

Under exchangeability assumptions on the graph, the authors prove an asymptotic connection to learning a graphon with a nuclear-norm-type penalty. They also provide guarantees describing the asymptotic distribution of the embedding vectors. Crucially, the resulting penalty depends on how graph samples are selected during stochastic gradient descent: the sampling procedure helps determine the effect of regularization.

The paper also empirically examines combining regularized node2vec embeddings with node attributes by simply concatenating them. This achieves comparable, and sometimes better, performance than methods that combine attributes and network structure nonlinearly. The findings give theoretical meaning to embedding regularization while supporting a relatively simple way to incorporate additional node information.
summary.tldr: Under graph exchangeability assumptions, squared-vector regularization induces a sampling-dependent structural penalty on network embeddings.

title: Asymptotics of $\ell_2$ Regularized Network Embeddings

abstract: 3D human pose and shape estimation (a.k.a. ``human mesh recovery'') has achieved substantial progress. Researchers mainly focus on the development of novel algorithms, while less attention has been paid to other critical factors involved. This could lead to less optimal baselines, hindering the fair and faithful evaluations of newly designed methodologies. To address this problem, this work presents the \textit{first} comprehensive benchmarking study from three under-explored perspectives beyond algorithms. \emph{1) Datasets.} An analysis on 31 datasets reveals the distinct impacts of data samples: datasets featuring critical attributes (\emph{i.e.} diverse poses, shapes, camera characteristics, backbone features) are more effective. Strategical selection and combination of high-quality datasets can yield a significant boost to the model performance. \emph{2) Backbones.} Experiments with 10 backbones, ranging from CNNs to transformers, show the knowledge learnt from a proximity task is readily transferable to human mesh recovery. \emph{3) Training strategies.} Proper augmentation techniques and loss designs are crucial. With the above findings, we achieve a PA-MPJPE of 47.3 \(mm\) on the 3DPW test set with a relatively simple model. More importantly, we provide strong baselines for fair comparisons of algorithms, and recommendations for building effective training configurations in the future. Codebase is available at \url{https://github.com/smplbody/hmr-benchmarks}.
