paragraphs: The paper studies whether a causal effect within a particular subpopulation can be computed from observational data collected in that same subpopulation. This is the subpopulation identification problem, or s-ID. Earlier work addressed the setting where every variable in the system is observable. The authors extend the problem to allow latent variables, meaning variables that are not observed.

Their approach begins by adapting graphical concepts used in the classical causal identification problem. In particular, they develop counterparts of c-components and Hedges for the subpopulation setting with latent variables. These definitions provide the structural language needed to reason about identification when both the restriction to a subpopulation and unobserved variables are present.

Using this extended framework, the authors propose a sound identification algorithm. Soundness means that the causal identification conclusions the algorithm produces are valid within the framework. The stated contribution therefore expands the setting in which correct identification can be established. The abstract claims soundness, so its result should be understood as a correctness guarantee for the algorithm’s conclusions, without assuming a stronger claim that it resolves every identifiable case.
summary.tldr: The paper extends subpopulation causal identification to latent-variable settings and provides a sound algorithm.

title: Causal Effect Identification in a Sub-Population with Latent Variables

abstract: With the remarkable achievements of large language models (LLMs), the demand for fine-tuning and deploying LLMs in various downstream tasks has garnered widespread interest. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques represented by LoRA and model quantization techniques represented by GPTQ and AWQ are of paramount significance. However, although these techniques have been widely adopted in single-task scenarios, research is scarce in multi-task scenarios. To be specific, we find that mainstream quantization methods would prevent the base LLM from being shared among tasks, so current LLM serving systems are infeasible to integrate LLM quantization with multiple LoRA adapters to achieve memory-efficient multi-task serving. Moreover, existing LLM serving systems lack support for dynamic task addition and overlook the workload differences among tasks, leading to inefficiencies in multi-task scenarios.This work proposes LoRA-Inlaid, an efficient multi-task LLM serving system. On the one hand, LoRA-Inlaid designs a flexible and efficient multi-task quantization algorithm (MLGPTQ) that facilitates the sharing of a single quantized model for multiple LoRA adapters, which significantly reduces the memory consumption for model deployment. Meanwhile, it supports adding LoRA adapters for new tasks on the fly, without sacrificing the stability of online services. On the other hand, LoRA-Inlaid develops a novel multi-task scheduling algorithm guided by output length prediction and grouping among different tasks, which effectively shrinks the memory consumption and avoids frequent switching of LoRA adapters. Empirical results verify that LoRA-Inlaid outperforms existing state-of-the-art LLM serving systems by up to 1.58 times in terms of throughput, 1.76 times in terms of average latency, 2 times in terms of job completion time, and 10 times in terms of SLO Attainment, while maintaining the same level of model quality.

paragraphs: Serving several tasks with one language model becomes difficult when task-specific LoRA adapters are combined with quantization. The authors find that mainstream quantization methods obstruct sharing the base model across tasks. They also identify serving inefficiencies caused by limited support for adding tasks dynamically and by scheduling that overlooks differences between task workloads.

New adapters can be added while services remain online. A separate scheduling algorithm predicts output lengths and groups work across tasks, reducing memory use and frequent adapter switching.

These are reported maxima, not gains promised for every workload. Together, the results show the value of coordinating quantization and scheduling around the requirements of multiple adapters.
summary.tldr: LoRA-Inlaid combines shared-model quantization and task-aware scheduling to serve multiple LoRA adapters more efficiently.

title: Efficient Multi-task LLM Quantization and Serving for Multiple LoRA Adapters

abstract: Finetuning large language models (LLMs) in federated learning (FL) settings has become increasingly important as it allows resource-constrained devices to finetune a model using private data. However, finetuning LLMs using backpropagation requires excessive memory (especially from intermediate activations) for resource-constrained devices. While Forward-mode Auto-Differentiation (AD) can significantly reduce memory footprint from activations, we observe that directly applying it to LLM finetuning results in slow convergence and poor accuracy. In this paper, we introduce Spry, an FL algorithm that splits trainable weights of an LLM among participating clients, such that each client computes gradients using forward-mode AD that are closer estimations of the true gradients. Spry achieves a low memory footprint, high accuracy, and fast convergence. We formally prove that the global gradients in Spry are unbiased estimators of true global gradients for homogeneous data distributions across clients, while heterogeneity increases bias of the estimates. We also derive Spry's convergence rate, showing that the gradients decrease inversely proportional to the number of FL rounds, indicating the convergence up to the limits of heterogeneity. Empirically, Spry reduces the memory footprint during training by 1.4-7.1$\times$ in contrast to backpropagation, while reaching comparable accuracy, across a wide range of language tasks, models, and FL settings. Spry reduces the convergence time by 1.2-20.3$\times$ and achieves 5.2-13.5\% higher accuracy against state-of-the-art zero-order methods. When finetuning Llama2-7B with LoRA, compared to the peak memory consumption of 33.9GB of backpropagation, Spry only consumes 6.2GB of peak memory. For OPT13B, the reduction is from 76.5GB to 10.8GB. Spry makes feasible previously impossible FL deployments on commodity mobile and edge devices. Our source code is available for replication at https://github.com/Astuary/Spry.
originalAbstract: Finetuning large language models (LLMs) in federated learning (FL) settings has become increasingly important as it allows resource-constrained devices to finetune a model using private data. However, finetuning LLMs using backpropagation requires excessive memory (especially from intermediate activations) for resource-constrained devices. While Forward-mode Auto-Differentiation (AD) can significantly reduce memory footprint from activations, we observe that directly applying it to LLM finetuning results in slow convergence and poor accuracy. In this paper, we introduce Spry, an FL algorithm that splits trainable weights of an LLM among participating clients, such that each client computes gradients using forward-mode AD that are closer estimations of the true gradients. Spry achieves a low memory footprint, high accuracy, and fast convergence. We formally prove that the global gradients in Spry are unbiased estimators of true global gradients for homogeneous data distributions across clients, while heterogeneity increases bias of the estimates. We also derive Spry's convergence rate, showing that the gradients decrease inversely proportional to the number of FL rounds, indicating the convergence up to the limits of heterogeneity. Empirically, Spry reduces the memory footprint during training by 1.4-7.1$\times$ in contrast to backpropagation, while reaching comparable accuracy, across a wide range of language tasks, models, and FL settings. Spry reduces the convergence time by 1.2-20.3$\times$ and achieves 5.2-13.5\% higher accuracy against state-of-the-art zero-order methods. When finetuning Llama2-7B with LoRA, compared to the peak memory consumption of 33.9GB of backpropagation, Spry only consumes 6.2GB of peak memory. For OPT13B, the reduction is from 76.5GB to 10.8GB. Spry makes feasible previously impossible FL deployments on commodity mobile and edge devices. Our source code is available for replication at https://github.com/Astuary/Spry.

paragraphs: Spry targets the memory burden of federated language-model fine-tuning on constrained devices. Backpropagation stores intermediate activations, while forward-mode automatic differentiation can reduce that storage. Directly using forward mode, however, produces slow convergence and poor accuracy in the authors' observations. Spry divides trainable weights among clients to obtain closer gradient estimates.

The analysis proves that global gradient estimates are unbiased when clients have homogeneous data distributions. Heterogeneity increases their bias, and the convergence result reflects that restriction: gradients decrease inversely with the number of federated rounds, up to limits imposed by heterogeneity. The guarantee therefore depends on how data differs across participating clients.

Experiments report 1.4–7.1 times lower training memory than backpropagation with comparable accuracy. Against state-of-the-art zero-order methods, Spry reduces convergence time by factors of 1.2–20.3 and reports 5.2–13.5% higher accuracy. For Llama2-7B with LoRA, peak memory falls from 33.9 GB to 6.2 GB. These results show how distributing the gradient-computation burden can expand feasible federated deployments.
summary.tldr: Spry distributes trainable weights across clients to make forward-mode federated fine-tuning more memory-efficient, with convergence affected by data heterogeneity.

title: Thinking Forward: Memory-Efficient Federated Finetuning of Language Models

abstract: Presently, pseudo-labeling stands as a prevailing approach in cross-domain semantic segmentation, enhancing model efficacy by training with pixels assigned with reliable pseudo-labels. However, we identify two key limitations within this paradigm: (1) under relatively severe domain shifts, most selected reliable pixels appear speckled and remain noisy. (2) when dealing with wild data, some pixels belonging to the open-set class may exhibit high confidence and also appear speckled. These two points make it difficult for the pixel-level selection mechanism to identify and correct these speckled close- and open-set noises. As a result, error accumulation is continuously introduced into subsequent self-training, leading to inefficiencies in pseudo-labeling. To address these limitations, we propose a novel method called Semantic Connectivity-driven Pseudo-labeling (SeCo). SeCo formulates pseudo-labels at the connectivity level, which makes it easier to locate and correct closed and open set noise. Specifically, SeCo comprises two key components: Pixel Semantic Aggregation (PSA) and Semantic Connectivity Correction (SCC). Initially, PSA categorizes semantics into ``stuff'' and ``things'' categories and aggregates speckled pseudo-labels into semantic connectivity through efficient interaction with the Segment Anything Model (SAM). This enables us not only to obtain accurate boundaries but also simplifies noise localization. Subsequently, SCC introduces a simple connectivity classification task, which enables us to locate and correct connectivity noise with the guidance of loss distribution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SeCo can be flexibly applied to various cross-domain semantic segmentation tasks, \textit{i.e.} domain generalization and domain adaptation, even including source-free, and black-box domain adaptation, significantly improving the performance of existing state-of-the-art methods. The code is provided in the appendix and will be open-source.

Semantic Connectivity-driven Pseudo-labeling, or SeCo, organizes predictions into connected semantic regions. Its Pixel Semantic Aggregation component separates semantics into stuff and things categories and interacts with the Segment Anything Model to assemble scattered labels into regions with accurate boundaries. This organization makes erroneous labels easier to locate at a meaningful spatial scale.

Experiments show improvements when SeCo is applied to domain generalization and several forms of domain adaptation, including source-free and black-box settings. The central finding is that connected structure provides useful evidence for correcting both known-class mistakes and noise involving unfamiliar classes.

title: Connectivity-Driven Pseudo-Labeling Makes Stronger Cross-Domain Segmenters

abstract: Color video snapshot compressive imaging (SCI) employs computational imaging techniques to capture multiple sequential video frames in a single Bayer-patterned measurement. With the increasing popularity of quad-Bayer pattern in mainstream smartphone cameras for capturing high-resolution videos, mobile photography has become more accessible to a wider audience. However, existing color video SCI reconstruction algorithms are designed based on the traditional Bayer pattern. When applied to videos captured by quad-Bayer cameras, these algorithms often result in color distortion and ineffective demosaicing, rendering them impractical for primary equipment. To address this challenge, we propose the MambaSCI method, which leverages the Mamba and UNet architectures for efficient reconstruction of quad-Bayer patterned color video SCI. To the best of our knowledge, our work presents the first algorithm for quad-Bayer patterned SCI reconstruction, and also the initial application of the Mamba model to this task. Specifically, we customize Residual-Mamba-Blocks, which residually connect the Spatial-Temporal Mamba (STMamba), Edge-Detail-Reconstruction (EDR) module, and Channel Attention (CA) module. Respectively, STMamba is used to model long-range spatial-temporal dependencies with linear complexity, EDR is for better edge-detail reconstruction, and CA is used to compensate for the missing channel information interaction in Mamba model. Experiments demonstrate that MambaSCI surpasses state-of-the-art methods with lower computational and memory costs. PyTorch style pseudo-code for the core modules is provided in the supplementary materials. Code is at https://github.com/PAN083/MambaSCI.

Existing color reconstruction methods assume a traditional Bayer sensor pattern. Applying them to quad-Bayer measurements can cause color distortion and poor demosaicing, motivating an algorithm designed for that sensor arrangement.

Channel attention supplies interactions between channels that the Mamba component otherwise lacks.

The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first quad-Bayer SCI reconstruction algorithm and the first use of Mamba for this task. Its significance is the combination of sensor-specific reconstruction and efficient temporal-spatial modeling: the architecture addresses the measurement pattern while also targeting detail preservation and computational cost.
summary.tldr: MambaSCI reconstructs quad-Bayer compressed video using efficient space-time modeling, edge reconstruction, and channel attention.

title: MambaSCI: Efficient Mamba-UNet for Quad-Bayer Patterned Video Snapshot Compressive Imaging

abstract: Public benchmarks play an essential role in the evaluation of large language models. However, data contamination can lead to inflated performance, rendering them unreliable for model comparison. It is therefore crucial to detect contamination and estimate its impact on measured performance. Unfortunately, existing detection methods can be easily evaded and fail to quantify contamination. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel definition of *contamination as artificially inflated and non-generalizing benchmark performance* instead of the inclusion of benchmark samples in the training data. This perspective enables us to detect *any* model with inflated performance, i.e., performance that does not generalize to rephrased samples, synthetic samples from the same distribution, or different benchmarks for the same task. Based on this insight, we develop ConStat, a statistical method that reliably detects and quantifies contamination by comparing performance between a primary and reference benchmark relative to a set of reference models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ConStat in an extensive evaluation of diverse model architectures, benchmarks, and contamination scenarios and find high levels of contamination in multiple popular models including Mistral, Llama, Yi, and the top-3 Open LLM Leaderboard models.

paragraphs: ConStat approaches benchmark contamination through its effect on measured ability. Instead of defining contamination solely as benchmark examples appearing in training data, the paper defines it as artificially elevated benchmark performance that fails to generalize. This shifts the focus toward whether a reported score reflects capability beyond the particular evaluation.

The method compares performance on a primary benchmark with performance on a reference benchmark, using a collection of reference models to interpret the relationship. Relevant checks can involve rephrased questions, synthetic examples from the same distribution, or another benchmark covering the same task. The statistical comparison is designed to both detect contamination and quantify its impact.

The authors evaluate ConStat across different architectures, benchmarks, and contamination scenarios. They report substantial contamination in evaluated models from the Mistral, Llama, and Yi families, as well as the three leading Open LLM Leaderboard models in their study. These findings concern inflated, non-generalizing performance under the paper's definition, making transfer between evaluations central to interpreting benchmark scores.
summary.tldr: ConStat detects and quantifies benchmark contamination by testing whether unusually strong performance carries over to related evaluations.

title: ConStat: Performance-Based Contamination Detection in Large Language Models

abstract: In multiclass classification over $n$ outcomes, we typically optimize some surrogate loss $L: \mathbb{R}^d \times\mathcal{Y} \to \mathbb{R}$ assigning real-valued error to predictions in $\mathbb{R}^d$. In this paradigm, outcomes must be embedded into the reals with dimension $d \approx n$ in order to design a consistent surrogate loss. Consistent losses are well-motivated theoretically, yet for large $n$, such as in information retrieval and structured prediction tasks, their optimization may be computationally infeasible. In practice, outcomes are typically embedded into some $\mathbb{R}^d$ for $d \ll n$, with little known about their suitability for multiclass classification. We investigate two approaches for trading off consistency and dimensionality in multiclass classification while using a convex surrogate loss. We first formalize partial consistency when the optimized surrogate has dimension $d \ll n$. We then check if partial consistency holds under a given embedding and low-noise assumption, providing insight into when to use a particular embedding into $\mathbb{R}^d$. Finally, we present a new method to construct (fully) consistent losses with $d \ll n$ out of multiple problem instances. Our practical approach leverages parallelism to sidestep lower bounds on $d$.

paragraphs: Multiclass learning commonly replaces classification error with a convex surrogate loss that is easier to optimize. Full consistency means that optimizing this surrogate supports the correct classification objective. In the setting studied here, achieving that guarantee ordinarily requires a prediction representation with dimension roughly comparable to the number of outcomes, which can be expensive when there are many classes.

The paper examines two ways to work with much smaller representations. First, it formalizes partial consistency and investigates whether a chosen embedding satisfies it under a specified low-noise assumption. This provides a way to reason about when a low-dimensional embedding is suitable, while making explicit that the resulting guarantee is weaker or more conditional than full consistency.

Second, the authors construct fully consistent losses with low-dimensional representations by combining multiple problem instances. Their approach uses parallelism to sidestep dimensionality lower bounds. The distinction matters: one route studies what a compact individual representation can guarantee, while the other reorganizes the overall computation across multiple instances to recover full consistency without requiring a single large representation.
summary.tldr: The paper studies conditional guarantees for compact convex surrogates and a parallel construction that recovers full consistency across multiple instances.

title: Trading off Consistency and Dimensionality of Convex Surrogates for Multiclass Classification

abstract: Mass transport problems arise in many areas of machine learning whereby one wants to compute a map transporting one distribution to another. Generative modeling techniques like Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Denoising Diffusion Models (DMMs) have been successfully adapted to solve such transport problems, resulting in CycleGAN and Bridge Matching respectively. However, these methods do not approximate Optimal Transport (OT) maps, which are known to have desirable properties. Existing techniques approximating OT maps for high-dimensional data-rich problems, including DDMs-based Rectified Flow and Schrodinger bridge procedures, require fully training a DDM-type model at each iteration, or use mini-batch techniques which can introduce significant errors. We propose a novel algorithm to compute the Schrodinger bridge, a dynamic entropy-regularized version of OT, that eliminates the need to train multiple DDMs-like models. This algorithm corresponds to a discretization of a flow of path measures, referred to as the Schrodinger Bridge Flow, whose only stationary point is the Schrodinger bridge. We demonstrate the performance of our algorithm on a variety of unpaired data translation tasks.

paragraphs: Unpaired data translation requires mapping between distributions without matched examples specifying each desired transformation. Optimal transport offers a principled way to construct such mappings. The paper focuses on the Schrödinger bridge, a dynamic, entropy-regularized version of optimal transport, and the computational burden of existing approaches for high-dimensional data.

Existing methods can require fully training a diffusion-type model at every iteration or use mini-batch approximations that introduce substantial errors. The proposed algorithm avoids training multiple diffusion-type models. It arises by discretizing a flow of path measures, meaning that the mathematical object being updated describes distributions over entire transformation trajectories.

The authors show that the Schrödinger bridge is the only stationary point of this flow. That property identifies the intended equilibrium of the construction without itself asserting that every discretized run reaches it. The paper demonstrates the algorithm on several unpaired translation tasks, connecting the mathematical framework with practical transformations between data distributions.
summary.tldr: Schrödinger Bridge Flow supports unpaired data translation without repeatedly training multiple diffusion-type models.

title: Schrodinger Bridge Flow for Unpaired Data Translation

abstract: Editing biological sequences has extensive applications in synthetic biology and medicine, such as designing regulatory elements for nucleic-acid therapeutics and treating genetic disorders. The primary objective in biological-sequence editing is to determine the optimal modifications to a sequence which augment certain biological properties while adhering to a minimal number of alterations to ensure predictability and potentially support safety. In this paper, we propose GFNSeqEditor, a novel biological-sequence editing algorithm which builds on the recently proposed area of generative flow networks (GFlowNets). Our proposed GFNSeqEditor identifies elements within a starting seed sequence that may compromise a desired biological property. Then, using a learned stochastic policy, the algorithm makes edits at these identified locations, offering diverse modifications for each sequence to enhance the desired property. The number of edits can be regulated through specific hyperparameters. We conducted extensive experiments on a range of real-world datasets and biological applications, and our results underscore the superior performance of our proposed algorithm compared to existing state-of-the-art sequence editing methods.

paragraphs: Biological sequence editing seeks changes that improve a desired property while keeping the number of alterations small. Limiting edits helps preserve predictability and may support safety, making the extent of modification part of the design problem. GFNSeqEditor addresses this task using generative flow networks to produce multiple candidate edits from a starting sequence.

The algorithm first identifies elements of the seed sequence that may weaken the desired biological property. A learned stochastic policy then edits those locations, allowing different modifications to be proposed for the same starting point. Specific hyperparameters regulate the number of changes, giving the method a way to control how extensively it alters a sequence.

Experiments across real-world datasets and biological applications report better performance than existing state-of-the-art sequence-editing methods. The approach brings together targeted selection of edit locations, diversity among proposed modifications, and control over edit count. The abstract presents limited editing as potentially supportive of safety; the reported performance results establish advantages in the evaluated editing tasks rather than a general safety guarantee.
summary.tldr: GFNSeqEditor uses a learned stochastic editing policy to propose diverse biological sequence improvements with a controllable number of changes.

title: GFlowNet Assisted Biological Sequence Editing

abstract: Data *quality* is a crucial factor in the performance of machine learning models, a principle that dataset distillation methods exploit by compressing training datasets into much smaller counterparts that maintain similar downstream performance. Understanding how and why data distillation methods work is vital not only for improving these methods but also for revealing fundamental characteristics of "good” training data. However, a major challenge in achieving this goal is the observation that distillation approaches, which rely on sophisticated but mostly disparate methods to generate synthetic data, have little in common with each other. In this work, we highlight a largely overlooked aspect common to most of these methods: the use of soft (probabilistic) labels. Through a series of ablation experiments, we study the role of soft labels in depth. Our results reveal that the main factor explaining the performance of state-of-the-art distillation methods is not the specific techniques used to generate synthetic data but rather the use of soft labels. Furthermore, we demonstrate that not all soft labels are created equal; they must contain *structured information* to be beneficial. We also provide empirical scaling laws that characterize the effectiveness of soft labels as a function of images-per-class in the distilled dataset and establish an empirical Pareto frontier for data-efficient learning. Combined, our findings challenge conventional wisdom in dataset distillation, underscore the importance of soft labels in learning, and suggest new directions for improving distillation methods. Code for all experiments is available at https://github.com/sunnytqin/no-distillation.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation compresses a training collection into a much smaller dataset while aiming to preserve downstream performance. Different methods construct their synthetic images in very different ways, making their success difficult to explain through a shared mechanism. This paper investigates a common ingredient: soft labels, which assign probabilities across classes instead of providing a single class label.

Through ablation experiments, the authors examine how much these labels contribute to performance. Their results identify soft labels as the main explanation for the performance of the state-of-the-art distillation methods they study. The information inside the labels matters: merely making labels probabilistic is insufficient; beneficial labels must carry structured information.

The paper also develops empirical scaling relationships between soft-label effectiveness and the number of images per class. An empirical Pareto frontier describes achievable tradeoffs in data-efficient learning. Together, these findings shift attention toward the supervision attached to distilled examples and suggest that improving label information could be a productive direction for improving distillation.
summary.tldr: Ablation experiments identify structured soft labels as a major driver of the performance of the dataset distillation methods studied.

title: A Label is Worth A Thousand Images in Dataset Distillation

abstract: Causal inference is essential for developing and evaluating medical interventions, yet real-world medical datasets are often difficult to access due to regulatory barriers. This makes synthetic data a potentially valuable asset that enables these medical analyses, along with the development of new inference methods themselves. Generative models can produce synthetic data that closely approximate real data distributions, yet existing methods do not consider the unique challenges that downstream causal inference tasks, and specifically those focused on treatments, pose. We establish a set of desiderata that synthetic data containing treatments should satisfy to maximise downstream utility: preservation of (i) the covariate distribution, (ii) the treatment assignment mechanism, and (iii) the outcome generation mechanism. Based on these desiderata, we propose a set of evaluation metrics to assess such synthetic data. Finally, we present STEAM: a novel method for generating Synthetic data for Treatment Effect Analysis in Medicine that mimics the data-generating process of data containing treatments and optimises for our desiderata. We empirically demonstrate that STEAM achieves state-of-the-art performance across our metrics as compared to existing generative models, particularly as the complexity of the true data-generating process increases.

paragraphs: Synthetic medical data could support treatment-effect research when access to real patient data is restricted. This paper argues that matching a dataset’s overall distribution does not adequately address the specific needs of downstream causal analysis. Data containing treatments has an internal structure that a useful generator should preserve.

The authors identify three targets: the distribution of covariates, the mechanism assigning treatments, and the mechanism producing outcomes. They introduce evaluation metrics organized around these targets. This makes the intended use explicit: a synthetic dataset should retain the relationships needed for treatment analysis, alongside the characteristics of the population it represents.

Their generation method, STEAM, follows the structure of a treatment-containing data-generating process and optimizes for these requirements. In the reported experiments, it outperforms existing generative models on the proposed metrics, particularly as the underlying data-generating process becomes more complex. The work therefore pairs a purpose-specific generator with a corresponding evaluation framework, so that synthetic-data quality is judged in relation to its intended causal-inference use.
summary.tldr: STEAM generates and evaluates synthetic medical data around preserving the mechanisms needed for treatment-effect analysis.

title: Improving the Generation and Evaluation of Synthetic Data for Downstream Medical Causal Inference

abstract: In the adaptive sampling model of online learning, future prediction tasks can be arbitrarily dependent on the past. Every round, an adversary selects an instance to test the learner. After the learner makes a prediction, a noisy label is drawn from an underlying conditional label distribution and is revealed to both learner and adversary. A learner is consistent if it eventually performs no worse than the Bayes predictor. We study the $k_n$-nearest neighbor learner within this setting. In the worst-case, the learner will fail because an adaptive process can generate spurious patterns out of noise. However, under the mild smoothing assumption that the process generating the instances is uniformly absolutely continuous and that choice of $(k_n)_n$ is reasonable, the $k_n$-nearest neighbor rule is online consistent.

A learner is consistent if it eventually performs no worse than the Bayes predictor. We study the $k_n$-nearest neighbor learner within this setting. In the worst-case, the learner will fail because an adaptive process can generate spurious patterns out of noise. However, under the mild smoothing assumption that the process generating the instances is uniformly absolutely continuous and that choice of $(k_n)_n$ is reasonable, the $k_n$-nearest neighbor rule is online consistent.

paragraphs: This paper studies nearest-neighbor prediction when incoming examples can depend on everything that happened previously. In each round, an adversary chooses the next instance, the learner predicts its label, and a noisy label is then drawn from an underlying conditional distribution. Both parties observe that label before the next round begins.

The central question is whether the learner eventually performs no worse than the Bayes predictor, the reference predictor defined by the underlying label distribution. Under unrestricted adaptive sampling, nearest-neighbor learning can fail. The adaptive process can exploit past noise to create misleading patterns, so accumulating more observations does not by itself ensure reliable learning.

The authors establish consistency under a smoothing condition: the process selecting instances must be uniformly absolutely continuous, and the sequence specifying how many neighbors to use must be chosen reasonably. The guarantee is therefore conditional, not a claim about every adaptive sequence. Its significance is that dependence on past observations need not destroy nearest-neighbor consistency when the stated regularity and neighbor-count requirements hold.
summary.tldr: Nearest-neighbor learning remains online consistent under adaptive sampling when a smoothing assumption and suitable neighbor-count choices hold.

title: Consistency of the $k_n$-nearest neighbor rule under adaptive sampling

abstract: Template-based molecular generation offers a promising avenue for drug design by ensuring generated compounds are synthetically accessible through predefined reaction templates and building blocks. In this work, we tackle three core challenges in template-based GFlowNets: (1) minimizing synthesis cost, (2) scaling to large building block libraries, and (3) effectively utilizing small fragment sets. We propose **Recursive Cost Guidance**, a backward policy framework that employs auxiliary machine learning models to approximate synthesis cost and viability. This guidance steers generation toward low-cost synthesis pathways, significantly enhancing cost-efficiency, molecular diversity, and quality, especially when paired with an **Exploitation Penalty** that balances the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. To enhance performance in smaller building block libraries, we develop a **Dynamic Library** mechanism that reuses intermediate high-reward states to construct full synthesis trees. Our approach establishes state-of-the-art results in template-based molecular generation.

title: Scalable and Cost-Efficient de Novo Template-Based Molecular Generation

abstract: Online tensor decompositions are powerful and proven techniques that address the challenges in processing high-velocity streaming tensor data, such as traffic flow and weather system. The main aim of this work is to propose a novel online functional tensor decomposition (OFTD) framework, which represents a spatial-temporal continuous function using the CP tensor decomposition parameterized by coordinate-based implicit neural representations (INRs). The INRs allow for natural characterization of continually expanded streaming data by simply adding new coordinates into the network. Particularly, our method transforms the classical online tensor decomposition algorithm into a more dynamic continual learning paradigm of updating the INR weights to fit the new data without forgetting the previous tensor knowledge. To this end, we introduce a long-tail memory replay method that adapts to the local continuity property of INR. Extensive experiments for streaming tensor completion using traffic, weather, user-item, and video data verify the effectiveness of the OFTD approach for streaming data analysis. This endeavor serves as a pivotal inspiration for future research to connect classical online tensor tools with continual learning paradigms to better explore knowledge underlying streaming tensor data.

paragraphs: Streaming measurements often form multidimensional arrays, or tensors, with missing entries that need to be estimated as new data arrive. Traffic and weather are examples where the data continually expand across space and time. This paper proposes Online Functional Tensor Decomposition to represent that expanding information as a continuous function.

The method combines CP tensor decomposition with coordinate-based implicit neural representations. These networks parameterize the decomposition using coordinates, so newly arriving observations can be incorporated through new coordinate inputs. Updating the representation becomes a continual-learning problem: adjust the network to fit recent data while retaining knowledge of earlier observations.

To address forgetting, the authors introduce a long-tail memory replay method adapted to the local continuity of the neural representation. Replaying stored information supports retention as the model changes. Experiments on traffic, weather, user-item, and video data verify the approach’s effectiveness for streaming tensor completion. The contribution is a connection between classical tensor structure and continually updated neural functions, giving the model a way to accommodate an expanding stream without treating each update as an isolated reconstruction problem.
summary.tldr: OFTD combines tensor decomposition, coordinate-based neural representations, and memory replay to complete streaming data while retaining earlier knowledge.

title: Online Functional Tensor Decomposition via Continual Learning for Streaming Data Completion

abstract: A major goal of neuroscience is to understand brain computations during visual processing in naturalistic settings. A dominant approach is to use image-computable deep neural networks trained with different task objectives as a basis for linear encoding models. However, in addition to requiring estimation of a large number of linear encoding parameters, this approach ignores the structure of the feature maps both in the brain and the models. Recently proposed alternatives factor the linear mapping into separate sets of spatial and feature weights, thus finding static receptive fields for units, which is appropriate only for early visual areas. In this work, we employ the attention mechanism used in the transformer architecture to study how retinotopic visual features can be dynamically routed to category-selective areas in high-level visual processing. We show that this computational motif is significantly more powerful than alternative methods in predicting brain activity during natural scene viewing, across different feature basis models and modalities. We also show that this approach is inherently more interpretable as the attention-routing signals for different high-level categorical areas can be easily visualized for any input image. Given its high performance at predicting brain responses to novel images, the model deserves consideration as a candidate mechanistic model of how visual information from retinotopic maps is routed in the human brain based on the relevance of the input content to different category-selective regions. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/Hosseinadeli/transformer_brain_encoder/}{https://github.com/Hosseinadeli/transformer\_brain\_encoder/}.

paragraphs: Predicting brain responses to natural images often involves mapping neural-network features to measured brain activity. The paper argues that conventional linear mappings overlook the spatial and feature structure of those representations. Alternatives with fixed spatial receptive fields are also poorly suited to the dynamic routing involved in high-level visual processing.

The authors use transformer attention to route features organized by visual location toward category-selective brain areas. Because the routing depends on the input image, the model can represent changing relationships between image content and high-level regions. The attention signals can also be visualized, making it possible to inspect how different images direct information toward different categorical areas.

The method predicts brain activity during natural-scene viewing significantly better than the compared alternatives across feature models and measurement modalities. Its performance on novel images motivates the authors to propose it as a candidate mechanistic account of visual routing. That is a proposal supported by predictive and interpretability results, rather than a claim that the brain's routing mechanism has been definitively established.
summary.tldr: Attention-based brain encoders improve visual-response prediction and offer an interpretable candidate model of content-dependent visual routing.

title: Transformer brain encoders explain human high-level visual responses

abstract: While conditional diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in various applications, they require abundant data to train from scratch, which is often infeasible in practice. To address this issue, transfer learning has emerged as an essential paradigm in small data regimes. Despite its empirical success, the theoretical underpinnings of transfer learning conditional diffusion models remain unexplored. In this paper, we take the first step towards understanding the sample efficiency of transfer learning conditional diffusion models through the lens of representation learning. Inspired by practical training procedures, we assume that there exists a low-dimensional representation of conditions shared across all tasks. Our analysis shows that with a well-learned representation from source tasks, the sample complexity of target tasks can be reduced substantially. Numerical experiments are also conducted to verify our results.

paragraphs: Conditional diffusion models often need substantial training data, making training from scratch difficult when a new task has few examples. This paper investigates why transferring knowledge from other tasks can reduce that data requirement. Its focus is theoretical sample efficiency: how learning a reusable representation affects the amount of target-task data needed.

The analysis assumes that the conditions across all tasks share a low-dimensional representation. Under that assumption, source tasks can provide a useful representation before learning the target task. The authors show that a well-learned source representation can substantially reduce the target task’s sample complexity. Both the shared structure and the quality of the learned representation are central to the result.

Numerical experiments are included to verify the theoretical findings. The contribution is an initial explanation of conditional diffusion transfer through representation learning: source-task training can supply compact conditional structure that makes subsequent learning more data-efficient. The stated conclusion concerns tasks satisfying that shared-representation setting, with a sufficiently well-learned representation available for transfer.
summary.tldr: A well-learned shared low-dimensional condition representation can substantially reduce the target-task data needed for conditional diffusion learning.

title: Provable Sample-Efficient Transfer Learning Conditional Diffusion Models via Representation Learning

abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) reasoning tasks require agents to interpret multimodal instructions, perform long-horizon planning, and act adaptively in dynamic environments. Existing approaches typically train VLA models in an end-to-end fashion, directly mapping inputs to actions without explicit reasoning, which hinders their ability to plan over multiple steps or adapt to complex task variations. In this paper, we propose ThinkAct, a dual-system framework that bridges high-level reasoning with low-level action execution via reinforced visual latent planning. ThinkAct trains a multimodal LLM to generate embodied reasoning plans guided by reinforcing action-aligned visual rewards based on goal completion and trajectory consistency. These reasoning plans are compressed into a visual plan latent that conditions a downstream action model for robust action execution on target environments. Extensive experiments on embodied reasoning and robot manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that ThinkAct enables few-shot adaptation, long-horizon planning, and self-correction behaviors in complex embodied AI tasks.

paragraphs: Agents acting from visual and language instructions need to understand goals, plan across several steps, and respond to changing environments. Directly mapping inputs to actions can make those demands difficult to handle. ThinkAct introduces a dual-system design that connects explicit high-level reasoning with a separate model responsible for executing actions.

A multimodal language model learns to produce embodied reasoning plans using reinforcement signals tied to visual evidence of goal completion and trajectory consistency. The plans are compressed into a visual latent representation, which conditions the downstream action model. This intermediate representation provides a connection between the reasoning process and the actions carried out in the target environment.

Experiments on embodied reasoning and robot manipulation benchmarks demonstrate few-shot adaptation, planning over long horizons, and self-correction behavior. The contribution is the combination of planning rewards aligned with action outcomes and a compact representation that carries plans into execution. The reported behaviors indicate that this connection can help agents handle complex tasks requiring more than a direct response to the current input.
summary.tldr: ThinkAct links reinforced multimodal reasoning plans to action execution through a compact visual representation.

title: ThinkAct: Vision-Language-Action Reasoning via Reinforced Visual Latent Planning

abstract: AI systems must adapt to the evolving visual landscape, especially in domains where object appearance shifts over time. While prior work on time-aware vision models has primarily addressed commonsense-level categories, we introduce Car Models in Time (CaMiT). This fine-grained dataset captures the temporal evolution of this representative subset of technological artifacts. CaMiT includes 787K labeled samples of 190 car models (2007–2023) and 5.1M unlabeled samples (2005–2023), supporting supervised and self-supervised learning. We show that static pretraining on in-domain data achieves competitive performance with large-scale generalist models, offering a more resource-efficient solution. However, accuracy degrades when testing a year's models backward and forward in time. To address this, we evaluate CaMiT in a time-incremental classification setting, a realistic continual learning scenario with emerging, evolving, and disappearing classes. We investigate two mitigation strategies: time-incremental pretraining, which updates the backbone model, and time-incremental classifier learning, which updates the final classification layer, with positive results in both cases. Finally, we introduce time-aware image generation by consistently using temporal metadata during training. Results indicate improved realism compared to standard generation. CaMiT provides a rich resource for exploring temporal adaptation in a fine-grained visual context for discriminative and generative AI systems.

paragraphs: Car recognition presents a moving target: models appear, change appearance, and disappear over time. CaMiT makes this temporal evolution available for studying fine-grained vision. It contains 787,000 labeled examples covering 190 car models from 2007–2023, alongside 5.1 million unlabeled examples from 2005–2023. The two portions support learning both with and without explicit labels.

The authors find that static pretraining on car data can compete with large general-purpose models while using resources more efficiently. However, recognition accuracy deteriorates when a model trained for one year's data is evaluated on earlier or later years. They therefore examine continual classification in which the available classes themselves emerge, evolve, or disappear.

Two updating strategies produce positive results: progressively updating the backbone representation and progressively updating the final classifier. The paper also uses temporal metadata consistently during image-generation training, reporting more realistic images than standard generation. Together, these studies make CaMiT useful for investigating how both recognition and generation can adapt to changing object appearance, rather than treating a dataset's visual categories as fixed.
summary.tldr: CaMiT tracks car models through time and shows benefits from updating recognition models and incorporating temporal information into image generation.

title: CaMiT: A Time-Aware Car Model Dataset for Classification and Generation

abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a popular method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of generative models, valued for its simplicity and effectiveness. Despite recent enhancements, LoRA still suffers from a fundamental limitation: overfitting when the bottleneck is widened. It performs best at ranks 32–64, yet its accuracy stagnates or declines at higher ranks, still falling short of full fine-tuning (FFT) performance. We identify the root cause as LoRA’s structural bottleneck, which introduces gradient entanglement to the unrelated input channels and distorts gradient propagation. To address this, we introduce a novel structure, Granular Low-Rank Adaptation (GraLoRA) that partitions weight matrices into sub-blocks, each with its own low-rank adapter. With negligible computational or storage cost, GraLoRA overcomes LoRA’s limitations, effectively increases the representational capacity, and more closely approximates FFT behavior. Experiments on code generation, commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, general language understanding, and image generation benchmarks show that GraLoRA consistently outperforms LoRA and other baselines, achieving up to +8.5\% absolute gain in Pass@1 on HumanEval+. These improvements hold across model sizes and rank settings, making GraLoRA a scalable and robust solution for PEFT.

paragraphs: LoRA adapts a generative model through low-rank updates, reducing the number of parameters that need training. The paper examines why increasing the rank does not reliably improve accuracy. It reports that performance often stagnates or declines beyond the most effective rank range, and attributes this behavior to a structural bottleneck that entangles gradients from unrelated input channels.

title: GraLoRA: Granular Low-Rank Adaptation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning

abstract: Recent efforts to apply Large Language Models (LLMs) to time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) have yielded limited success, often performing worse than even simple methods. While prior work has focused solely on downstream performance evaluation, the fundamental question—why do LLMs struggle with TSAD?—has remained largely unexplored. In this paper, we present an in-depth analysis that identifies two core challenges in understanding complex temporal dynamics and accurately localizing anomalies. To address these challenges, we propose a simple yet effective method that combines statistical decomposition with index-aware prompting. Our method outperforms 21 existing prompting strategies on the AnomLLM benchmark, achieving up to a 66.6\% improvement in F1 score. We further compare LLMs with 16 non-LLM baselines on the TSB-AD benchmark, highlighting scenarios where LLMs offer unique advantages via contextual reasoning. Our findings provide empirical insights into how and when LLMs can be effective for TSAD. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/junwoopark92/LLM-TSAD

paragraphs: Detecting anomalies in a time series requires understanding how measurements evolve and identifying where unusual behavior occurs. The paper investigates why language models have struggled with this task, sometimes trailing simple methods. Its analysis identifies two central difficulties: interpreting complex temporal dynamics and accurately locating anomalies within the sequence.

The proposed method combines statistical decomposition with index-aware prompting. Decomposition separates aspects of the time series to make its structure easier to analyze, while index-aware prompts explicitly address positions in the sequence. The pairing targets both identified weaknesses: understanding the pattern and connecting an anomaly judgment to the appropriate location.

On AnomLLM, the method outperforms 21 existing prompting strategies, with F1 improvements reaching 66.6%. A separate comparison against 16 non-language-model baselines on TSB-AD identifies situations where contextual reasoning gives language models distinctive advantages. The findings therefore concern both how to improve these models and when their reasoning capabilities can be useful; they do not establish that language models dominate every anomaly-detection setting.
summary.tldr: Statistical decomposition and index-aware prompting address language models' temporal understanding and localization weaknesses, improving anomaly detection in the reported benchmarks.

title: Delving into Large Language Models for Effective Time-Series Anomaly Detection

abstract: Recent research on Reasoning of Large Language Models (LLMs) has sought to further enhance their performance by integrating meta-thinking—enabling models to monitor, evaluate, and control their reasoning processes for more adaptive and effective problem-solving. However, current single-agent work lacks a specialized design for acquiring meta-thinking, resulting in low efficacy. To address this challenge, we introduce Reinforced Meta-thinking Agents (ReMA), a novel framework that leverages Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) to elicit meta-thinking behaviors, encouraging LLMs to think about thinking. ReMA decouples the reasoning process into two hierarchical agents: a high-level meta-thinking agent responsible for generating strategic oversight and plans, and a low-level reasoning agent for detailed executions. Through iterative reinforcement learning with aligned objectives, these agents explore and learn collaboration, leading to improved generalization and robustness. Empirical results from single-turn experiments demonstrate that ReMA outperforms single-agent RL baselines on complex reasoning tasks, including competitive-level mathematical benchmarks and LLM-as-a-Judge benchmarks. Additionally, we further extend ReMA to multi-turn interaction settings, leveraging turn-level ratio and parameter sharing to improve efficiency. Comprehensive ablation studies further illustrate the evolving dynamics of each distinct agent, providing valuable insights into how the meta-thinking reasoning process enhances the reasoning capabilities of LLMs.

paragraphs: Meta-thinking means monitoring, evaluating, and directing a reasoning process. ReMA makes this responsibility explicit by dividing problem-solving between two hierarchical language-model agents. A high-level agent develops strategy and oversight, while a low-level agent carries out detailed reasoning. This creates a specialized structure for learning how to manage reasoning.

The agents train through iterative multi-agent reinforcement learning with aligned objectives. They learn to collaborate as planning and execution influence the shared task outcome. The framework aims to improve generalization and robustness through this interaction, giving strategic control a distinct role within the learning process rather than expecting it to emerge within an undifferentiated single-agent procedure.

In single-turn experiments, ReMA outperforms single-agent reinforcement-learning baselines on competitive mathematics and tasks where language models act as judges. The authors also extend the framework to multi-turn interactions, using a turn-level ratio and shared parameters to improve efficiency. Ablation studies examine how the two agents evolve, providing evidence about how their distinct roles contribute to the reported reasoning gains.
summary.tldr: ReMA trains separate planning and execution agents together, improving complex reasoning over single-agent reinforcement-learning baselines in the reported experiments.

title: ReMA: Learning to Meta-Think for LLMs with Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: While large language models (LLMs) are driving the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, effectively and reliably training these large models remains one of the field's most significant challenges. To address this challenge, we propose POET, a novel reParameterized training algorithm that uses Orthogonal Equivalence Transformation to optimize neurons. Specifically, POET reparameterizes each neuron with two learnable orthogonal matrices and a fixed random weight matrix. Because of its provable preservation of spectral properties of weight matrices, POET can stably optimize the objective function with improved generalization. We further develop efficient approximations that make POET flexible and scalable for training large-scale neural networks. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness and scalability of POET in training LLMs.

paragraphs: Training a large language model requires optimizing a large collection of weights reliably. POET approaches this challenge by changing how those weights are represented during optimization. Instead of treating the weight representation as unrestricted, it reparameterizes each neuron using two learnable orthogonal matrices together with a fixed random weight matrix.

The key mathematical feature is that these orthogonal transformations provably preserve the spectral properties of the weight matrices. Training can therefore change the learned representation while maintaining this structure. The authors connect that preservation to stable optimization of the training objective and improved generalization. The proposed benefit comes from constraining the form of learning, with the fixed random matrix and learnable transformations playing distinct roles.

To make the approach practical for large networks, the paper also develops efficient approximations of the training method. These are intended to provide flexibility and scalability beyond the basic formulation. Extensive language-model training experiments support POET’s effectiveness and scalability, presenting structured reparameterization as a promising way to improve the training process itself.
summary.tldr: POET trains language models through learnable orthogonal transformations that preserve weight-matrix spectral properties, supporting stable optimization and improved generalization.

title: Reparameterized LLM Training via Orthogonal Equivalence Transformation

abstract: Adapting a pretrained diffusion model to new objectives at inference time remains an open problem in generative modeling. Existing steering methods suffer from inaccurate value estimation, especially at high noise levels, which biases guidance. Moreover, information from past runs is not reused to improve sample quality, leading to inefficient use of compute. Inspired by the success of Monte Carlo Tree Search, we address these limitations by casting inference-time alignment as a search problem that reuses past computations. We introduce a tree-based approach that _samples_ from the reward-aligned target density by propagating terminal rewards back through the diffusion chain and iteratively refining value estimates with each additional generation. Our proposed method, Diffusion Tree Sampling (DTS), produces asymptotically exact samples from the target distribution in the limit of infinite rollouts, and its greedy variant Diffusion Tree Search (DTS*) performs a robust search for high reward samples. On MNIST and CIFAR-10 class-conditional generation, DTS matches the FID of the best-performing baseline with up to $5\times$ less compute. In text-to-image generation and language completion tasks, DTS* effectively searches for high reward samples that match best-of-N with $2\times$ less compute. By reusing information from previous generations, we get an _anytime algorithm_ that turns additional compute budget into steadily better samples, providing a scalable approach for inference-time alignment of diffusion models.

paragraphs: Diffusion Tree Sampling addresses how to steer a pretrained diffusion model toward a new reward during generation. Earlier steering methods can estimate future value poorly when samples are still very noisy. They also fail to reuse information from previous generations, leaving useful evidence unavailable when deciding where to spend additional computation.

The method organizes generation as a tree search. Rewards from completed samples are passed backward through the diffusion chain, improving value estimates as more generations accumulate. DTS targets sampling from the reward-aligned distribution and becomes exact in the limit of infinitely many rollouts. Its greedy variant, DTS*, instead searches for individual samples with high rewards; these are distinct objectives.

For class-conditional generation on MNIST and CIFAR-10, DTS matches the best baseline's FID using up to five times less computation. For text-to-image generation and language completion, DTS* matches best-of-N reward search with two times less computation. Reusing earlier results makes the approach an anytime algorithm, allowing additional computation to progressively improve samples rather than repeatedly starting independent searches.
summary.tldr: Diffusion Tree Sampling reuses rewards from previous generations to improve diffusion guidance and reduce the computation needed for aligned outputs.

title: Diffusion Tree Sampling: Scalable inference‑time alignment of diffusion models

abstract: Diffusion- and flow-based models have emerged as state-of-the-art generative modeling approaches, but they require many sampling steps. Consistency models can distill these models into efficient one-step generators; however, unlike flow- and diffusion-based methods, their performance inevitably degrades when increasing the number of steps, which we show both analytically and empirically. Flow maps generalize these approaches by connecting any two noise levels in a single step and remain effective across all step counts. In this paper, we introduce two new continuous-time objectives for training flow maps, along with additional novel training techniques, generalizing existing consistency and flow matching objectives. We further demonstrate that autoguidance can improve performance, using a low-quality model for guidance during distillation, and an additional boost can be achieved by adversarial finetuning, with minimal loss in sample diversity. We extensively validate our flow map models, called *Align Your Flow*, on challenging image generation benchmarks and achieve state-of-the-art few-step generation performance on both ImageNet 64x64 and 512x512, using small and efficient neural networks. Finally, we show text-to-image flow map models that outperform all existing non-adversarially trained few-step samplers in text-conditioned synthesis.

paragraphs: Diffusion and flow models generate strong images but often require many sampling steps. Consistency models compress generation into one step, yet the authors show analytically and empirically that their performance degrades as the number of steps increases. This motivates flow maps, which connect any two noise levels in one step and remain effective across step counts.

Align Your Flow introduces two continuous-time objectives for learning these maps, together with additional training techniques. The objectives generalize existing consistency and flow-matching objectives. The authors also use autoguidance, where a lower-quality model supplies guidance during distillation. Adversarial fine-tuning provides another improvement, with a reported minimal reduction in sample diversity.

On ImageNet at 64-by-64 and 512-by-512 resolution, the resulting models achieve state-of-the-art few-step generation performance using small, efficient networks. The text-to-image models also outperform existing few-step samplers that were trained without adversarial methods. These findings support flow maps as a way to make compressed generators effective under different sampling budgets, instead of optimizing only for a single generation step.
summary.tldr: Align Your Flow trains continuous-time flow maps for strong few-step image generation across different sampling step counts.

title: Align Your Flow: Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation

abstract: Structural pruning enhances hardware-agnostic inference efficiency for large language models (LLMs) yet often fails to maintain comparable performance. Local pruning performs efficient layer-by-layer compression but ignores global topology. Although global pruning aims to identify an optimal sparse model, intuitive methods typically adopt a two-stage paradigm that first evaluates substructure saliency and then applies global pruning, which ignores inter-structure dependencies and fails to achieve end-to-end optimization. To address these limitations, we propose Týr-the-Pruner, an efficient end-to-end search-based global structural pruning framework. This framework constructs a supernet by repeatedly applying local pruning across a range of sparsity ratios to each layer in an LLM, with the core goal of determining the optimal sparsity distribution under a target overall sparsity ratio. Concretely, we introduce an effective local pruning and an expectation error accumulation approach to improve supernet construction. Furthermore, we employ an iterative prune-and-search strategy with coarse-to-fine sparsity granularity to ensure efficient search convergence. Experimental results show that Týr-the-Pruner achieves state-of-the-art structural pruning, retaining 97% of the dense model's performance while removing a challenging 50% of Llama-3.1-70B's parameters.

paragraphs: Structural pruning removes parts of a language model to improve inference efficiency, but deciding what to remove can sharply affect performance. Layer-by-layer pruning overlooks the model's global structure. The paper also critiques global methods that first score components and then prune them, because separating these stages can miss dependencies between structures.

Týr-the-Pruner searches for how sparsity should be distributed across layers under an overall pruning target. It builds a supernet containing locally pruned alternatives at different sparsity levels for each layer. Improved local pruning and expectation error accumulation support supernet construction. An iterative prune-and-search process starts with coarse sparsity choices and refines them to make convergence efficient.

The authors report state-of-the-art structural pruning results, including retention of 97% of the dense model's performance after removing 50% of Llama-3.1-70B's parameters. That result concerns the reported performance evaluation. The broader contribution is to treat compression as a coordinated allocation problem across the whole network, using end-to-end search to account for interactions that isolated pruning decisions overlook.
summary.tldr: Týr-the-Pruner searches globally for layerwise sparsity allocations, retaining 97% of reported dense-model performance while pruning half of Llama-3.1-70B's parameters.

title: Týr-the-Pruner: Structural Pruning LLMs via Global Sparsity Distribution Optimization

abstract: We consider the problem of diversity maximization from the perspective of individual fairness: given a set $P$ of $n$ points in a metric space, we aim to extract a subset $S$ of size $k$ from $P$ so that (1) the diversity of $S$ is maximized and (2) $S$ is \emph{individually fair} in the sense that every point in $P$ has at least one of its $\frac{n}{k}$-nearest neighbors as its ``representative'' in $S$. We propose $\left(O(1), 3\right)$-bicriteria approximation algorithms for the individually fair variants of the three most common diversity maximization problems, namely, max-min diversification, max-sum diversification, and sum-min diversification. Specifically, the proposed algorithms provide a set of points where every point in the dataset finds a point within a distance at most $3$ times its distance to its $\frac{n}{k}$-nearest neighbor while achieving a diversity value at most $O(1)$ times lower than the optimal solution. Numerical experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed algorithms generate solutions that are individually fairer than those produced by unconstrained algorithms and incur only modest losses in diversity.

paragraphs: Selecting a diverse subset can leave some members of a dataset poorly represented. This paper combines diversity maximization with an individual fairness requirement: every point should have a selected representative among its n/k nearest neighbors, where n is the dataset size and k is the number selected. Representation is therefore judged relative to each point's local neighborhood.

The authors develop approximation algorithms for three common diversity objectives: max-min, max-sum, and sum-min diversification. Their guarantees allow controlled compromises on both goals. Every point receives a representative within three times its distance to its n/k-th nearest neighbor, while the selected subset's diversity stays within a constant factor of the optimal value.

This is a bicriteria guarantee because it bounds both the relaxation of fairness and the loss in diversity. It does not promise exact satisfaction of the original nearest-neighbor requirement. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show fairer representation than unconstrained algorithms, with only modest diversity losses, illustrating how the two goals can be balanced in practice.
summary.tldr: The paper gives diversity-selection algorithms with constant-factor diversity guarantees and a threefold relaxation of an individual representation requirement.

title: Individually Fair Diversity Maximization

abstract: We propose two simple, principled and practical algorithms that enjoy provable scaling laws for the test-time compute of large language models (LLMs). The first one is a two-stage knockout-style algorithm: given an input problem, it first generates multiple candidate solutions, and then aggregate them via a knockout tournament for the final output. Assuming that the LLM can generate a correct solution with non-zero probability and do better than a random guess in comparing a pair of correct and incorrect solutions, we prove theoretically that the failure probability of this algorithm decays to zero exponentially or by a power law (depending on the specific way of scaling) as its test-time compute grows. The second one is a two-stage league-style algorithm, where each candidate is evaluated by its average win rate against multiple opponents, rather than eliminated upon loss to a single opponent. Under analogous but more robust assumptions, we prove that its failure probability also decays to zero exponentially with more test-time compute. Both algorithms require a black-box LLM and nothing else (e.g., no verifier or reward model) for a minimalistic implementation, which makes them appealing for practical applications and easy to adapt for different tasks. Through extensive experiments with diverse models and datasets, we validate the proposed theories and demonstrate the outstanding scaling properties of both algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies how additional inference computation can systematically reduce a language model’s chance of producing an incorrect answer. Both proposed algorithms first generate candidate solutions and then use the model to compare them. A minimal implementation needs only black-box access to the model, without a separate verifier or reward model.

The first algorithm selects a winner through a knockout tournament. Its guarantee assumes that the model has a nonzero chance of generating a correct solution and is better than random when comparing a correct solution with an incorrect one. Under those assumptions, failure probability approaches zero exponentially or according to a power law, depending on how computation is increased.

The second algorithm uses a league structure, scoring each candidate by its average win rate against multiple opponents. Under analogous but more robust assumptions, its failure probability decreases exponentially with additional computation. Experiments across multiple models and datasets support the predicted scaling behavior. The contribution provides conditional guarantees for turning generation and comparison into increasingly reliable answers, together with simple procedures for implementing that allocation of compute.
summary.tldr: Knockout and league-style candidate selection provide provable reductions in failure probability as inference compute grows, under stated generation and comparison assumptions.

title: Provable Scaling Laws for the Test-Time Compute of Large Language Models

abstract: Empirical evaluation of trust and manipulation in large-scale collective intelligence processes is challenging. The datasets involved are too large for thorough manual study, and current automated options are limited. We introduce a statistical framework which classifies point of view based on user interactions. The framework works on Web-scale datasets and is applicable to a wide variety of collective intelligence processes. It enables principled study of such issues as manipulation, trustworthiness of information, and potential bias. We demonstrate the model’s effectiveness in determining point of view on both synthetic data and a dataset of Wikipedia user interactions. We build a combined model of topics and points-of-view on the entire history of English Wikipedia, and show how it can be used to find potentially biased articles and visualize user interactions at a high level.

paragraphs: Large collaborative information systems contain more activity than researchers can thoroughly inspect by hand. This makes it difficult to study manipulation, information trustworthiness, and possible bias. The paper introduces a statistical framework that classifies points of view from user interactions, providing an automated way to investigate these questions at Web scale.

The central move is to use interactions as evidence about viewpoint. The framework is intended for a variety of collective intelligence processes, and the authors demonstrate its effectiveness on synthetic data and Wikipedia interactions. This connects the statistical task of identifying viewpoints with the practical task of understanding how participants relate to one another in a large collaborative setting.

The authors also construct a joint model of topics and points of view using the entire history of English Wikipedia. They show how this model can flag potentially biased articles and produce high-level visualizations of user interactions. Those outputs support investigation: identifying potential bias does not itself establish that an article is biased or that a participant is manipulating information.
summary.tldr: A scalable statistical framework infers viewpoints from user interactions and helps identify potentially biased content in collaborative systems.

title: Automated inference of point of view from user interactions in collective intelligence venues

abstract: This paper presents Yinyang K-means, a new algorithm for K-means clustering. By clustering the centers in the initial stage, and leveraging efficiently maintained lower and upper bounds between a point and centers, it more effectively avoids unnecessary distance calculations than prior algorithms. It significantly outperforms classic K-means and prior alternative K-means algorithms consistently across all experimented data sets, cluster numbers, and machine configurations. The consistent, superior performance—plus its simplicity, user-control of overheads, and guarantee in producing the same clustering results as the standard K-means does—makes Yinyang K-means a drop-in replacement of the classic K-means with an order of magnitude higher performance.
