paragraphs: Yinyang K-means accelerates K-means clustering by avoiding distance calculations that are unnecessary for the final result. The method first groups the cluster centers. It then maintains lower and upper distance bounds between data points and centers, using those bounds to determine when further distance evaluation can be skipped.

The bounds are maintained efficiently, and the paper reports that this organization eliminates unnecessary calculations more effectively than earlier algorithms. Crucially, the method guarantees the same clustering results as standard K-means. Its acceleration therefore comes from reducing computation while preserving the clustering outcome, making it suitable as a replacement within an existing K-means workflow.

Across all tested datasets, cluster counts, and machine configurations, the authors report significant speed improvements over classic K-means and prior alternatives, describing an order-of-magnitude performance gain. The abstract also highlights simplicity and user control over overheads. These findings support the method’s practical appeal across the evaluated settings, with the result-preservation guarantee providing a separate reason that adopting the faster computation can be straightforward.
summary.tldr: Yinyang K-means skips unnecessary distance calculations while preserving standard K-means results and delivering consistent speedups across the tested settings.

title: Yinyang K-Means: A Drop-In Replacement of the Classic K-Means with Consistent Speedup

abstract: We consider the problem of building probabilistic models that jointly model short natural language utterances and source code snippets. The aim is to bring together recent work on statistical modelling of source code and work on bimodal models of images and natural language. The resulting models are useful for a variety of tasks that involve natural language and source code. We demonstrate their performance on two retrieval tasks: retrieving source code snippets given a natural language query, and retrieving natural language descriptions given a source code query (i.e., source code captioning). The experiments show there to be promise in this direction, and that modelling the structure of source code is helpful towards the retrieval tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to connect short descriptions in ordinary language with snippets of source code. It builds probabilistic models that represent both kinds of information jointly. The motivation is to bring together statistical modeling of code and the idea of learning relationships between two different forms of data, previously explored for images and language.

The authors evaluate the models in two retrieval directions. In one, a natural language query is used to retrieve a relevant code snippet. In the other, a code query retrieves a natural language description. The paper calls this second task source code captioning, but the demonstrated task is retrieval of descriptions rather than a claim about unrestricted generation of new explanations.

The experiments indicate that joint modeling is promising for these tasks. They also show that representing the structure of source code helps retrieval. That finding gives the work a specific methodological message: the organization of code contributes useful information when connecting programs to language, beyond simply placing the two kinds of data in a shared modeling problem.
summary.tldr: Joint probabilistic models connect code snippets with natural language, with code structure helping retrieval in both directions.

title: Bimodal Modelling of Source Code and Natural Language

abstract: Over the past decade, Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and specifically Upper Confidence Bound in Trees (UCT) have proven to be quite effective in large probabilistic planning domains. In this paper, we focus on how values are backpropagated in the MCTS tree, and apply complex return strategies from the Reinforcement Learning (RL) literature to MCTS, producing 4 new MCTS variants. We demonstrate that in some probabilistic planning benchmarks from the International Planning Competition (IPC), selecting a MCTS variant with a backup strategy different from Monte Carlo averaging can lead to substantially better results. We also propose a hypothesis for why different backup strategies lead to different performance in particular environments, and manipulate a carefully structured grid-world domain to provide empirical evidence supporting our hypothesis.

In this paper, we focus on how values are backpropagated in the MCTS tree, and apply complex return strategies from the Reinforcement Learning (RL) literature to MCTS, producing 4 new MCTS variants. We demonstrate that in some probabilistic planning benchmarks from the International Planning Competition (IPC), selecting a MCTS variant with a backup strategy different from Monte Carlo averaging can lead to substantially better results. We also propose a hypothesis for why different backup strategies lead to different performance in particular environments, and manipulate a carefully structured grid-world domain to provide empirical evidence supporting our hypothesis.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo tree search uses simulated outcomes to guide planning, and its backup strategy determines how those outcomes update values within the search tree. This paper focuses on that update process. It asks whether more complex return strategies from reinforcement learning can improve planning compared with backing up values through Monte Carlo averaging.

The authors transfer these strategies into tree search and construct four new variants. On some probabilistic planning benchmarks from the International Planning Competition, choosing a variant with a different backup strategy produces substantially better results. The qualification is central: the finding concerns particular benchmark environments, rather than identifying one backup strategy as uniformly best.

The paper also proposes a hypothesis explaining why backup strategies perform differently across environments. To investigate it, the authors manipulate a carefully structured grid-world and obtain empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis. This adds an explanatory component to the comparisons, connecting the choice of value update to environmental characteristics and showing that backup design can materially affect search performance.
summary.tldr: Alternative value-backup strategies substantially improve Monte Carlo tree search on some planning benchmarks.

title: On the Analysis of Complex Backup Strategies in Monte Carlo Tree Search

abstract: Labeled training data is an essential part of any supervised machine learning framework. In practice, there is a trade-off between the quality of a label and its cost. In this paper, we consider a problem of learning to rank on a large-scale dataset with low-quality relevance labels aiming at maximizing the quality of a trained ranker on a small validation dataset with high-quality ground truth relevance labels. Motivated by the classical Gauss-Markov theorem for the linear regression problem, we formulate the problems of (1) reweighting training instances and (2) remapping learning targets. We propose meta–gradient decision tree learning framework for optimizing weight and target functions by applying gradient-based hyperparameter optimization. Experiments on a large-scale real-world dataset demonstrate that we can significantly improve state-of-the-art machine-learning algorithms by incorporating our framework.

In this paper, we consider a problem of learning to rank on a large-scale dataset with low-quality relevance labels aiming at maximizing the quality of a trained ranker on a small validation dataset with high-quality ground truth relevance labels. Motivated by the classical Gauss-Markov theorem for the linear regression problem, we formulate the problems of (1) reweighting training instances and (2) remapping learning targets. We propose meta–gradient decision tree learning framework for optimizing weight and target functions by applying gradient-based hyperparameter optimization. Experiments on a large-scale real-world dataset demonstrate that we can significantly improve state-of-the-art machine-learning algorithms by incorporating our framework.

paragraphs: The paper studies ranking when a large training dataset has low-quality relevance labels but a smaller validation dataset has high-quality labels. The objective is to use the abundant training data in a way that maximizes ranking quality on the more trustworthy validation set. This directly addresses the practical trade-off between label quality and acquisition cost.

The authors formulate two adjustments: changing the weights assigned to training instances and remapping their learning targets. Motivated by the Gauss–Markov theorem for linear regression, they develop a meta-gradient decision-tree framework that learns these weight and target functions through gradient-based hyperparameter optimization.

The higher-quality validation labels guide how the lower-quality training information is used. Weight learning changes the influence of examples, while target learning changes what the ranker is asked to predict from them. Experiments on a large real-world dataset report significant improvements when the framework is incorporated into state-of-the-art learning algorithms. The results support optimizing the treatment of imperfect labels as part of training the ranker.
summary.tldr: A meta-gradient tree framework uses high-quality validation labels to learn training weights and targets for ranking with noisy labels.

title: Meta–Gradient Boosted Decision Tree Model for Weight and Target Learning

abstract: In the context of supervised tensor learning, preserving the structural information and exploiting the discriminative nonlinear relationships of tensor data are crucial for improving the performance of learning tasks. Based on tensor factorization theory and kernel methods, we propose a novel Kernelized Support Tensor Machine (KSTM) which integrates kernelized tensor factorization with maximum-margin criterion. Specifically, the kernelized factorization technique is introduced to approximate the tensor data in kernel space such that the complex nonlinear relationships within tensor data can be explored. Further, dual structural preserving kernels are devised to learn the nonlinear boundary between tensor data. As a result of joint optimization, the kernels obtained in KSTM exhibit better generalization power to discriminative analysis. The experimental results on real-world neuroimaging datasets show the superiority of KSTM over the state-of-the-art techniques.

Based on tensor factorization theory and kernel methods, we propose a novel Kernelized Support Tensor Machine (KSTM) which integrates kernelized tensor factorization with maximum-margin criterion. Specifically, the kernelized factorization technique is introduced to approximate the tensor data in kernel space such that the complex nonlinear relationships within tensor data can be explored. Further, dual structural preserving kernels are devised to learn the nonlinear boundary between tensor data. As a result of joint optimization, the kernels obtained in KSTM exhibit better generalization power to discriminative analysis. The experimental results on real-world neuroimaging datasets show the superiority of KSTM over the state-of-the-art techniques.

paragraphs: The paper addresses supervised learning from tensor data, where retaining structural information and capturing nonlinear relationships are both important. Its Kernelized Support Tensor Machine combines tensor factorization with kernel methods and a maximum-margin learning criterion. The aim is to make those aspects work together in a discriminative model.

Kernelized factorization approximates the tensor data in kernel space, giving the model a way to explore complex nonlinear relationships within the data. Two structure-preserving kernels are then designed to learn nonlinear boundaries between tensor examples. Joint optimization connects the learned kernels with the task of distinguishing those examples.

The authors report that this joint treatment produces kernels with better generalization for discriminative analysis. Experiments on real-world neuroimaging datasets show superior performance to the state-of-the-art techniques considered. The contribution brings structural preservation and nonlinear discrimination into one learning formulation, with empirical evidence from neuroimaging that the combined approach improves the evaluated prediction tasks.
summary.tldr: Kernelized Support Tensor Machines jointly learn structure-preserving nonlinear representations and maximum-margin discrimination for tensor data.

title: Kernelized Support Tensor Machines

abstract: We propose a novel approach to the problem of multilevel clustering, which aims to simultaneously partition data in each group and discover grouping patterns among groups in a potentially large hierarchically structured corpus of data. Our method involves a joint optimization formulation over several spaces of discrete probability measures, which are endowed with Wasserstein distance metrics. We propose a number of variants of this problem, which admit fast optimization algorithms, by exploiting the connection to the problem of finding Wasserstein barycenters. Consistency properties are established for the estimates of both local and global clusters. Finally, experiment results with both synthetic and real data are presented to demonstrate the flexibility and scalability of the proposed approach.
originalAbstract: We propose a novel approach to the problem of multilevel clustering, which aims to simultaneously partition data in each group and discover grouping patterns among groups in a potentially large hierarchically structured corpus of data. Our method involves a joint optimization formulation over several spaces of discrete probability measures, which are endowed with Wasserstein distance metrics. We propose a number of variants of this problem, which admit fast optimization algorithms, by exploiting the connection to the problem of finding Wasserstein barycenters. Consistency properties are established for the estimates of both local and global clusters. Finally, experiment results with both synthetic and real data are presented to demonstrate the flexibility and scalability of the proposed approach.

The paper addresses these questions together for hierarchically organized data. This joint view matters because local clusters and broader relationships among groups are parts of the same modeling problem.

The authors formulate an optimization problem over several spaces of discrete probability measures, using Wasserstein distances to compare them. They connect this formulation to Wasserstein barycenters, which serve as representative centers for distributions. That connection leads to several variants of the problem with fast optimization algorithms.

The paper establishes consistency properties for estimates of both local and global clusters, giving theoretical support at each level of the hierarchy. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate the proposed approach's flexibility and scalability. The contribution is a shared mathematical framework for discovering structure within groups and across groups, together with computational variants and statistical results that address both levels rather than treating them as unrelated clustering tasks.
summary.tldr: A Wasserstein-based framework jointly discovers clusters within groups and patterns across groups, with consistency results and fast optimization variants.

title: Multilevel Clustering via Wasserstein Means

abstract: We propose a randomized first order optimization algorithm Gradient Projection Iterative Sketch (GPIS) and an accelerated variant for efficiently solving large scale constrained Least Squares (LS). We provide the first theoretical convergence analysis for both algorithms. An efficient implementation using a tailored line-search scheme is also proposed. We demonstrate our methods’ computational efficiency compared to the classical accelerated gradient method, and the variance-reduced stochastic gradient methods through numerical experiments in various large synthetic/real data sets.
originalAbstract: We propose a randomized first order optimization algorithm Gradient Projection Iterative Sketch (GPIS) and an accelerated variant for efficiently solving large scale constrained Least Squares (LS). We provide the first theoretical convergence analysis for both algorithms. An efficient implementation using a tailored line-search scheme is also proposed. We demonstrate our methods’ computational efficiency compared to the classical accelerated gradient method, and the variance-reduced stochastic gradient methods through numerical experiments in various large synthetic/real data sets.

paragraphs: This paper targets large-scale constrained least-squares problems, where an optimization method must reduce fitting error while respecting restrictions on the solution. Its proposed method, Gradient Projection Iterative Sketch, is a randomized first-order algorithm. The authors also develop an accelerated version, providing two related approaches to the same computational task.

The theoretical contribution is a convergence analysis for both algorithms. Such analysis connects the proposed iterative procedures to their behavior as optimization proceeds. The paper also addresses implementation through a tailored line-search scheme. This gives the method a concrete way to choose update sizes as part of an efficient implementation.

Numerical experiments cover multiple large synthetic and real datasets. The authors report computational efficiency relative to a classical accelerated gradient method and variance-reduced stochastic gradient methods. These comparisons place the proposed algorithms alongside established approaches to large optimization problems. The overall contribution combines algorithm design, convergence theory, and an implementation strategy, with experiments supporting the computational usefulness of the resulting methods for constrained least squares.
summary.tldr: Gradient Projection Iterative Sketch and its accelerated variant combine randomized first-order optimization with convergence guarantees for large constrained least-squares problems.

title: Gradient Projection Iterative Sketch for Large-Scale Constrained Least-Squares

abstract: Prediction suffix trees (PST) provide an effective tool for sequence modelling and prediction. Current prediction techniques for PSTs rely on exact matching between the suffix of the current sequence and the previously observed sequence. We present a provably correct algorithm for learning a PST with approximate suffix matching by relaxing the exact matching condition. We then present a self-bounded enhancement of our algorithm where the depth of suffix tree grows automatically in response to the model performance on a training sequence. Through experiments on synthetic datasets as well as three real-world datasets, we show that the approximate matching PST results in better predictive performance than the other variants of PST.

paragraphs: Prediction suffix trees model sequences using patterns at the ends of previously observed sequences. Existing prediction techniques rely on an exact match between the current suffix and an observed one. This paper relaxes that requirement, allowing approximate suffix matches to contribute to sequence modeling and prediction.

The authors present a learning algorithm for this approximate-matching setting and prove its correctness. They then add a self-bounded version in which the tree’s depth grows automatically in response to performance on the training sequence. Depth controls how much preceding sequence information the tree can represent, so this enhancement connects model growth to observed learning behavior.

Experiments use synthetic data and three real-world datasets. The approximate-matching prediction suffix tree achieves better predictive performance than the other suffix-tree variants evaluated. The findings support relaxing exact matching as a useful change to this model family, while the self-bounded enhancement provides a mechanism for adapting the amount of sequence history represented during training.
summary.tldr: Approximate suffix matching improves reported sequence predictions, with an enhancement that grows tree depth in response to training performance.

title: Self-Bounded Prediction Suffix Tree via Approximate String Matching

abstract: K-means clustering algorithm using Lloyd’s heuristic is one of the most commonly used tools in data mining and machine learning that shows promising performance. However, it suffers from a high computational cost resulting from pairwise Euclidean distance computations between data points and cluster centers in each iteration of Lloyd’s heuristic. Main contributing factor of this computational bottle neck is a matrix-vector multiplication step, where the matrix contains all the data points and the vector is a cluster center. In this paper we show that we can randomly sparsify the original data matrix resulting in a sparse data matrix which can significantly speed up the above mentioned matrix vector multiplication step without significantly affecting cluster quality. In particular, we show that optimal k-means clustering solution of the sparse data matrix, obtained by applying random matrix sparsification, results in an approximately optimal k-means clustering objective of the original data matrix. Our empirical studies on three real world datasets corroborate our theoretical findings and demonstrate that our proposed sparsification method can indeed achieve satisfactory clustering performance.

paragraphs: Lloyd's heuristic for k-means repeatedly compares data points with cluster centers. These distance calculations can be expensive, with a major bottleneck arising from multiplying the data matrix by vectors representing centers. The paper targets this numerical operation by randomly sparsifying the original data matrix before clustering.

A sparse matrix permits faster matrix-vector multiplication, but the essential question is whether the modified data still support good clusters for the original data. The authors establish that an optimal k-means solution on the sparsified matrix gives an approximately optimal objective value on the original matrix. This is a guarantee about the optimal solution of the sparse problem; it does not turn Lloyd's heuristic into an exact optimizer.

Experiments on three real-world datasets support the theoretical findings and show satisfactory clustering performance. The practical appeal is that reducing the amount of matrix data involved in computation can accelerate an expensive step without significantly harming cluster quality. The paper thus links a numerical simplification to an explicit guarantee about the original clustering objective.
summary.tldr: Randomly sparsifying the data matrix speeds k-means computations while preserving an approximate-optimality connection to the original clustering problem.

title: K-means clustering using random matrix sparsification

abstract: In the context of individual-level causal inference, we study the problem of predicting whether someone will respond or not to a treatment based on their features and past examples of features, treatment indicator (e.g., drug/no drug), and a binary outcome (e.g., recovery from disease). As a classification task, the problem is made difficult by not knowing the example outcomes under the opposite treatment indicators. We assume the effect is monotonic, as in advertising’s effect on a purchase or bail-setting’s effect on reappearance in court: either it would have happened regardless of treatment, not happened regardless, or happened only depending on exposure to treatment. Predicting whether the latter is latently the case is our focus. While previous work focuses on conditional average treatment effect estimation, formulating the problem as a classification task allows us to develop new tools more suited to this problem. By leveraging monotonicity, we develop new discriminative and generative algorithms for the responder-classification problem. We explore and discuss connections to corrupted data and policy learning. We provide an empirical study with both synthetic and real datasets to compare these specialized algorithms to standard benchmarks.

We assume the effect is monotonic, as in advertising’s effect on a purchase or bail-setting’s effect on reappearance in court: either it would have happened regardless of treatment, not happened regardless, or happened only depending on exposure to treatment. Predicting whether the latter is latently the case is our focus. While previous work focuses on conditional average treatment effect estimation, formulating the problem as a classification task allows us to develop new tools more suited to this problem. By leveraging monotonicity, we develop new discriminative and generative algorithms for the responder-classification problem. We explore and discuss connections to corrupted data and policy learning. We provide an empirical study with both synthetic and real datasets to compare these specialized algorithms to standard benchmarks.

paragraphs: Predicting whether an outcome will occur differs from predicting whether treatment will change that outcome. A person might experience the outcome regardless of treatment, or never experience it either way. This paper focuses on identifying responders: people whose binary outcome depends on whether they receive treatment. Training examples reveal only the outcome under the treatment actually received.

The authors assume monotonicity of the treatment effect, excluding effects in the opposite direction. Under this assumption, the relevant categories are those whose outcome occurs either way, those whose outcome never occurs, and those whose outcome changes with treatment. The task is to predict membership in the last category from features despite the unobserved alternative outcome.

The paper formulates this as classification and develops both discriminative and generative algorithms using monotonicity. This changes the target from estimating a conditional average treatment effect to recognizing individual response categories. It also explores connections with corrupted data and policy learning. Synthetic and real datasets provide comparisons with standard benchmarks, although the abstract does not claim a particular performance advantage.
summary.tldr: Under a monotonicity assumption, the paper develops classifiers for identifying people whose binary outcomes would change because of treatment.

title: Classifying Treatment Responders Under Causal Effect Monotonicity

abstract: We present algorithms for efficiently learning regularizers that improve generalization. Our approach is based on the insight that regularizers can be viewed as upper bounds on the generalization gap, and that reducing the slack in the bound can improve performance on test data. For a broad class of regularizers, the hyperparameters that give the best upper bound can be computed using linear programming. Under certain Bayesian assumptions, solving the LP lets us "jump" to the optimal hyperparameters given very limited data. This suggests a natural algorithm for tuning regularization hyperparameters, which we show to be effective on both real and synthetic data.

Our approach is based on the insight that regularizers can be viewed as upper bounds on the generalization gap, and that reducing the slack in the bound can improve performance on test data. For a broad class of regularizers, the hyperparameters that give the best upper bound can be computed using linear programming. Under certain Bayesian assumptions, solving the LP lets us "jump" to the optimal hyperparameters given very limited data. This suggests a natural algorithm for tuning regularization hyperparameters, which we show to be effective on both real and synthetic data.

paragraphs: Regularization aims to improve how a learned model performs beyond its training data, but choosing its strength or other hyperparameters can be difficult. This paper approaches that choice through the generalization gap. It views regularizers as upper bounds on that gap and seeks to reduce the extra slack in those bounds.

For a broad class of regularizers, the hyperparameters producing the best upper bound can be found with linear programming. This turns the bound-based selection problem into a structured optimization task. Tightening the bound can improve test performance, providing the motivation for using this calculation to guide regularization.

Under certain Bayesian assumptions, solving the linear program allows a direct move to optimal hyperparameters using very limited data. That conditional result motivates a practical tuning algorithm, whose effectiveness is demonstrated on real and synthetic datasets. The distinction matters: the optimality claim relies on the stated assumptions, while the experiments support the usefulness of the resulting tuning approach in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: The paper tunes regularizers through linear-programming bounds on generalization, with direct optimal selection under certain Bayesian assumptions.

title: Learning Optimal Linear Regularizers

abstract: Motivated by high-stakes decision-making domains like personalized medicine where user information is inherently sensitive, we design privacy preserving exploration policies for episodic reinforcement learning (RL). We first provide a meaningful privacy formulation using the notion of joint differential privacy (JDP)–a strong variant of differential privacy for settings where each user receives their own sets of output (e.g., policy recommendations). We then develop a private optimism-based learning algorithm that simultaneously achieves strong PAC and regret bounds, and enjoys a JDP guarantee. Our algorithm only pays for a moderate privacy cost on exploration: in comparison to the non-private bounds, the privacy parameter only appears in lower-order terms. Finally, we present lower bounds on sample complexity and regret for reinforcement learning subject to JDP.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can involve sensitive information when different users receive personalized decisions. This paper develops privacy-preserving exploration for episodic learning, motivated by settings such as personalized medicine. It formulates privacy using joint differential privacy, a variant designed for situations where each user receives their own outputs, including policy recommendations.

The authors introduce an optimism-based private learning algorithm with both PAC and regret guarantees. These capture complementary aspects of learning performance: obtaining sufficiently good behavior and controlling the accumulated cost of learning. The algorithm provides these guarantees while satisfying the proposed joint differential privacy requirement.

Compared with the non-private bounds, the privacy parameter appears only in lower-order terms. This supports the authors’ conclusion that privacy adds a moderate exploration cost within their analysis. The paper also derives lower bounds on sample complexity and regret under joint differential privacy. Together, these results characterize both an achievable learning performance and fundamental constraints on private episodic reinforcement learning, connecting privacy protection directly to the cost of exploration.
summary.tldr: An episodic reinforcement learning algorithm achieves joint differential privacy with PAC and regret guarantees whose privacy costs appear only in lower-order terms.

title: Private Reinforcement Learning with PAC and Regret Guarantees

abstract: In learning with noisy labels, for every instance, its label can randomly walk to other classes following a transition distribution which is named a noise model. Well-studied noise models are all instance-independent, namely, the transition depends only on the original label but not the instance itself, and thus they are less practical in the wild. Fortunately, methods based on instance-dependent noise have been studied, but most of them have to rely on strong assumptions on the noise models. To alleviate this issue, we introduce confidence-scored instance-dependent noise (CSIDN), where each instance-label pair is equipped with a confidence score. We find that with the help of confidence scores, the transition distribution of each instance can be approximately estimated. Similarly to the powerful forward correction for instance-independent noise, we propose a novel instance-level forward correction for CSIDN. We demonstrate the utility and effectiveness of our method through multiple experiments on datasets with synthetic label noise and real-world unknown noise.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can arise differently for different examples, even when those examples belong to the same class. Many established noise models simplify this situation by making label corruption depend only on the original class. Models that account for the example itself are more flexible, but existing approaches often require strong assumptions about how the corruption occurs.

The paper introduces confidence-scored instance-dependent noise, in which every example and its observed label come with a confidence score. The authors show that these scores help approximately estimate each example's transition distribution: the probabilities governing how its label could change to other classes. This additional information provides a way to handle variation in label reliability across individual examples.

Using those estimates, the authors develop an instance-level version of forward correction, extending an approach previously used for instance-independent noise. Experiments with synthetic corruption and real-world unknown noise demonstrate the method's usefulness. The contribution is therefore a confidence-assisted correction framework; its transition estimates remain approximate, and the setting explicitly includes confidence scores as additional information.
summary.tldr: Confidence scores enable approximate estimation of example-specific label noise and support a corresponding training correction.

title: Confidence Scores Make Instance-dependent Label-noise Learning Possible

abstract: Understanding the fundamental mechanism behind the success of deep neural networks is one of the key challenges in the modern machine learning literature. Despite numerous attempts, a solid theoretical analysis is yet to be developed. In this paper, we develop a novel unified framework to reveal a hidden regularization mechanism through the lens of convex optimization. We first show that the training of multiple three-layer ReLU sub-networks with weight decay regularization can be equivalently cast as a convex optimization problem in a higher dimensional space, where sparsity is enforced via a group $\ell_1$-norm regularization. Consequently, ReLU networks can be interpreted as high dimensional feature selection methods. More importantly, we then prove that the equivalent convex problem can be globally optimized by a standard convex optimization solver with a polynomial-time complexity with respect to the number of samples and data dimension when the width of the network is fixed. Finally, we numerically validate our theoretical results via experiments involving both synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: This paper uses convex optimization to examine the structure hidden inside a neural network training problem. It considers multiple three-layer ReLU subnetworks trained with weight decay. The authors show that this training problem has an equivalent convex formulation in a higher-dimensional space, providing another way to understand both its optimization and its regularization.

In the convex formulation, regularization takes the form of a group l1 penalty that promotes sparsity across groups. This reveals a feature-selection interpretation of the networks: the equivalent problem selects among high-dimensional features while controlling their complexity. The equivalence makes the regularizing effect of weight decay visible through a different mathematical representation.

The authors further prove that a standard convex solver can globally optimize the equivalent problem in time polynomial in sample count and data dimension when network width is fixed. That fixed-width condition is part of the computational guarantee. Experiments using synthetic and real datasets numerically validate the theoretical results, supporting this convex perspective on the specified three-layer training setup.
summary.tldr: Training the studied three-layer ReLU subnetworks is equivalent to convex group-sparse feature selection, with polynomial-time global optimization at fixed width.

title: Global Optimality Beyond Two Layers: Training Deep ReLU Networks via Convex Programs

abstract: In recent years, various notions of capacity and complexity have been proposed for characterizing the generalization properties of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in deep learning. Some of the popular notions that correlate well with the performance on unseen data are (i) the ‘flatness’ of the local minimum found by SGD, which is related to the eigenvalues of the Hessian, (ii) the ratio of the stepsize $\eta$ to the batch-size $b$, which essentially controls the magnitude of the stochastic gradient noise, and (iii) the ‘tail-index’, which measures the heaviness of the tails of the network weights at convergence. In this paper, we argue that these three seemingly unrelated perspectives for generalization are deeply linked to each other. We claim that depending on the structure of the Hessian of the loss at the minimum, and the choices of the algorithm parameters $\eta$ and $b$, the SGD iterates will converge to a \emph{heavy-tailed} stationary distribution. We rigorously prove this claim in the setting of quadratic optimization: we show that even in a simple linear regression problem with independent and identically distributed data whose distribution has finite moments of all order, the iterates can be heavy-tailed with infinite variance. We further characterize the behavior of the tails with respect to algorithm parameters, the dimension, and the curvature. We then translate our results into insights about the behavior of SGD in deep learning. We support our theory with experiments conducted on synthetic data, fully connected, and convolutional neural networks.

paragraphs: Several properties of stochastic gradient descent have been associated with generalization: the flatness of a solution, the ratio of step size to batch size, and the heaviness of the distribution’s tails for learned weights. This paper argues that these perspectives are linked through the behavior of SGD’s iterates.

The central claim is conditional: depending on loss curvature and algorithm parameters, the iterates can converge to a heavy-tailed stationary distribution. The authors rigorously establish this phenomenon for quadratic optimization. Even linear regression with independent, identically distributed data having finite moments of every order can produce iterates with heavy tails and infinite variance. Thus, heavy-tailed iterates need not originate in heavy-tailed observations.

The analysis characterizes how tail behavior varies with step size, batch size, dimension, and curvature. The authors then draw insights for deep learning and support their theory with synthetic experiments and fully connected and convolutional networks. The rigorous quadratic results provide a mechanism connecting these quantities, while the neural-network experiments explore its relevance beyond that theoretical setting.
summary.tldr: SGD can generate heavy-tailed iterates even from well-behaved data, linking tail behavior to curvature, step size, and batch size.

title: The Heavy-Tail Phenomenon in SGD

abstract: We consider large-scale Markov decision processes with an unknown cost function and address the problem of learning a policy from a finite set of expert demonstrations. We assume that the learner is not allowed to interact with the expert and has no access to reinforcement signal of any kind. Existing inverse reinforcement learning methods come with strong theoretical guarantees, but are computationally expensive, while state-of-the-art policy optimization algorithms achieve significant empirical success, but are hampered by limited theoretical understanding. To bridge the gap between theory and practice, we introduce a novel bilinear saddle-point framework using Lagrangian duality. The proposed primal-dual viewpoint allows us to develop a model-free provably efficient algorithm through the lens of stochastic convex optimization. The method enjoys the advantages of simplicity of implementation, low memory requirements, and computational and sample complexities independent of the number of states. We further present an equivalent no-regret online-learning interpretation.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning a decision policy from a finite collection of expert demonstrations in a large Markov decision process. The learner does not know the cost function, cannot interact with the expert, and receives no reinforcement signal. These restrictions make the demonstrations the available evidence about how the expert behaves.

The authors reformulate the problem as a bilinear saddle-point problem using Lagrangian duality. This provides a primal-dual perspective from which they derive a model-free algorithm using stochastic convex optimization. The purpose is to connect efficient policy learning with theoretical guarantees, addressing the gap between computationally expensive inverse reinforcement learning methods and empirically successful methods with less developed theory.

The resulting algorithm is described as provably efficient, straightforward to implement, and economical in memory. Its computational and sample complexities do not depend on the number of states, an especially relevant property for large problems. The authors also give an equivalent interpretation through no-regret online learning, connecting the same method to another framework for understanding sequential improvement.
summary.tldr: A primal-dual formulation yields a provably efficient method for learning from expert demonstrations without access to rewards.

title: Efficient Performance Bounds for Primal-Dual Reinforcement Learning from Demonstrations

abstract: Recently, learning a model that generalizes well on out-of-distribution (OOD) data has attracted great attention in the machine learning community. In this paper, after defining OOD generalization by Wasserstein distance, we theoretically justify that a model robust to input perturbation also generalizes well on OOD data. Inspired by previous findings that adversarial training helps improve robustness, we show that models trained by adversarial training have converged excess risk on OOD data. Besides, in the paradigm of pre-training then fine-tuning, we theoretically justify that the input perturbation robust model in the pre-training stage provides an initialization that generalizes well on downstream OOD data. Finally, various experiments conducted on image classification and natural language understanding tasks verify our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: The paper connects robustness to input perturbations with generalization beyond the training distribution. It defines the out-of-distribution setting using Wasserstein distance, giving distribution shift a mathematical form. Within that formulation, the authors theoretically justify why a model that resists input perturbations can also generalize well to shifted data.

This connection motivates an analysis of adversarial training, which is used to improve perturbation robustness. The authors show convergence of excess risk on out-of-distribution data for adversarially trained models. They also study pre-training followed by fine-tuning, arguing theoretically that robustness during pre-training provides an initialization that generalizes well to downstream out-of-distribution data.

Experiments on image classification and natural language understanding support the theoretical findings. The contribution links a property of individual-input behavior to a property of performance across distributions, and extends that link to transfer through pre-training. The generalization claims are grounded in the paper’s Wasserstein-based formulation, which supplies the setting for the theoretical connection.
summary.tldr: Under a Wasserstein-based formulation, the paper connects input robustness and adversarial pre-training to improved out-of-distribution generalization.

title: Improved OOD Generalization via Adversarial Training and Pretraing

abstract: This work investigates the compatibility between label smoothing (LS) and knowledge distillation (KD). Contemporary findings addressing this thesis statement take dichotomous standpoints: Muller et al. (2019) and Shen et al. (2021b). Critically, there is no effort to understand and resolve these contradictory findings, leaving the primal question \text{-} to smooth or not to smooth a teacher network? \text{-} unanswered. The main contributions of our work are the discovery, analysis and validation of systematic diffusion as the missing concept which is instrumental in understanding and resolving these contradictory findings. This systematic diffusion essentially curtails the benefits of distilling from an LS-trained teacher, thereby rendering KD at increased temperatures ineffective. Our discovery is comprehensively supported by large-scale experiments, analyses and case studies including image classification, neural machine translation and compact student distillation tasks spanning across multiple datasets and teacher-student architectures. Based on our analysis, we suggest practitioners to use an LS-trained teacher with a low-temperature transfer to achieve high performance students. Code and models are available at https://keshik6.github.io/revisiting-ls-kd-compatibility/

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student using a teacher model’s outputs, while label smoothing changes the targets used to train that teacher. Earlier findings disagreed about whether these techniques work well together. This paper investigates that disagreement to clarify when a label-smoothed teacher is useful.

The authors identify and analyze a phenomenon they call systematic diffusion. According to their analysis, it reduces the benefits of transferring knowledge from a teacher trained with label smoothing, making distillation at increased temperatures ineffective. Temperature is therefore central to resolving the conflicting conclusions: evaluating label smoothing without considering the transfer temperature can obscure the interaction.

The discovery is supported by large-scale experiments, analyses, and case studies covering image classification, neural machine translation, and compact student models across multiple datasets and teacher–student architectures. Based on those findings, the authors recommend combining a label-smoothed teacher with low-temperature transfer to obtain high-performing students. The practical conclusion concerns how the two techniques are configured together, rather than a universal instruction to always accept or reject label smoothing.
summary.tldr: Systematic diffusion helps explain conflicting distillation results and motivates using label-smoothed teachers with low-temperature transfer.

title: Revisiting Label Smoothing and Knowledge Distillation Compatibility: What was Missing?

abstract: In the correlation clustering problem the input is a signed graph where the sign indicates whether each pair of points should be placed in the same cluster or not. The goal of the problem is to compute a clustering which minimizes the number of disagreements with such recommendation. Thanks to its many practical applications, correlation clustering is a fundamental unsupervised learning problem and has been extensively studied in many different settings. In this paper we study the problem in the classic online setting with recourse; The vertices of the graphs arrive in an online manner and the goal is to maintain an approximate clustering while minimizing the number of times each vertex changes cluster. Our main contribution is an algorithm that achieves logarithmic recourse per vertex in the worst case. We also complement this result with a tight lower bound. Finally we show experimentally that our algorithm achieves better performances than state-of-the-art algorithms on real world data.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering starts with pairwise recommendations: some pairs should share a cluster, while others should be separated. Its objective is to minimize disagreements with those recommendations. This paper studies the online setting, where new vertices arrive over time and a clustering must be maintained as the input grows.

The additional concern is recourse, meaning how often an existing vertex changes clusters. Updating assignments may help maintain an approximate solution, but repeatedly moving the same vertex makes the clustering less consistent over time. The authors design an algorithm that bounds each vertex’s recourse logarithmically in the worst case while maintaining an approximate clustering.

A matching lower bound shows that the recourse guarantee is tight in the studied setting. Experiments on real-world data also show better performance than the compared state-of-the-art algorithms. The contribution combines a theoretical account of how much reassignment is required with an algorithm that reaches that bound, addressing stability of membership alongside the clustering objective.
summary.tldr: An online correlation clustering algorithm achieves a tight logarithmic bound on how often each vertex changes clusters.

title: Online and Consistent Correlation Clustering

abstract: Generative models trained with Differential Privacy (DP) can be used to generate synthetic data while minimizing privacy risks. We analyze the impact of DP on these models vis-a-vis underrepresented classes/subgroups of data, specifically, studying: 1) the size of classes/subgroups in the synthetic data, and 2) the accuracy of classification tasks run on them. We also evaluate the effect of various levels of imbalance and privacy budgets. Our analysis uses three state-of-the-art DP models (PrivBayes, DP-WGAN, and PATE-GAN) and shows that DP yields opposite size distributions in the generated synthetic data. It affects the gap between the majority and minority classes/subgroups; in some cases by reducing it (a "Robin Hood" effect) and, in others, by increasing it (a "Matthew" effect). Either way, this leads to (similar) disparate impacts on the accuracy of classification tasks on the synthetic data, affecting disproportionately more the underrepresented subparts of the data. Consequently, when training models on synthetic data, one might incur the risk of treating different subpopulations unevenly, leading to unreliable or unfair conclusions.

paragraphs: Differentially private generative models produce synthetic data while reducing privacy risks. This paper investigates how that process affects underrepresented groups, looking separately at their prevalence in generated data and the accuracy of classifiers trained on it. The analysis also varies data imbalance and privacy budgets.

Using PrivBayes, DP-WGAN, and PATE-GAN, the authors find that differential privacy can change group proportions in opposite directions. Sometimes it narrows the size gap between majority and minority groups, called a Robin Hood effect. In other cases, it widens that gap, called a Matthew effect. Thus, the direction of the distributional change is not uniform.

Despite those opposite changes in representation, the study finds similar disparities in downstream classification accuracy, with underrepresented portions affected disproportionately. A more balanced synthetic dataset therefore does not by itself establish more equitable predictive performance in these experiments. The findings identify a risk when learning from private synthetic data: different subpopulations may be treated unevenly, potentially producing unreliable or unfair conclusions.
summary.tldr: Differential privacy can either narrow or widen synthetic-data group imbalances while disproportionately affecting classification accuracy for underrepresented groups.

title: Robin Hood and Matthew Effects: Differential Privacy Has Disparate Impact on Synthetic Data

abstract: Importance sampling is a promising strategy for improving the convergence rate of stochastic gradient methods. It is typically used to precondition the optimization problem, but it can also be used to reduce the variance of the gradient estimator. Unfortunately, this latter point of view has yet to lead to practical methods that provably improve the asymptotic error of stochastic gradient methods. In this work, we propose stochastic reweighted gradient descent (SRG), a stochastic gradient method based solely on importance sampling that can reduce the variance of the gradient estimator and improve on the asymptotic error of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in the strongly convex and smooth case. We show that SRG can be extended to combine the benefits of both importance-sampling-based preconditioning and variance reduction. When compared to SGD, the resulting algorithm can simultaneously reduce the condition number and the asymptotic error, both by up to a factor equal to the number of component functions. We demonstrate improved convergence in practice on regularized logistic regression problems.

paragraphs: Importance sampling changes how component functions are sampled during stochastic optimization. It can improve the problem's conditioning or reduce noise in the estimated gradient. This paper focuses on the second benefit, asking how sampling alone can yield a practical method with a provable improvement in the long-run error of stochastic gradient descent.

The proposed stochastic reweighted gradient descent method, SRG, uses importance sampling to reduce gradient-estimation variance. For strongly convex, smooth problems, it can improve asymptotic error relative to SGD. Those mathematical assumptions define the setting of the stated guarantee. The authors also extend SRG to combine variance reduction with importance-sampling-based preconditioning.

The combined algorithm can reduce both the condition number and the asymptotic error, each by up to the number of component functions. This is an upper extent of possible improvement, rather than a uniform gain for every problem. Experiments on regularized logistic regression demonstrate improved convergence in practice, supporting the idea that carefully chosen sampling can address both optimization geometry and gradient noise.
summary.tldr: SRG uses importance sampling to reduce gradient variance and can improve both conditioning and asymptotic error in strongly convex, smooth optimization.

title: Stochastic Reweighted Gradient Descent

abstract: While message-passing graph neural networks have clear limitations in approximating permutation-equivariant functions over graphs or general relational data, more expressive, higher-order graph neural networks do not scale to large graphs. They either operate on $k$-order tensors or consider all $k$-node subgraphs, implying an exponential dependence on $k$ in memory requirements, and do not adapt to the sparsity of the graph. By introducing new heuristics for the graph isomorphism problem, we devise a class of universal, permutation-equivariant graph networks, which, unlike previous architectures, offer a fine-grained control between expressivity and scalability and adapt to the sparsity of the graph. These architectures lead to vastly reduced computation times compared to standard higher-order graph networks in the supervised node- and graph-level classification and regression regime while significantly improving standard graph neural network and graph kernel architectures in terms of predictive performance.

paragraphs: Graph networks should respond consistently when nodes are relabeled, a property called permutation equivariance. Ordinary message-passing networks have limits on the equivariant functions they can approximate. More expressive higher-order alternatives often require large tensors or consideration of every group of k nodes, creating memory costs that grow exponentially with order.

SpeqNets use new heuristics for graph isomorphism to construct a class of universal, permutation-equivariant networks. The architectures adapt to graph sparsity and offer fine-grained control over the balance between expressivity and scalability. This addresses the cost of higher-order modeling by making graph structure relevant to how much computation the network requires.

In supervised node-level and graph-level classification and regression, the authors report substantially shorter computation times than standard higher-order graph networks. They also report significantly better predictive performance than standard graph neural networks and graph kernels. These findings support the architecture family as a practical way to explore richer graph representations while controlling their computational demands.
summary.tldr: SpeqNets adapt higher-order graph modeling to sparsity, offering adjustable expressivity and scalability with strong reported predictive results.

title: SpeqNets: Sparsity-aware permutation-equivariant graph networks

abstract: Learning partial differential equations’ (PDEs) solution operators is an essential problem in machine learning. However, there are several challenges for learning operators in practical applications like the irregular mesh, multiple input functions, and complexity of the PDEs’ solution. To address these challenges, we propose a general neural operator transformer (GNOT), a scalable and effective transformer-based framework for learning operators. By designing a novel heterogeneous normalized attention layer, our model is highly flexible to handle multiple input functions and irregular meshes. Besides, we introduce a geometric gating mechanism which could be viewed as a soft domain decomposition to solve the multi-scale problems. The large model capacity of the transformer architecture grants our model the possibility to scale to large datasets and practical problems. We conduct extensive experiments on multiple challenging datasets from different domains and achieve a remarkable improvement compared with alternative methods. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/thu-ml/GNOT.

paragraphs: Learning a PDE solution operator means learning a mapping from input functions to the corresponding solutions. Practical problems complicate this task through irregular meshes, multiple input functions, and solution behavior spanning different scales. GNOT is a Transformer-based framework designed to address these difficulties within one operator-learning model.

The architecture introduces a heterogeneous normalized attention layer that accommodates different input functions and irregular spatial discretizations. It also uses geometric gating, which the authors interpret as a soft decomposition of the domain. This provides a mechanism for handling multiscale problems by organizing processing according to geometry without requiring a hard division into separate regions.

Experiments across challenging datasets from different domains show substantial improvements over the alternative methods evaluated. The authors also identify the Transformer’s large capacity as offering the possibility of scaling to larger datasets and practical applications. That scaling potential complements the demonstrated results: the empirical evidence establishes improvements on the studied problems, while the architecture supplies a flexible basis for broader use.
summary.tldr: GNOT combines flexible attention and geometric gating to learn PDE solution operators with irregular meshes, multiple inputs, and multiscale behavior.

title: GNOT: A General Neural Operator Transformer for Operator Learning

abstract: Understanding the impact of exploration on the behaviour of multi-agent learning has, so far, benefited from the restriction to potential, or network zero-sum games in which convergence to an equilibrium can be shown. Outside of these classes, learning dynamics rarely converge and little is known about the effect of exploration in the face of non-convergence. To progress this front, we study the smooth Q- Learning dynamics. We show that, in any network game, exploration by agents results in the convergence of Q-Learning to a neighbourhood of an equilibrium. This holds independently of whether the dynamics reach the equilibrium or display complex behaviours. We show that increasing the exploration rate decreases the size of this neighbourhood and also decreases the ability of all agents to improve their payoffs. Furthermore, in a broad class of games, the payoff performance of Q-Learning dynamics, measured by Social Welfare, decreases when the exploration rate increases. Our experiments show this to be a general phenomenon, namely that exploration leads to improved convergence of Q-Learning, at the cost of payoff performance.

paragraphs: When several agents learn together, their behavior may continue changing rather than settle at an equilibrium. Previous understanding often relied on special game classes where convergence could be established. This paper studies smooth Q-learning to examine what exploration does in broader network games, including those with complex, nonconvergent dynamics.

The authors show that exploration brings Q-learning into a neighborhood of an equilibrium in any network game. This does not require the dynamics to reach the equilibrium itself. Increasing exploration shrinks that neighborhood and reduces the ability of all agents to improve their payoffs, giving a precise sense in which exploration improves convergence behavior.

That improvement can have a performance cost. For a broad class of games, the paper shows that social welfare decreases as exploration increases. Experiments suggest the same tradeoff is more general: stronger exploration improves convergence while reducing payoff performance. The findings distinguish being closer to equilibrium from achieving higher collective rewards, showing why a more stable learning process need not be the more rewarding one.
summary.tldr: Greater exploration brings multi-agent Q-learning closer to equilibrium but can reduce collective payoff performance.

title: The Impact of Exploration on Convergence and Performance of Multi-Agent Q-Learning Dynamics

abstract: This work develops analysis and algorithms for solving a class of bilevel optimization problems where the lower-level (LL) problems have linear constraints. Most of the existing approaches for constrained bilevel problems rely on value function-based approximate reformulations, which suffer from issues such as non-convex and non-differentiable constraints. In contrast, in this work, we develop an implicit gradient-based approach, which is easy to implement, and is suitable for machine learning applications. We first provide an in-depth understanding of the problem, by showing that the implicit objective for such problems is in general non-differentiable. However, if we add some small (linear) perturbation to the LL objective, the resulting implicit objective becomes differentiable almost surely. This key observation opens the door for developing (deterministic and stochastic) gradient-based algorithms similar to the state-of-the-art ones for unconstrained bi-level problems. We show that when the implicit function is assumed to be strongly-convex, convex, and weakly-convex, the resulting algorithms converge with guaranteed rate. Finally, we experimentally corroborate the theoretical findings and evaluate the performance of the proposed framework on numerical and adversarial learning problems.

This paper studies cases where the lower level has linear constraints. Such constraints complicate differentiation, and common approximate reformulations can introduce constraints that are themselves non-convex and non-differentiable.

The approach matters because it addresses the differentiability obstacle directly and yields an implementable gradient framework, with its convergence guarantees linked to the stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: Small linear perturbations enable implicit-gradient algorithms for bilevel problems with linearly constrained lower levels.

title: Linearly Constrained Bilevel Optimization: A Smoothed Implicit Gradient Approach

abstract: Neural pruning, which involves identifying the optimal sparse subnetwork, is a key technique for reducing the complexity and improving the efficiency of deep neural networks. To address the challenge of solving neural pruning at a specific sparsity level directly, we investigate the evolution of optimal subnetworks with continuously increasing sparsity, which can provide insight into how to transform an unpruned dense model into an optimal subnetwork with any desired level of sparsity. In this paper, we proposed a novel pruning framework, coined Sparsity-indexed ODE (SpODE) that provides explicit guidance on how to best preserve model performance while ensuring an infinitesimal increase in model sparsity. On top of this, we develop a pruning algorithm, termed Pruning via Sparsity-indexed ODE (PSO), that enables effective pruning via traveling along the SpODE path. Empirical experiments show that PSO achieves either better or comparable performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines across various pruning settings.

paragraphs: Neural pruning aims to reduce a network’s complexity by finding a sparse subnetwork that preserves useful performance. Directly choosing such a subnetwork at a particular sparsity level is difficult. This paper instead studies how optimal subnetworks evolve as sparsity increases continuously, treating the desired sparse model as the destination of a path.

The proposed Sparsity-indexed ODE, or SpODE, describes how to best preserve performance while making an infinitesimal increase in sparsity. It gives local guidance for moving away from the original dense model. The authors turn this formulation into a practical algorithm, Pruning via Sparsity-indexed ODE, or PSO, which prunes by following the path.

Experiments across multiple pruning settings show that PSO performs better than or comparably to state-of-the-art baselines. The findings support using continuous changes in sparsity to guide a pruning algorithm. The distinction between formulation and evidence is useful: the framework investigates paths of optimal subnetworks, while the practical algorithm’s reported success is its empirical performance relative to other methods.
summary.tldr: PSO prunes networks by following a differential-equation path through increasing sparsity, achieving competitive or better performance in evaluated settings.

title: Pruning via Sparsity-indexed ODE: a Continuous Sparsity Viewpoint

abstract: We study the problems of distributed online and bandit convex optimization against an adaptive adversary. We aim to minimize the average regret on $M$ machines working in parallel over $T$ rounds with $R$ intermittent communications. Assuming the underlying cost functions are convex and can be generated adaptively, our results show that collaboration is not beneficial when the machines have access to the first-order gradient information at the queried points . This is in contrast to the case for stochastic functions, where each machine samples the cost functions from a fixed distribution. Furthermore, we delve into the more challenging setting of federated online optimization with bandit (zeroth-order) feedback , where the machines can only access values of the cost functions at the queried points. The key finding here is identifying the high-dimensional regime where collaboration is beneficial and may even lead to a linear speedup in the number of machines . We further illustrate our findings through federated adversarial linear bandits by developing novel distributed single and two-point feedback algorithms. Our work is the first attempt towards a systematic understanding of federated online optimization with limited feedback, and it attains tight regret bounds in the intermittent communication setting for both first and zeroth-order feedback. Our results thus bridge the gap between stochastic and adaptive settings in federated online optimization.

paragraphs: This paper asks when multiple machines benefit from collaborating on an online optimization problem. The machines work in parallel, communicate intermittently, and face convex costs that an adaptive adversary can generate. The objective is to minimize average regret, measuring the cost of their sequential decisions relative to a comparison decision.

The answer depends on the feedback available. When each machine receives gradient information at its queried points, the authors find that collaboration is not beneficial in this adaptive setting. This differs from the stochastic setting, where cost functions are sampled from a fixed distribution. When machines receive only function values, the authors identify a high-dimensional regime where collaboration helps and may provide speedup linear in the number of machines.

The paper also develops distributed algorithms for adversarial linear bandits with single-point and two-point feedback. Tight regret bounds cover both gradient and function-value feedback under intermittent communication. Together, these results clarify why the benefits of federated optimization depend on both the information returned by each query and whether the sequence of costs can adapt.
summary.tldr: Under adaptive convex costs, collaboration offers no benefit with gradient feedback but can yield linear speedup in a high-dimensional bandit regime.

title: Federated Online and Bandit Convex Optimization

abstract: Due to privacy, storage, and other constraints, there is a growing need for unsupervised domain adaptation techniques in machine learning that do not require access to the data used to train a collection of source models. Existing methods for multi-source-free domain adaptation (MSFDA) typically train a target model using pseudo-labeled data produced by the source models, which focus on improving the pseudo-labeling techniques or proposing new training objectives. Instead, we aim to analyze the fundamental limits of MSFDA. In particular, we develop an information-theoretic bound on the generalization error of the resulting target model, which illustrates an inherent bias-variance trade-off. We then provide insights on how to balance this trade-off from three perspectives, including domain aggregation, selective pseudo-labeling, and joint feature alignment, which leads to the design of novel algorithms. Experiments on multiple datasets validate our theoretical analysis and demonstrate the state-of-art performance of the proposed algorithm, especially on some of the most challenging datasets, including Office-Home and DomainNet.

Instead, we aim to analyze the fundamental limits of MSFDA. In particular, we develop an information-theoretic bound on the generalization error of the resulting target model, which illustrates an inherent bias-variance trade-off. We then provide insights on how to balance this trade-off from three perspectives, including domain aggregation, selective pseudo-labeling, and joint feature alignment, which leads to the design of novel algorithms. Experiments on multiple datasets validate our theoretical analysis and demonstrate the state-of-art performance of the proposed algorithm, especially on some of the most challenging datasets, including Office-Home and DomainNet.

paragraphs: Multi-source-free domain adaptation learns a target model using existing source models without accessing their original training data. That restriction matters when privacy or storage constraints make source datasets unavailable. Existing approaches commonly use source models to assign pseudo-labels to target data, then train a new model from those generated labels.

This paper examines the underlying limits of that process through an information-theoretic bound on target-model generalization error. The bound exposes a bias–variance tradeoff, giving a theoretical basis for reasoning about adaptation quality. The authors use it to study three choices: how to aggregate source domains, which pseudo-labels to select, and how to align features jointly.

Those insights lead to new algorithms designed to balance the tradeoff. Experiments on multiple datasets support the analysis and show state-of-the-art performance for the proposed algorithm, particularly on challenging datasets including Office-Home and DomainNet. The contribution links practical adaptation decisions to a generalization analysis, providing a rationale for how source-model information should be combined and used when the underlying source data cannot be revisited.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic bias–variance analysis guides improved domain adaptation using source models without their training data.

title: On Balancing Bias and Variance in Unsupervised Multi-Source-Free Domain Adaptation

abstract: A big convergence of model architectures across language, vision, speech, and multimodal is emerging. However, under the same name ”Transformers”, the above areas use different implementations for better performance, e.g., Post-LayerNorm for BERT, and Pre-LayerNorm for GPT and vision Transformers. We call for the development of Foundation Transformer for true general-purpose modeling, which serves as a go-to architecture for various tasks and modalities with guaranteed training stability. In this work, we introduce a Transformer variant, named Magneto, to fulfill the goal. Specifically, we propose Sub-LayerNorm for good expressivity, and the initialization strategy theoretically derived from DeepNet for stable scaling up. Extensive experiments demonstrate its superior performance and better stability than the de facto Transformer variants designed for various applications, including language modeling (i.e., BERT, and GPT), machine translation, vision pretraining (i.e., BEiT), speech recognition, and multimodal pretraining (i.e., BEiT-3).

paragraphs: Transformers are used across language, vision, speech, and multimodal learning, but their implementations differ between applications. One important difference is where normalization occurs within the network. Magneto seeks a common architecture that performs well across these settings and supports stable training as model scale increases.

The proposed design introduces Sub-LayerNorm to support expressivity and pairs it with an initialization strategy theoretically derived from DeepNet. These components address complementary concerns: how the architecture represents complex functions and how its parameters are initialized for stable scaling. The goal is a broadly useful Transformer design that reduces the need for different architectural variants across modalities.

Experiments span BERT-style and GPT-style language modeling, machine translation, BEiT vision pretraining, speech recognition, and BEiT-3 multimodal pretraining. The authors report stronger performance and better training stability than the established Transformer variants used for these applications. This breadth supports Magneto’s proposed role as a shared architecture across the evaluated tasks, with initialization and normalization treated as central design choices.
summary.tldr: Magneto combines Sub-LayerNorm and a theoretically derived initialization strategy to improve Transformer performance and stability across multiple modalities.

title: Magneto: A Foundation Transformer

abstract: Transformer-based models have delivered impressive results on many tasks, particularly vision and language tasks. In many model training situations, conventional configurations are often adopted. For example, we usually set the base model with hidden size (i.e. model width) to be 768 and the number of transformer layers (i.e. model depth) to be 12. In this paper, we revisit these conventional configurations by studying the the relationship between transformer configuration and training objective. We show that the optimal transformer configuration is closely related to the training objective. Specifically, compared with the simple classification objective, the masked autoencoder is effective in alleviating the over-smoothing issue in deep transformer training. Based on this finding, we propose “Bamboo”, a notion of using deeper and narrower transformer configurations, for masked autoencoder training. On ImageNet, with such a simple change in configuration, the re-designed Base-level transformer achieves 84.2% top-1 accuracy and outperforms SoTA models like MAE by $0.9%$. On language tasks, re-designed model outperforms BERT with the default setting by 1.1 points on average, on GLUE benchmark with 8 datasets.

paragraphs: Transformer designs often inherit familiar choices about width and depth, such as a hidden size of 768 and 12 layers. This paper asks whether those defaults suit different training objectives equally well. Its central finding is that the best configuration depends closely on what the model is trained to do.

The authors compare classification training with masked autoencoder training and find that the latter better alleviates over-smoothing in deep transformers. Over-smoothing concerns representations becoming too similar as processing proceeds through layers. This observation motivates Bamboo: using more layers with narrower representations when training with a masked autoencoder objective.

The redesigned Base-level vision transformer reaches 84.2% ImageNet top-1 accuracy, with a reported 0.9% improvement over MAE.
