summary.tldr: Bamboo uses deeper, narrower transformers to improve results when the training objective supports effective learning at greater depth.

title: A Study on Transformer Configuration and Training Objective

abstract: Extracting informative representations from videos is fundamental for effectively learning various downstream tasks. We present a novel approach for unsupervised learning of meaningful representations from videos, leveraging the concept of image spatial entropy (ISE) that quantifies the per-pixel information in an image. We argue that local entropy of pixel neighborhoods and their temporal evolution create valuable intrinsic supervisory signals for learning prominent features. Building on this idea, we abstract visual features into a concise representation of keypoints that act as dynamic information transmitters, and design a deep learning model that learns, purely unsupervised, spatially and temporally consistent representations directly from video frames. Two original information-theoretic losses, computed from local entropy, guide our model to discover consistent keypoint representations; a loss that maximizes the spatial information covered by the keypoints and a loss that optimizes the keypoints’ information transportation over time. We compare our keypoint representation to strong baselines for various downstream tasks, e.g., learning object dynamics. Our empirical results show superior performance for our information-driven keypoints that resolve challenges like attendance to static and dynamic objects or objects abruptly entering and leaving the scene.

paragraphs: This paper learns compact video representations as keypoints without labeled supervision. Its starting idea is that the information within local pixel neighborhoods, and how that information evolves over time, can supply a training signal. The model is guided by two losses computed from local entropy. One encourages keypoints to cover spatial information in each frame. The other optimizes how keypoints carry information through time. This pairs a requirement to represent informative image regions with a requirement for temporal consistency, rather than learning isolated locations independently in each frame.

The authors evaluate the resulting representations on downstream tasks, including learning object dynamics, and report better performance than strong baselines. They also report handling static and moving objects, as well as objects that abruptly enter or leave a scene. These findings support local information content as a useful source of unsupervised guidance for learning keypoints that remain meaningful across changing video frames.
summary.tldr: Two entropy-based objectives learn informative, temporally consistent video keypoints without labeled supervision.

title: Entropy-driven Unsupervised Keypoint Representation Learning in Videos

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) with hundreds of billions of parameters have transformed the field of machine learning. However, serving these models at inference time is both compute and memory intensive, where a single request can require multiple GPUs and tens of Gigabytes of memory. Multi-head attention is one of the key components of LLMs, which can for over 50% of LLMs memory and compute requirement. We observe that there is a high amount of redundancy across heads on which tokens they pay attention to. Based on this insight, we propose Clustered HeadAttention ( CHAI ). CHAI combines heads with a high amount of correlation for self-attention at runtime, thus reducing both memory and compute. In our experiments, we show that CHAI is able to reduce the memory requirements for storing K,V cache by up to 21.4% and inference time latency by up to 1.73× without any fine-tuning required. CHAI achieves this with a maximum 3.2% deviation in accuracy across 3 different models (i.e. OPT-66B, LLAMA-7B, LLAMA-33B) and 5 different evaluation datasets.

paragraphs: Serving large language models requires substantial computation and memory, and multi-head attention can account for more than half of those requirements. This paper identifies redundancy among attention heads: different heads often focus on highly similar sets of tokens. CHAI uses that correlation as an opportunity to reduce the work performed during inference.

The method combines highly correlated heads for self-attention at runtime. It reduces both memory use and computation without requiring fine-tuning. Its memory results concern the stored key and value cache, an important distinction from a claim about reducing the entire model’s memory footprint by the same percentage.

Across OPT-66B, LLAMA-7B, and LLAMA-33B on five evaluation datasets, the authors report key-value cache memory reductions of up to 21.4% and inference speedups of up to 1.73 times. The maximum reported accuracy deviation is 3.2%. These results show an empirical tradeoff between exploiting head redundancy and preserving predictions, with the strongest savings representing observed maxima rather than guarantees for every request.
summary.tldr: CHAI combines correlated attention heads at inference time to reduce cache memory and latency without fine-tuning.

title: CHAI: Clustered Head Attention for Efficient LLM Inference

abstract: A fundamental approach to semi-supervised learning is to leverage the structure of the sample space to diffuse label information from annotated examples to unlabeled points. Traditional methods model the input data points as a graph and rely on fast algorithms for solving Laplacian systems of equations, such as those defining PageRank. However, previous work has demonstrated that graph-based models fail to capture higher-order relations, such as group membership, which are better modeled by hypergraphs. Unfortunately, the scalable application of hypergraph models has been hampered by the non-linearity of the hypergraph Laplacian. In this paper, we present highly scalable algorithms for hypergraph primitives, such as hypergraph PageRank vectors and hypergraph Laplacian systems, over general families of hypergraphs. In addition to giving strong theoretical guarantees, we empirically showcase the speed of our algorithms on benchmark instances of semi-supervised learning on categorical data. We exploit their generality to improve semi-supervised manifold clustering via hypergraph models. By providing significant speed-ups on fundamental hypergraph tasks, our algorithms enable the deployment of hypergraph models on a massive scale.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning can spread label information from annotated examples to unlabeled data using relationships among samples. Ordinary graphs represent pairwise relationships, while hypergraphs can directly represent connections involving whole groups. This richer representation is useful for relationships such as group membership, but the nonlinear hypergraph Laplacian has made large-scale computation difficult.

The paper develops scalable algorithms for core hypergraph computations, including PageRank vectors and Laplacian systems. These operations provide the computational machinery needed to diffuse information through hypergraph models. The algorithms apply to general families of hypergraphs and come with theoretical guarantees, addressing a bottleneck that previously restricted the practical use of these richer structures.

The authors demonstrate speed on semi-supervised learning benchmarks involving categorical data. They also use the algorithms’ generality to improve semi-supervised manifold clustering with hypergraph models. The stated significance is both computational and representational: speeding up fundamental operations makes it more practical to use group relationships in learning problems at massive scale.
summary.tldr: Fast hypergraph PageRank and Laplacian algorithms make higher-order relationships more practical for large-scale semi-supervised learning.

title: Fast Algorithms for Hypergraph PageRank with Applications to Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: It is by now well-established that modern over-parameterized models seem to elude the bias-variance tradeoff and generalize well despite overfitting noise. Many recent works attempt to analyze this phenomenon in the relatively tractable setting of kernel regression. However, as we argue in detail, most past works on this topic either make unrealistic assumptions, or focus on a narrow problem setup. This work aims to provide a unified theory to upper bound the excess risk of kernel regression for nearly all common and realistic settings. When applied to common kernels, our results imply benign overfitting in high input dimensions, nearly tempered overfitting in fixed dimensions, and explicit convergence rates for regularized regression. As a by-product, we obtain time-dependent bounds for neural networks trained in the kernel regime. Our results rely on new relative perturbation bounds for the eigenvalues of kernel matrices, which may be of independent interest. These reveal a self-regularization phenomenon, whereby a heavy tail in the eigendecomposition of the kernel implicitly leads to good generalization.

paragraphs: Models can sometimes fit training noise and still predict well on new data, challenging a simple reading of the bias–variance tradeoff. This paper examines that behavior through kernel regression. The authors seek a unified theory covering nearly all common realistic settings, addressing what they describe as restrictive assumptions or narrow scope in much earlier work.

Their main results upper-bound excess risk, measuring how far prediction performance is from the relevant optimal reference. Applied to common kernels, the bounds imply benign overfitting in high input dimensions, nearly tempered overfitting in fixed dimensions, and explicit convergence rates when regularization is used. The distinctions matter: the theory does not assign the same overfitting behavior to every dimensional setting.

The analysis relies on new relative perturbation bounds for kernel-matrix eigenvalues. These reveal a self-regularization effect in which a heavy tail in the kernel’s eigendecomposition can implicitly support good generalization. As an additional consequence, the authors obtain time-dependent bounds for neural networks trained in the kernel regime, extending the analysis to that particular neural-network setting.
summary.tldr: A unified kernel-regression analysis links generalization and overfitting behavior to dimension, regularization, and the kernel’s eigenvalue structure.

title: Generalization in Kernel Regression Under Realistic Assumptions

abstract: In reinforcement learning, it is crucial to have an accurate environment dynamics model to evaluate different policies’ value in downstream tasks like offline policy optimization and policy evaluation. However, the learned model is known to be inaccurate in predictions when evaluating target policies different from data-collection policies. In this work, we found that utilizing policy representation for model learning, called policy-conditioned model (PCM) learning, is useful to mitigate the problem, especially when the offline dataset is collected from diversified behavior policies. The reason beyond that is in this case, PCM becomes a meta-dynamics model that is trained to be aware of and focus on the evaluation policies that on-the-fly adjust the model to be suitable to the evaluation policies’ state-action distribution, thus improving the prediction accuracy. Based on that intuition, we propose an easy-to-implement yet effective algorithm of PCM for accurate model learning. We also give a theoretical analysis and experimental evidence to demonstrate the feasibility of reducing value gaps by adapting the dynamics model under different policies. Experiment results show that PCM outperforms the existing SOTA off-policy evaluation methods in the DOPE benchmark by a large margin, and derives significantly better policies in offline policy selection and model predictive control compared with the standard model learning method.

paragraphs: An environment model learned from one collection of behavior policies can become inaccurate when used to evaluate a different policy. This matters because policy evaluation and optimization depend on predicting what that policy will experience. The paper proposes conditioning the learned dynamics model on a representation of the policy being evaluated.

This policy-conditioned model, or PCM, learns to adapt its predictions to the target policy’s state-action distribution. The authors describe it as a meta-dynamics model that adjusts to the evaluation policy. They find this especially useful when the offline dataset contains diverse behavior policies, providing a setting in which policy-aware model learning can mitigate prediction mismatch.

The paper supplies an algorithm, theoretical analysis, and experimental evidence for reducing policy-value gaps through this adaptation. PCM reportedly outperforms state-of-the-art off-policy evaluation methods by a large margin on DOPE. It also produces better policies in offline policy selection and model predictive control than standard model learning. The findings support adapting the learned model to its downstream policy-evaluation use.
summary.tldr: Conditioning environment models on the evaluation policy improves reported prediction, policy evaluation, and policy selection results.

title: Policy-conditioned Environment Models are More Generalizable

abstract: Many neural network architectures are known to be Turing Complete, and can thus, in principle implement arbitrary algorithms. However, Transformers are unique in that they can implement gradient-based learning algorithms under simple parameter configurations. This paper provides theoretical and empirical evidence that (non-linear) Transformers naturally learn to implement gradient descent in function space, which in turn enable them to learn non-linear functions in context. Our results apply to a broad class of combinations of non-linear architectures and non-linear in-context learning tasks. Additionally, we show that the optimal choice of non-linear activation depends in a natural way on the class of functions that need to be learned.

paragraphs: A neural architecture’s ability to represent arbitrary algorithms does not by itself explain which algorithms it readily learns. This paper investigates a more specific property of transformers: their ability to implement gradient-based learning under simple parameter configurations. The focus is on learning nonlinear functions from information provided in context.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that nonlinear transformers naturally learn to carry out gradient descent in function space. In this interpretation, the learning process adjusts a candidate function through successive improvements, providing a mechanism for nonlinear in-context learning. Their results cover a broad class of combinations of nonlinear architectures and nonlinear learning tasks.

The paper also finds that the optimal nonlinear activation depends naturally on the class of functions being learned. This connects an architectural choice to the structure of the target task. Together, the findings offer an algorithmic account of nonlinear in-context learning, grounded in both analysis and experiments. The account applies to the studied class of architecture-task combinations rather than asserting one mechanism for every transformer behavior.
summary.tldr: Theory and experiments support functional gradient descent as a mechanism for nonlinear in-context learning in a broad class of transformers.

title: Transformers Implement Functional Gradient Descent to Learn Non-Linear Functions In Context

abstract: Can we pre-train a generalist agent from a large amount of unlabeled offline trajectories such that it can be immediately adapted to any new downstream tasks in a zero-shot manner? In this work, we present a functional reward encoding (FRE) as a general, scalable solution to this zero-shot RL problem. Our main idea is to learn functional representations of any arbitrary tasks by encoding their state-reward samples using a transformer-based variational auto-encoder. This functional encoding not only enables the pre-training of an agent from a wide diversity of general unsupervised reward functions, but also provides a way to solve any new downstream tasks in a zero-shot manner, given a small number of reward-annotated samples. We empirically show that FRE agents trained on diverse random unsupervised reward functions can generalize to solve novel tasks in a range of simulated robotic benchmarks, often outperforming previous zero-shot RL and offline RL methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to pretrain a generalist agent from unlabeled offline trajectories and then use it for new tasks without further task-specific training. Its proposed functional reward encoding represents a task through samples pairing states with rewards. A transformer-based variational autoencoder learns to turn these samples into a functional representation.

The same representation supports pretraining across diverse unsupervised reward functions and specifying a downstream task using a small number of reward-annotated samples. This provides a common interface between the tasks used during pretraining and those encountered later. Zero-shot adaptation here still receives reward information describing the new task through those samples.

Experiments on simulated robotic benchmarks show that agents pretrained with diverse random reward functions can solve novel tasks. They often outperform earlier zero-shot reinforcement learning and offline reinforcement learning methods. The findings support functional reward encoding as a scalable approach to task representation, with empirical evidence that diversity in unsupervised pretraining rewards can support later generalization to new objectives.
summary.tldr: Functional reward encodings let pretrained agents tackle new tasks from a few reward-annotated samples, with strong results on simulated robotics benchmarks.

title: Unsupervised Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning via Functional Reward Encodings

abstract: The Sliced-Wasserstein (SW) distance between probability measures is defined as the average of the Wasserstein distances resulting for the associated one-dimensional projections. As a consequence, the SW distance can be written as an integral with respect to the uniform measure on the sphere and the Monte Carlo framework can be employed for calculating the SW distance. Spherical harmonics are polynomials on the sphere that form an orthonormal basis of the set of square-integrable functions on the sphere. Putting these two facts together, a new Monte Carlo method, hereby referred to as Spherical Harmonics Control Variates (SHCV), is proposed for approximating the SW distance using spherical harmonics as control variates. The resulting approach is shown to have good theoretical properties, e.g., a no-error property for Gaussian measures under a certain form of linear dependency between the variables. Moreover, an improved rate of convergence, compared to Monte Carlo, is established for general measures. The convergence analysis relies on the Lipschitz property associated to the SW integrand. Several numerical experiments demonstrate the superior performance of SHCV against state-of-the-art methods for SW distance computation.

paragraphs: Sliced-Wasserstein distance compares probability distributions by averaging Wasserstein distances between their one-dimensional projections. Computing it therefore involves averaging over directions on a sphere, a task naturally suited to Monte Carlo estimation. This paper improves that estimation by using spherical harmonics, a structured family of polynomial functions on the sphere.

The proposed Spherical Harmonics Control Variates method uses these functions as control variates in the Monte Carlo calculation. Their mathematical structure provides a way to improve the estimate of the spherical integral. The authors establish a better convergence rate than ordinary Monte Carlo for general measures, using a Lipschitz property of the sliced-Wasserstein integrand in the analysis.

They also prove a no-error property for Gaussian measures under a particular form of linear dependence between variables. That exactness is conditional on the stated Gaussian structure. Numerical experiments show better performance than leading methods for computing sliced-Wasserstein distance. The contribution combines general convergence improvements with a stronger special-case result and empirical evidence for more effective distance computation.
summary.tldr: Spherical-harmonic control variates improve sliced-Wasserstein estimation, with faster theoretical convergence and conditional exactness for certain Gaussian measures.

title: Sliced-Wasserstein Estimation with Spherical Harmonics as Control Variates

abstract: Model-based offline reinforcement Learning (RL) is a promising approach that leverages existing data effectively in many real-world applications, especially those involving high-dimensional inputs like images and videos. To alleviate the distribution shift issue in offline RL, existing model-based methods heavily rely on the uncertainty of learned dynamics. However, the model uncertainty estimation becomes significantly biased when observations contain complex distractors with non-trivial dynamics. To address this challenge, we propose a new approach - Separated Model-based Offline Policy Optimization (SeMOPO) - decomposing latent states into endogenous and exogenous parts via conservative sampling and estimating model uncertainty on the endogenous states only. We provide a theoretical guarantee of model uncertainty and performance bound of SeMOPO. To assess the efficacy, we construct the Low-Quality Vision Deep Data-Driven Datasets for RL (LQV-D4RL), where the data are collected by non-expert policy and the observations include moving distractors. Experimental results show that our method substantially outperforms all baseline methods, and further analytical experiments validate the critical designs in our method. The project website is https://sites.google.com/view/semopo.

paragraphs: Model-based offline reinforcement learning uses existing experience to learn dynamics and train a policy. To manage distribution shift, such methods often depend on uncertainty estimates from the learned dynamics. When visual observations contain moving distractors, those estimates can become biased by changes that complicate the image without representing the relevant system dynamics.

SeMOPO addresses this by separating latent states into endogenous and exogenous components through conservative sampling. It estimates model uncertainty only on the endogenous component. This makes the separation directly relevant to policy learning: uncertainty is computed from a selected part of the representation rather than from all observed visual dynamics. The authors provide an uncertainty guarantee and a performance bound.

For evaluation, they construct LQV-D4RL, containing data collected by a nonexpert policy and observations with moving distractors. SeMOPO substantially outperforms all compared baselines in the reported experiments. Further analytical experiments support the importance of its central design choices, connecting the proposed separation with improved learning from these challenging offline visual datasets.
summary.tldr: SeMOPO separates latent dynamics and estimates uncertainty on endogenous states to improve offline reinforcement learning with moving visual distractors.

title: SeMOPO: Learning High-quality Model and Policy from Low-quality Offline Visual Datasets

abstract: In order to enhance the generalization ability towards unseen domains, universal cross-domain image retrieval methods require a training dataset encompassing diverse domains, which is costly to assemble. Given this constraint, we introduce a novel problem of data-free adaptive cross-domain retrieval, eliminating the need for real images during training. Towards this goal, we propose a novel Text-driven Knowledge Integration (TKI) method, which exclusively utilizes a pre-trained vision-language model to implement an “aggregation after expansion" training strategy. Specifically, we extract diverse implicit domain-specific information through a set of learnable domain word vectors. Subsequently, a domain-agnostic universal projection, equipped with a non-Euclidean multi-layer perceptron, can be optimized using these assorted text descriptions through the text-proxied domain aggregation. Leveraging the cross-modal transferability phenomenon of the shared latent space, we can integrate the trained domain-agnostic universal projection with the pre-trained visual encoder to extract the features of the input image for the following retrieval during testing. Extensive experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method.

Specifically, we extract diverse implicit domain-specific information through a set of learnable domain word vectors. Subsequently, a domain-agnostic universal projection, equipped with a non-Euclidean multi-layer perceptron, can be optimized using these assorted text descriptions through the text-proxied domain aggregation. Leveraging the cross-modal transferability phenomenon of the shared latent space, we can integrate the trained domain-agnostic universal projection with the pre-trained visual encoder to extract the features of the input image for the following retrieval during testing. Extensive experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method.

paragraphs: Cross-domain image retrieval aims to find relevant images even when their domains differ from those encountered during training. Assembling diverse image collections for this purpose can be costly. This paper introduces a retrieval adaptation setting that uses no real training images, relying instead on an existing pretrained vision-language model.

The proposed Text-driven Knowledge Integration method first uses learnable domain word vectors to extract varied domain-specific information. It then aggregates these text descriptions to train a domain-agnostic projection containing a non-Euclidean multilayer perceptron. The training strategy expands the available domain information before learning a shared representation from it.

At test time, the learned projection is combined with the pretrained visual encoder to produce image features for retrieval. This transfer relies on the shared latent space connecting text and images. Experiments on several benchmark datasets report superior performance. The contribution is a way to adapt retrieval through textual information already accessible in a pretrained model, without requiring real images for the adaptation training.
summary.tldr: TKI adapts cross-domain image retrieval without real training images by transferring learned text-domain structure through a pretrained vision-language model.

title: Retrieval Across Any Domains via Large-scale Pre-trained Model

abstract: A plethora of jailbreaking attacks have been proposed to obtain harmful responses from safety-tuned LLMs. These methods largely succeed in coercing the target output in their original settings, but their attacks vary substantially in fluency and computational effort. In this work, we propose a unified threat model for the principled comparison of these methods. Our threat model checks if a given jailbreak is likely to occur in the distribution of text. For this, we build an N-gram language model on 1T tokens, which, unlike model-based perplexity, allows for an LLM-agnostic, nonparametric, and inherently interpretable evaluation. We adapt popular attacks to this threat model, and, for the first time, benchmark these attacks on equal footing with it. After an extensive comparison, we find attack success rates against safety-tuned modern models to be lower than previously presented and that attacks based on discrete optimization significantly outperform recent LLM-based attacks. Being inherently interpretable, our threat model allows for a comprehensive analysis and comparison of jailbreak attacks. We find that effective attacks exploit and abuse infrequent bigrams, either selecting the ones absent from real-world text or rare ones, e.g., specific to Reddit or code datasets.

This paper introduces a shared threat model to make comparisons more principled. Its central question is whether an attack resembles text that is likely to occur in the underlying text distribution.

The authors build an N-gram language model using one trillion tokens. This model evaluates short sequences of words or tokens through their observed frequency, providing an interpretable measure that does not depend on a particular large language model. They then adapt existing attacks to this common evaluation framework.

Under these comparisons, attack success against modern safety-tuned models is lower than previously reported, and discrete optimization attacks substantially outperform recent attacks driven by language models. summary.tldr: An interpretable N-gram threat model enables comparable jailbreak evaluations and reveals lower success rates and frequent exploitation of rare token pairs.

title: An Interpretable N-gram Perplexity Threat Model for Large Language Model Jailbreaks

abstract: Batch Normalisation (BN) is widely used in conventional deep neural network training to harmonise the input-output distributions for each batch of data. However, federated learning, a distributed learning paradigm, faces the challenge of dealing with non-independent and identically distributed data among the client nodes. Due to the lack of a coherent methodology for updating BN statistical parameters, standard BN degrades the federated learning performance. To this end, it is urgent to explore an alternative normalisation solution for federated learning. In this work, we resolve the dilemma of the BN layer in federated learning by developing a customised normalisation approach, Hybrid Batch Normalisation (HBN). HBN separates the update of statistical parameters (i.e., means and variances used for evaluation) from that of learnable parameters (i.e., parameters that require gradient updates), obtaining unbiased estimates of global statistical parameters in distributed scenarios. In contrast with the existing solutions, we emphasise the supportive power of global statistics for federated learning. The HBN layer introduces a learnable hybrid distribution factor, allowing each computing node to adaptively mix the statistical parameters of the current batch with the global statistics. Our HBN can serve as a powerful plugin to advance federated learning performance. It reflects promising merits across a wide range of federated learning settings, especially for small batch sizes and heterogeneous data. Code is available at https://github.com/Hongyao-Chen/HybridBN.

paragraphs: Batch normalization becomes difficult in federated learning because different clients can have different data distributions. Means and variances estimated across these clients need a coherent update procedure. Standard batch normalization can otherwise degrade performance. Hybrid Batch Normalisation addresses this by reworking how statistical information is maintained and used.

HBN separates updates to statistical parameters, such as evaluation means and variances, from gradient-based updates to learnable parameters. This separation produces unbiased estimates of global statistics in distributed settings. A learnable mixing factor then lets each computing node combine statistics from its current batch with global statistics, adapting the balance to the node.

The approach emphasizes that global information can support learning even when clients have heterogeneous data. Experiments show promising results across a broad range of federated settings, with particular benefits for small batches and heterogeneous distributions. HBN is presented as a plugin layer, making the normalization mechanism itself the intervention rather than requiring an entirely new federated learning system.
summary.tldr: HBN improves federated normalization by separating statistical updates and learning how to mix local batch statistics with global estimates.

title: Hybrid Batch Normalisation: Resolving the Dilemma of Batch Normalisation in Federated Learning

abstract: The memory challenges associated with training Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a critical concern, particularly when using the Adam optimizer. To address this issue, numerous memory-efficient techniques have been proposed, with GaLore standing out as a notable example designed to reduce the memory footprint of optimizer states. However, these approaches do not alleviate the memory burden imposed by activations, rendering them unsuitable for scenarios involving long context sequences or large mini-batches. Moreover, their convergence properties are still not well-understood in the literature. In this work, we introduce a Randomized Subspace Optimization framework for pre-training and fine-tuning LLMs. Our approach decomposes the high-dimensional training problem into a series of lower-dimensional subproblems. At each iteration, a random subspace is selected, and the parameters within that subspace are optimized. This structured reduction in dimensionality allows our method to simultaneously reduce memory usage for both activations and optimizer states. We establish comprehensive convergence guarantees and derive rates for various scenarios, accommodating different optimization strategies to solve the subproblems. Extensive experiments validate the superior memory and communication efficiency of our method, achieving performance comparable to GaLore and Adam.

paragraphs: Training large language models requires memory for both optimizer states and activations. Methods that reduce only the optimizer’s storage can leave a substantial obstacle when training uses long sequences or large batches. This paper introduces Randomized Subspace Optimization to address both sources of memory use within one training framework.

The method breaks a high-dimensional optimization problem into a succession of smaller problems. At each iteration, it chooses a random subspace and optimizes parameters within that subspace. This changes the scope of each update, allowing the method to reduce activation memory alongside optimizer-state memory. The framework supports both pre-training and fine-tuning.

The authors establish convergence guarantees and rates across several scenarios, including different ways of solving the smaller optimization problems. Their experiments report better memory and communication efficiency while achieving performance comparable to GaLore and Adam. The contribution therefore combines resource savings with theoretical analysis of the training procedure, rather than relying solely on empirical evidence that smaller updates work.
summary.tldr: Randomized Subspace Optimization reduces activation and optimizer-state memory while matching GaLore and Adam performance in reported experiments.

title: A Memory Efficient Randomized Subspace Optimization Method for Training Large Language Models

abstract: Current mathematical reasoning benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) are approaching saturation, with some achieving $>$ 90% accuracy, and are increasingly compromised by training-set contamination. We introduce Putnam-AXIOM, a benchmark of 522 university-level competition problems drawn from the prestigious William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition, and Putnam-AXIOM Variation, an unseen companion set of 100 functional variants generated by programmatically perturbing variables, and constants. The variation protocol produces an unlimited stream of equally difficult, unseen instances – yielding a contamination-resilient test bed. On the Original set, OpenAI’s o1-preview – the strongest evaluated model – scores 41.9%, but its accuracy drops by 19.6 % (46.8% relative decrease) on the paired Variations. The remaining eighteen models show the same downward trend, ten of them with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals. These gaps suggest memorization and highlight the necessity of dynamic benchmarks. We complement ("boxed") accuracy with Teacher-Forced Accuracy (TFA), a lightweight metric that directly scores reasoning traces and automates natural language proof evaluations. Putnam-AXIOM therefore provides a rigorous, contamination-resilient evaluation framework for assessing advanced mathematical reasoning of LLMs. Data and evaluation code are publicly available at https://github.com/brando90/putnam-axiom.

paragraphs: Mathematical benchmarks become less informative when scores approach saturation or problems may have appeared in training data. Putnam-AXIOM addresses both issues with 522 university-level competition problems and a companion set of 100 unseen variants. The variants are created by programmatically changing variables and constants while preserving difficulty.

The variation protocol can generate an unlimited stream of new instances, supporting evaluation that is more resilient to contamination. Among the evaluated models, o1-preview performs best on the original set at 41.9%, but its accuracy falls by 19.6 percentage points on paired variations. All eighteen other models also decline, with ten showing non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals.

These gaps suggest memorization may contribute to performance and motivate dynamic evaluation; they do not by themselves establish memorization as the sole explanation. The benchmark also introduces Teacher-Forced Accuracy, a lightweight measure that scores reasoning traces and automates natural-language proof evaluation. Together, varied problems and reasoning-sensitive scoring broaden the assessment beyond correctness of a final boxed answer.
summary.tldr: Putnam-AXIOM combines difficult competition problems, generated variants, and reasoning-trace scoring, revealing performance drops that suggest memorization.

title: Putnam-AXIOM: A Functional & Static Benchmark for Measuring Higher Level Mathematical Reasoning in LLMs

abstract: We address the problem of code generation from multi-turn execution feedback. Existing methods either generate code without feedback or use complex, hierarchical reinforcement learning to optimize multi-turn rewards. We propose a simple yet scalable approach, $\mu$CODE, that solves multi-turn code generation using only single-step rewards. Our key insight is that code generation is a one-step recoverable MDP, where the correct code can be recovered from any intermediate code state in a single turn. $\mu$CODE iteratively trains both a generator to provide code solutions conditioned on multi-turn execution feedback and a verifier to score the newly generated code. Experimental evaluations show that our approach achieves significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. We provide analysis of the design choices of the reward models and policy, and show the efficacy of $\mu$CODE at utilizing the execution feedback.

paragraphs: Code generation can involve repeated attempts, with execution feedback helping a model revise earlier solutions. Training for this interaction can become complicated when rewards must account for an entire sequence of revisions. This paper proposes μCODE, which learns to use multi-turn feedback while relying only on single-step rewards.

The approach rests on viewing code generation as a one-step recoverable decision process: from any intermediate code state, a correct program can be produced in one turn. This makes immediate candidate quality useful even within a longer interaction. μCODE iteratively trains a generator conditioned on the accumulated execution feedback and a verifier that scores newly produced code.

The experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines and show that the method uses execution feedback effectively. The paper also analyzes choices concerning the reward models and generation policy. Its main contribution is a simpler training approach for iterative code generation, grounded in the ability to replace an unsuccessful program with a correct solution in a single revision.
summary.tldr: μCODE trains a feedback-conditioned code generator and verifier with single-step rewards to improve multi-turn code generation.

title: Multi-Turn Code Generation Through Single-Step Rewards

abstract: Deep learning survival models often outperform classical methods in time-to-event predictions, particularly in personalized medicine, but their "black box" nature hinders broader adoption. We propose a framework for gradient-based explanation methods tailored to survival neural networks, extending their use beyond regression and classification. We analyze the implications of their theoretical assumptions for time-dependent explanations in the survival setting and propose effective visualizations incorporating the temporal dimension. Experiments on synthetic data show that gradient-based methods capture the magnitude and direction of local and global feature effects, including time dependencies. We introduce GradSHAP(t), a gradient-based counterpart to SurvSHAP(t), which outperforms SurvSHAP(t) and SurvLIME in a computational speed vs. accuracy trade-off. Finally, we apply these methods to medical data with multi-modal inputs, revealing relevant tabular features and visual patterns, as well as their temporal dynamics.

paragraphs: Survival models predict time to an event, so explaining their predictions requires attention to when an input matters as well as how it matters. This paper adapts gradient-based explanation methods to survival neural networks. It examines how the methods' theoretical assumptions affect explanations that vary over time and develops visualizations that include that temporal dimension.

In synthetic experiments, the methods recover the magnitude and direction of feature effects at both local and global levels, including effects that depend on time. The authors also introduce GradSHAP(t), a gradient-based counterpart to SurvSHAP(t). They report a better computational speed-versus-accuracy trade-off than SurvSHAP(t) and SurvLIME.

The framework is then applied to medical data containing multiple input types. The resulting explanations identify relevant tabular features and visual patterns, together with their temporal dynamics. These findings show how explanations can convey changes in a model's use of information across time. The contribution therefore covers both computing feature explanations and presenting them in a form suited to time-to-event predictions.
summary.tldr: A gradient-based framework explains time-varying survival predictions, with GradSHAP(t) improving the reported speed–accuracy trade-off.

title: Gradient-based Explanations for Deep Learning Survival Models

abstract: Despite the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), a fundamental challenge persists: the lack of high-quality optimization modeling datasets hampers LLMs’ robust modeling of practical optimization problems from natural language descriptions (NL). This data scarcity also contributes to the generalization difficulties experienced by learning-based methods. To address these challenges, we propose a scalable framework for synthesizing a high-quality dataset, named OptMATH. Starting from curated seed data with mathematical formulations (MF), this framework automatically generates problem data (PD) with controllable complexity. Then, a back-translation step is employed to obtain NL. To verify the correspondence between the NL and the PD, a forward modeling step followed by rejection sampling is used. The accepted pairs constitute the training part of OptMATH. Then a collection of rejected pairs is identified and further filtered. This collection serves as a new benchmark for optimization modeling, containing difficult instances whose lengths are much longer than these of NL4OPT and MAMO. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that models of various sizes (0.5B-32B parameters) trained on OptMATH achieve superior results on multiple modeling benchmarks, thereby validating the effectiveness and scalability of our approach. The OptMATH dataset and related resources are available at https://github.com/optsuite/OptMATH.

paragraphs: Turning a natural-language problem into a mathematical optimization model requires preserving the problem’s meaning through a formal representation. The paper identifies a shortage of high-quality training data as an obstacle to reliable modeling and generalization. OptMATH addresses that shortage through an automated synthesis process with checks in both directions.

The framework starts from curated mathematical formulations and generates problem data with controllable complexity. It then produces natural-language descriptions through back-translation. A forward modeling step checks correspondence between those descriptions and the problem data, and rejection sampling selects pairs for training. Thus, generating a plausible description is only one part of constructing an accepted example.

The authors also further filter a collection of rejected pairs to create a difficult evaluation benchmark, with instances much longer than those in NL4OPT and MAMO. Models ranging from 0.5 billion to 32 billion parameters trained on OptMATH achieve superior results across multiple modeling benchmarks. These experiments support both the usefulness of the synthesized training data and the framework’s applicability across model sizes.
summary.tldr: OptMATH generates and verifies optimization-modeling data in both directions, improving models across sizes and producing a challenging benchmark.

title: OptMATH: A Scalable Bidirectional Data Synthesis Framework for Optimization Modeling

abstract: The use of parallel actors for data collection has been an effective technique used in reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. The manner in which data is collected in these algorithms, controlled via the number of parallel environments and the rollout length, induces a form of bias-variance trade-off; the number of training passes over the collected data, on the other hand, must strike a balance between sample efficiency and overfitting. We conduct an empirical analysis of these trade-offs on PPO, one of the most popular RL algorithms that uses parallel actors, and establish connections to network plasticity and, more generally, optimization stability. We examine its impact on network architectures, as well as the hyper-parameter sensitivity when scaling data. Our analyses indicate that larger dataset sizes can increase final performance across a variety of settings, and that scaling parallel environments is more effective than increasing rollout lengths. These findings highlight the critical role of data collection strategies in improving agent performance.

paragraphs: Parallel reinforcement learning actors can gather experience from many environments at once, but the way that experience is collected changes learning behavior. This paper examines those choices empirically in PPO, focusing on the number of parallel environments, rollout length, and repeated training passes over the collected data.

Environment count and rollout length induce a bias-variance trade-off. Reusing a collected dataset creates a separate balance between sample efficiency and overfitting. The authors connect these decisions to network plasticity, meaning its ability to keep adapting, and to optimization stability. They also examine how architecture and sensitivity to hyperparameters interact with larger data collections.

The analyses indicate that larger datasets can improve final performance across a variety of settings. Increasing the number of parallel environments is more effective than extending rollout lengths in the reported comparisons. The findings make data collection a substantive part of algorithm design: both the amount of experience and how that experience is distributed across parallel environments and time affect learning outcomes.
summary.tldr: PPO experiments indicate that larger datasets can improve performance and that adding parallel environments is more effective than lengthening rollouts.

title: The Impact of On-Policy Parallelized Data Collection on Deep Reinforcement Learning Networks

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents can solve diverse tasks but often exhibit unsafe behavior. Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) address this by enforcing safety constraints, yet existing methods either sacrifice reward maximization or allow unsafe training. We introduce Constrained Trust Region Policy Optimization (C-TRPO), which reshapes the policy space geometry to ensure trust regions contain only safe policies, guaranteeing constraint satisfaction throughout training. We analyze its theoretical properties and connections to TRPO, Natural Policy Gradient (NPG), and Constrained Policy Optimization (CPO). Experiments show that C-TRPO reduces constraint violations while maintaining competitive returns.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents can achieve high rewards while violating safety requirements during training. Constrained Markov decision processes express such requirements as explicit constraints, but existing methods can either compromise reward maximization or permit unsafe training behavior. This paper introduces Constrained Trust Region Policy Optimization, or C-TRPO, to incorporate those constraints into the structure of policy updates.

The central idea is to reshape the geometry of policy space so that a trust region contains only safe policies. A trust region determines the set of policies considered in an update. By making that region safe by construction, C-TRPO provides a guarantee of constraint satisfaction throughout training within its formulation.

The authors analyze the method theoretically and explain its connections to TRPO, Natural Policy Gradient, and Constrained Policy Optimization. Experiments report fewer constraint violations while maintaining competitive returns. The contribution links the mathematical design of permissible updates to safety during learning, with empirical evidence that reducing violations can coexist with competitive task performance.
summary.tldr: C-TRPO reshapes trust regions to contain only safe policies, providing training-time constraint guarantees and competitive experimental returns.

title: Embedding Safety into RL: A New Take on Trust Region Methods

abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting enhances mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) by enabling detailed step-by-step solutions. However, due to the verbosity of LLMs, the resulting reasoning chains can be long, making it harder to verify the reasoning steps and trace issues resulting from dependencies between the steps that may be farther away in the sequence of steps. Importantly, mathematical reasoning allows each step to be derived from a small set of premises, which are a subset of the preceding steps in the reasoning chain. In this paper, we present a framework that identifies the premises for each step, to improve the evaluation of reasoning. We restructure conventional linear reasoning chains into Premise Augmented Reasoning Chains (PARC) by introducing premise links, resulting in a directed acyclic graph where the nodes are the steps and the edges are the premise links. Through experiments with a PARC-based dataset that we built, namely (Premises and ERrors identification in LLMs), we demonstrate that LLMs can reliably identify premises within complex reasoning chains. In particular, even open-source LLMs achieve 90% recall in premise identification. We also show that PARC helps to identify errors in reasoning chains more reliably. The accuracy of error identification improves by 6% to 16% absolute when step-by-step verification is carried out in PARC under the premises. Our findings highlight the utility of premise-centric representations in addressing complex problem-solving tasks and open new avenues for improving the reliability of LLM-based reasoning evaluations.

paragraphs: Long mathematical reasoning chains can be difficult to check because a step may depend on statements much earlier in the solution. This paper makes those dependencies explicit. Its starting observation is that a mathematical step can be derived from a small set of premises drawn from preceding steps.

Premise Augmented Reasoning Chains, or PARC, add links from each step to its supporting premises. The resulting representation is a directed acyclic graph: steps become nodes, and premise dependencies become edges. Verification can then examine a step together with the particular statements it relies on, making the relevant context directly available.

Checking steps under their linked premises improves error-identification accuracy by 6 to 16 percentage points. These findings support dependency-aware representations as a practical way to improve the evaluation of mathematical reasoning.
summary.tldr: Linking mathematical reasoning steps to their premises improves reported error-identification accuracy by 6 to 16 percentage points.

title: Premise-Augmented Reasoning Chains Improve Error Identification in Math reasoning with LLMs

abstract: Humans are often modeled as rational actors by interactive agents when they are in fact frequently observed to make biased decisions. This erroneous assumption may cause an agent’s model of the human to fail, especially when interaction occurs in bias-inducing settings that prompt risky decisions. To address this, this paper formulates a risk-sensitive multi-agent coordination problem and presents the novel Risk-Sensitive Theory of Mind (RS-ToM) framework that allows an autonomous agent to reason about and adapt to a partner of unknown risk-sensitivity. In simulated studies, we show that an agent with an RS-ToM is able to better coordinate with such a partner when compared to an agent that assumes their partner is rational. Thus, we observe significant improvements to team performance, coordination fluency, compliance with partner risk-preferences, and predictability. The presented results suggest that an RS-ToM will be able to model and plan with partners that exhibit these risk-sensitive biases in the real world.

The proposed Risk-Sensitive Theory of Mind framework allows an agent to reason about and adapt to a partner whose risk sensitivity is initially unknown. The work formulates a risk-sensitive coordination problem using cumulative prospect theory. Its central aim is to incorporate the partner’s response to risk into the agent’s model and planning.

The authors report significant improvements in team performance, coordination fluency, respect for the partner’s risk preferences, and predictability. These findings establish benefits in the simulated settings. They also suggest potential for coordinating with real-world partners who exhibit similar risk-sensitive biases, with that transfer presented as a prospective implication.
summary.tldr: Risk-Sensitive Theory of Mind improves simulated coordination by adapting to a partner’s unknown risk sensitivity.

title: Risk-Sensitive Theory of Mind: Coordinating with Agents of Unknown Bias using Cumulative Prospect Theory

abstract: In-context learning based on attention models is examined for data with categorical outcomes, with inference in such models viewed from the perspective of functional gradient descent (GD). We develop a network composed of attention blocks, with each block employing a self-attention layer followed by a cross-attention layer, with associated skip connections. This model can exactly perform multi-step functional GD inference for in-context inference with categorical observations. We perform a theoretical analysis of this setup, generalizing many prior assumptions in this line of work, including the class of attention mechanisms for which it is appropriate. We demonstrate the framework empirically on synthetic data, image classification and language generation.

They show that this model can exactly implement multiple steps of functional gradient descent during in-context inference. The result establishes an exact computational correspondence for the proposed architecture, giving its attention operations a specific optimization interpretation.

These examples show the framework in several categorical-data settings, while the central theoretical claim concerns the constructed network’s ability to perform the specified inference procedure exactly.
summary.tldr: A constructed attention network exactly implements multistep functional gradient descent for in-context inference with categorical outcomes.

title: On Understanding Attention-Based In-Context Learning for Categorical Data

abstract: This paper presents SANA-1.5, a linear Diffusion Transformer for efficient scaling in text-to-image generation. Building upon SANA-1.0, we introduce three key innovations: (1) Efficient Training Scaling: A depth-growth paradigm that enables scaling from 1.6B to 4.8B parameters with significantly reduced computational resources, combined with a memory-efficient 8-bit optimizer. (2) Model Depth Pruning: A block importance analysis technique for efficient model compression to arbitrary sizes with minimal quality loss. (3) Inference-time Scaling: A repeated sampling strategy that trades computation for model capacity, enabling smaller models to match larger model quality at inference time. Through these strategies, SANA-1.5 achieves a text-image alignment score of 0.72 on GenEval, which can be further improved to 0.80 through inference scaling, establishing a new SoTA on GenEval benchmark. These innovations enable efficient model scaling across different compute budgets while maintaining high quality, making high-quality image generation more accessible.

paragraphs: SANA-1.5 addresses how to allocate computation when building and using text-to-image models. summary.tldr: SANA-1.5 combines depth growth, pruning, and repeated sampling to improve text-to-image quality across training and inference compute budgets.

title: SANA 1.5: Efficient Scaling of Training-Time and Inference-Time Compute in Linear Diffusion Transformer

abstract: Deep neural networks often develop spurious bias, reliance on correlations between non-essential features and classes for predictions. For example, a model may identify objects based on frequently co-occurring backgrounds rather than intrinsic features, resulting in degraded performance on data lacking these correlations. Existing mitigation approaches typically depend on external annotations of spurious correlations, which may be difficult to obtain and are not relevant to the spurious bias in a model. In this paper, we take a step towards self-guided mitigation of spurious bias by proposing NeuronTune, a post hoc method that directly intervenes in a model’s internal decision process. Our method probes in a model’s latent embedding space to identify and regulate neurons that lead to spurious prediction behaviors. We theoretically justify our approach and show that it brings the model closer to an unbiased one. Unlike previous methods, NeuronTune operates without requiring spurious correlation annotations, making it a practical and effective tool for improving model robustness. Experiments across different architectures and data modalities demonstrate that our method significantly mitigates spurious bias in a self-guided way.

paragraphs: A neural network can learn to associate a class with an incidental feature, such as a background that frequently accompanies an object. Predictions then deteriorate when that association disappears. NeuronTune addresses these spurious correlations without requiring annotations that explicitly identify them, which can be difficult to obtain and may not match the biases a particular model has learned.

The method operates after training and intervenes directly in the model's internal decision process. It probes the latent embedding space to identify neurons associated with spurious prediction behavior, then regulates those neurons. This makes the model's own behavior the basis for intervention rather than depending on externally supplied descriptions of its shortcuts.

The authors theoretically justify the approach and show that it moves the model closer to an unbiased one. Experiments across multiple architectures and data modalities demonstrate significant mitigation of spurious bias. These findings support self-guided internal intervention as a practical route toward greater robustness, while the stated result is bias reduction rather than complete elimination.
summary.tldr: NeuronTune probes and regulates internal neurons to reduce spurious prediction behavior without annotations of the spurious correlations.

title: NeuronTune: Towards Self-Guided Spurious Bias Mitigation

abstract: The integration of Deep Neural Networks in Reinforcement Learning (RL) systems has led to remarkable progress in solving complex tasks but also introduced challenges like primacy bias and dead neurons. Primacy bias skews learning towards early experiences, while dead neurons diminish the network’s capacity to acquire new knowledge. Traditional reset mechanisms aimed at addressing these issues often involve maintaining large replay buffers to train new networks or selectively resetting subsets of neurons. However, these approaches either incur prohibitive computational costs or reset network parameters without ensuring stability through recovery mechanisms, ultimately impairing learning efficiency. In this work, we introduce the novel concept of neuron regeneration, which combines reset mechanisms with knowledge recovery techniques. We also propose a new framework called Sustainable Backup Propagation(SBP) that effectively maintains plasticity in neural networks through this neuron regeneration process. The SBP framework achieves whole network neuron regeneration through two key procedures: cycle reset and inner distillation. Cycle reset involves a scheduled renewal of neurons, while inner distillation functions as a knowledge recovery mechanism at the neuron level. To validate our framework, we integrate SBP with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and propose a novel distillation function for inner distillation. This integration results in Plastic PPO (P3O), a new algorithm that enables efficient cyclic regeneration of all neurons in the actor network. Extensive experiments demonstrate the approach effectively maintains policy plasticity and improves sample efficiency in reinforcement learning.

The resulting algorithm, Plastic PPO, cyclically regenerates all neurons in the actor network. Experiments report that the method preserves policy plasticity and improves sample efficiency. The findings support treating renewal and recovery as linked operations when maintaining an agent’s ability to keep learning.
summary.tldr: Plastic PPO combines scheduled neuron resets with knowledge recovery to preserve learning capacity and improve sample efficiency.

title: Stay Hungry, Keep Learning: Sustainable Plasticity for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Transformers rely on both content-based and position-based addressing mechanisms to make predictions, but existing positional encoding techniques often diminish the effectiveness of position-based addressing. Many current methods enforce rigid patterns in attention maps, limiting the ability to model long-range dependencies and adapt to diverse tasks. Additionally, most positional encodings are learned as general biases, lacking the specialization required for different instances within a dataset. To address this, we propose conTextualized equivariAnt Position Encoding (TAPE), a novel framework that enhances positional embeddings by incorporating sequence content across layers. TAPE introduces dynamic, context-aware positional encodings, overcoming the constraints of traditional fixed patterns. We show that TAPE can provably facilitate LLM reasoning ability by emulating a broader class of algorithms. By enforcing permutation and orthogonal equivariance, TAPE ensures the stability of positional encodings during updates, improving long-context ability. Our method can be easily integrated into pre-trained transformers, offering parameter-efficient fine-tuning with minimal overhead. Extensive experiments show that TAPE achieves superior performance in language modeling, arithmetic reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks compared to existing positional embedding techniques.

The paper argues that many positional encodings impose rigid attention patterns and learn general biases that do not adapt sufficiently to individual sequences. These restrictions can hinder long-range dependencies and specialization across different tasks.

TAPE makes positional encodings depend on sequence content across layers. Its dynamic positional representations can adapt to the current input, while permutation and orthogonal equivariance provide stability during updates. The paper also gives a theoretical result showing that TAPE can facilitate reasoning by allowing models to emulate a broader class of algorithms.

summary.tldr: TAPE makes positional encodings content-aware and equivariant, improving evaluated reasoning, language modeling, and long-context retrieval tasks.

title: Rethinking Addressing in Language Models via Contextualized Equivariant Positional Encoding

abstract: Developers often struggle to specify correct training labels and rewards. Perhaps they don’t need to. We propose recontextualization, which reduces how often language models "game" training signals, performing misbehaviors those signals mistakenly reinforce. We show recontextualization prevents models from learning to 1) overfit evaluation criteria at the expense of chat response quality; 2) special-case code to pass incorrect tests; 3) overwrite evaluation functions rather than write correct code; and 4) become sycophantic. Our method works by generating completions from prompts discouraging misbehavior and then recontextualizing them as though they were in response to prompts permitting misbehavior. Recontextualization trains language models to resist misbehavior even when instructions permit it. This mitigates the reinforcement of misbehavior from misspecified training signals, reducing specification gaming without improving the supervision signal.

paragraphs: Training signals can accidentally reward undesirable behavior. A model might satisfy an evaluation rule while lowering response quality, or exploit incorrect tests instead of producing correct code. This paper studies how to reduce such specification gaming without first correcting the labels or rewards responsible for reinforcing it.

The proposed method, recontextualization, generates completions using prompts that discourage misbehavior. It then treats those completions during training as responses to prompts that permit misbehavior. This changes the context associated with the desired behavior, teaching the model to resist gaming even when the instructions allow it. The supervision signal itself is not improved.

The authors show that this procedure prevents models from learning four studied behaviors: overfitting evaluation criteria at the expense of chat quality, special-casing code for incorrect tests, overwriting evaluation functions, and becoming sycophantic. The results identify prompt context as a useful training intervention. By changing how completions are presented, the method mitigates the reinforcement of behaviors that misspecified training signals would otherwise encourage.
summary.tldr: Recontextualization reduces specification gaming by training desirable completions under contexts that permit misbehavior, without correcting the reward signal.

title: Recontextualization Mitigates Specification Gaming Without Modifying the Specification

abstract: Large language models frequently exhibit hallucinations: fluent and confident outputs that are factually incorrect or unsupported by the input context. While recent hallucination detection methods have explored various features derived from attention maps, the underlying mechanisms they exploit remain poorly understood. In this work, we propose SinkProbe, a hallucination detection method grounded in the observation that hallucinations are deeply entangled with attention sinks - tokens that accumulate disproportionate attention mass during generation - indicating a transition from distributed, input-grounded attention to compressed, prior-dominated computation. Importantly, although sink scores are computed solely from attention maps, we find that the classifier preferentially relies on sinks whose associated value vectors have large norms. Moreover, we show that previous methods implicitly depend on attention sinks by establishing their mathematical relationship to sink scores. Our findings yield a novel hallucination detection method grounded in theory that produces state-of-the-art results across popular datasets and LLMs.

paragraphs: A language model can produce a confident answer that is false or unsupported by its input. Attention maps offer internal clues about this behavior, but the mechanisms behind existing attention-based detectors remain unclear. This paper investigates attention sinks: tokens that attract an unusually large share of attention during generation.

The authors connect hallucinations with a shift toward these sinks. They interpret the pattern as a transition from attention distributed across the input toward more compressed computation dominated by the model’s prior knowledge. Their detector, SinkProbe, uses sink scores calculated entirely from attention maps. They also find that its classifier preferentially relies on sinks associated with value vectors of large norm.

Beyond introducing a detector, the paper establishes mathematical relationships between sink scores and earlier detection methods, showing that those methods implicitly depend on attention sinks. SinkProbe achieves reported state-of-the-art results across the evaluated datasets and language models. The contribution thus combines a predictive signal with an account of what previous attention-based signals were capturing.
summary.tldr: SinkProbe uses attention concentrated on particular tokens to detect hallucinations and explain signals exploited by earlier attention-based detectors.

title: Attention Sinks as Internal Signals for Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models

abstract: We study the sample complexity of the best-case Empirical Risk Minimizer in the setting of stochastic convex optimization. We show that there exists an instance in which the sample size is linear in the dimension, learning is possible, but the Empirical Risk Minimizer is likely to be unique and to overfit. This resolves an open question by Feldman. We also extend this to approximate ERMs. Building on our construction we also show that (constrained) Gradient Descent potentially overfits when horizon and learning rate grow w.r.t sample size. Specifically we provide a novel generalization lower bound of $\Omega\left(\sqrt{\eta T/m^{1.5}}\right)$ for Gradient Descent, where $\eta$ is the learning rate, $T$ is the horizon and $m$ is the sample size. This narrows down, exponentially, the gap between the best known upper bound of $O(\eta T/m)$ and existing lower bounds from previous constructions.

paragraphs: Empirical risk minimization chooses parameters that minimize loss on the observed training sample. This paper asks whether even the best possible choice among those minimizers can generalize poorly in stochastic convex optimization. The distinction matters because a failure caused only by choosing the wrong minimizer would leave open the possibility of fixing the selection rule.

The authors construct an instance where the sample size grows linearly with dimension and learning is possible, yet the empirical minimizer is likely to be unique and to overfit. Uniqueness removes the opportunity to choose a better empirical minimizer. The construction resolves the stated open question and extends to approximate minimizers, so requiring only near-optimal training loss does not eliminate the demonstrated failure.

The paper also establishes a possible overfitting failure for constrained gradient descent as learning rate and training horizon grow relative to sample size. Its generalization lower bound is Ω(√(ηT/m^1.5)), with learning rate η, horizon T, and sample size m. This exponentially narrows the stated gap to known upper bounds; it does not claim that every convex problem or gradient-descent run overfits.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs learnable convex problems where even the best empirical risk minimizer can overfit and strengthens generalization lower bounds for gradient descent.

title: All ERMs Can Fail in Stochastic Convex Optimization Lower Bounds in Linear Dimension

abstract: Solving large-scale Generalized Eigenvalue Problems (GEPs) is a fundamental yet computationally prohibitive task in science and engineering. As a promising direction, contour integral (CI) methods offer an efficient and parallelizable framework. However, their performance is critically dependent on the selection of integration contours—improper selection without reliable prior knowledge of eigenvalue distribution can incur significant computational overhead and compromise numerical accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose Deepcontour, a novel hybrid framework that integrates a deep learning-based spectral predictor with Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) for principled contour design. Specifically, Deepcontour utilizes its specialized Eigen-Neural-Operator (ENO) to provide rapid spectral distribution priors, driving a KDE module to automatically construct the optimized integration contours, which guide the CI solver to efficiently find the desired eigenvalues. Deepcontour achieves up to a 5.63x speedup across diverse scientific datasets while maintaining strict numerical rigor. By merging the predictive power of deep learning with the numerical rigor of classical solvers, this work establishes an efficient and robust paradigm for solving large-scale GEPs.

paragraphs: Large generalized eigenvalue problems are computationally demanding across science and engineering. Contour-integral solvers offer an efficient, parallelizable approach, but their performance depends strongly on the integration contours they use. Choosing contours without useful knowledge of the eigenvalue distribution can increase computation and weaken numerical accuracy.

Deepcontour combines a learned prediction stage with a classical numerical solver. Its Eigen-Neural-Operator rapidly estimates information about the spectral distribution. A kernel density estimation module uses that information to construct suitable integration contours automatically. Those contours then guide the contour-integral solver toward the desired eigenvalues, giving the predictive model a specific role in configuring the numerical computation.

The result shows how learned spectral priors can improve an important solver design choice without asking the predictor to perform the entire eigenvalue calculation. Its contribution is the connection between fast distributional prediction, systematic contour construction, and the accuracy-preserving work of the classical solver.
summary.tldr: Deepcontour uses learned spectral priors to construct integration contours, accelerating generalized eigensolvers by up to 5.63 times.

title: Learning-Guided Integration Contours Construction for Fast Large-Scale Generalized Eigensolvers

abstract: We consider an online learning problem in environments with multiple change points. In contrast to the single change point problem that is widely studied using classical "high confidence" detection schemes, the multiple change point environment presents new learning-theoretic and algorithmic challenges. Specifically, we show that classical methods may exhibit catastrophic failure (high regret) due to a phenomenon we refer to as endogenous confounding. To overcome this, we propose a new class of learning algorithms dubbed Anytime Tracking CUSUM (ATC). These are horizon-free online algorithms that implement a selective detection principle, balancing the need to ignore "small" (hard-to-detect) shifts, while reacting "quickly" to significant ones. We prove that the performance of a properly tuned ATC algorithm is nearly minimax-optimal; its regret is guaranteed to closely match a novel information-theoretic lower bound on the achievable performance of any learning algorithm in the multiple change point problem. Experiments on synthetic as well as real-world data validate the aforementioned theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Online learning becomes difficult when the environment changes repeatedly. Methods designed around confidently detecting a single change may perform poorly when changes occur multiple times. This paper identifies a failure mechanism called endogenous confounding and shows that classical methods can consequently suffer high regret.

The proposed Anytime Tracking CUSUM algorithms use selective detection. They balance ignoring small changes that are difficult to distinguish from uncertainty against responding quickly to significant shifts. They are horizon-free, meaning the algorithm does not require a predetermined endpoint for the learning process. This makes repeated adaptation central to the design.

For a properly tuned algorithm, the authors prove regret close to a new information-theoretic lower bound on what any learner can achieve in the multiple-change setting. This establishes nearly minimax-optimal performance under the stated tuning requirement. Synthetic and real-world experiments support the theoretical findings. The result explains why detecting every shift with high confidence is not the sole organizing principle for effective learning in repeatedly changing environments.
summary.tldr: Anytime Tracking CUSUM selectively responds to significant changes and achieves nearly minimax-optimal regret when properly tuned.

title: The Cost of Learning Under Multiple Change Points

abstract: Simulation plays a central role in scientific discovery. In many applications, the bottleneck is no longer running a simulator—it is choosing among large families of plausible simulators, each corresponding to different forward models/hypotheses consistent with observations. Over large model families, classical Bayesian workflows for model-selection are impractical. Furthermore, amortized model-selection methods typically hard-code a fixed model prior—or complexity penalty—at training time, requiring users to commit to a particular parsimony assumption before seeing the data. We introduce PRISM, a simulation-based encoder-decoder that infers a joint posterior over both discrete model structures and associated continuous parameters, while enabling test-time control of model complexity via a tunable model prior that the network is conditioned on. We show that PRISM scales to families with combinatorially many (up to billions of) model instantiations on a synthetic symbolic regression task. As a scientific application, we evaluate PRISM on biophysical modeling for diffusion MRI data, showing the ability to perform model selection across several multi-compartment models, on both synthetic and in-vivo neuroimaging data.
