title: Scalable Simulation-Based Model Inference with Test-Time Complexity Control

abstract: Reassembling $N$ fragments in $n$-dimensional space is a shape reconstruction task that is invariant to global rigid motions. Training directly on $\mathcal{M}=\mathrm{SE}(n)^N$ can be ill-posed: standard losses penalize solutions that differ only by a global transform. Existing methods often address this with ad-hoc anchoring which breaks permutation invariance across fragments and can introduce biases that must be mitigated with extensive and costly data augmentation. We propose a geometric framework that enforces invariance by construction. First, a Global Gauge Fixing (GGF) strategy deterministically aligns configurations using an intrinsic generalized-inertia rule. Second, we introduce a quotient-invariant Flow Matching objective that operates via orthogonal projection onto the horizontal tangent bundle. This construction factors out global pose at each timestep, enabling the model to learn only shape-changing dynamics on the quotient space $\mathcal{M}/\mathrm{SE}(n)$. Our unified $\mathrm{SE}(n)$-invariant framework admits efficient closed-form 2D/3D instantiations and improves accuracy on polygonal jigsaw puzzles and 3D fracture reassembly benchmarks.

summary.tldr: This flow-matching framework factors out global rigid motion so object reassembly models learn relative shape changes without arbitrary fragment anchoring.

title: SE(n)-Invariant Flow Matching: A General Framework with Application to Object Reassembly

abstract: We address the challenge of uncovering systematic, and potentially controllable, dynamical structure underlying complex high-dimensional time-series data. Existing generative and autoregressive models have difficulty telling systematic content apart from distractors, while contrastive methods struggle to learn accurate dynamics. To address these shortcomings, we develop the Recognition-Parametrized Gaussian State-Space Model (RP-GSSM), a probabilistic framework that infers accurate latent dynamics without relying on a parametrized decoder. By eliminating explicit generative parameters, the model directs its entire representational capacity to encoding dynamically relevant state; and, being fully probabilistic, learns via maximum likelihood without auxiliary objectives or ad-hoc regularization. Combining the expressive power of a neural network encoder with exact inference under a jointly Gaussian prior allows the RP-GSSM to embed a broad class of intrinsically nonlinear dynamical systems. The RP-GSSM parameters are provably linearly identifiable in the infinite data limit. We show that the RP-GSSM recovers physically meaningful latent states from noisy video more faithfully than competing methods, more reliably identifies underlying controllable nonlinear dynamics, and remains substantially more robust to visual distractors.

title: Maximum-Likelihood Learning of Latent Dynamics Without Reconstruction

abstract: Real-world machine learning (ML) pipelines rarely produce a single model; instead, they produce a Rashomon set of many near-optimal ones. We show that this multiplicity reshapes key aspects of trustworthiness. At the individual-model level, sparse interpretable models tend to preserve privacy but are fragile to adversarial attacks. In contrast, the diversity within a large Rashomon set enables reactive robustness: even when an attack compromises one model, a practitioner can switch to a different near-optimal model that remains accurate, without retraining. However, the same diversity increases information leakage, as disclosing more near-optimal models provides an attacker with progressively richer views of the training data. This produces a robustness–privacy trade-off governed by diversity, which we analyze theoretically and empirically. Beyond this trade-off, Rashomon sets are stable under small distribution shifts, so a set computed once remains valid under such shifts without re-computation. Our results highlight the dual role of Rashomon sets as both a resource and a risk for trustworthy ML.

They additionally show stability of Rashomon sets under small distribution shifts, allowing a previously computed set to remain valid without recomputation under such shifts. The findings make model multiplicity both a practical resource for responding to attacks and a source of privacy risk when models are disclosed.
summary.tldr: Diverse near-optimal models support switching after attacks, but disclosing more of them increases training-data leakage.

title: The Double-Edged Nature of the Rashomon Set for Trustworthy Machine Learning

abstract: We study differentially private (DP) regression in settings where each data sample includes public, non-sensitive features—common in applications like recommendation or advertising systems. While such label DP or DP with semi-sensitive features settings have been primarily explored in the context of classification, effective approaches for regression remain underexplored. We introduce $\textsf{Cond-DP}$, a conditioned variant of $\textsf{DPSGD}$ that leverages the structure of public feature matrices to improve optimization under privacy constraints. Motivated by the observation that these public features often exhibit rapidly decaying spectra, $\textsf{Cond-DP}$ incorporates a data-driven conditioning matrix to reshape the optimization landscape and accelerate convergence. We provide convergence guarantees for convex, strongly convex and non-convex settings, and recover standard $\textsf{DPSGD}$ as a special case when the conditioning matrix is the identity. We show how to construct an effective conditioning matrix for $\textsf{Cond-DP}$ directly from public features, enabling faster convergence than $\textsf{DPSGD}$ in private linear regression, without incurring additional privacy cost. Empirically, $\textsf{Cond-DP}$ with this conditioning matrix consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across a wide range of datasets and model architectures under label DP, demonstrating strong and robust performance in practice.

The privacy setting is central: the conditioning information comes from features already designated public, while the learning task retains its stated protection for sensitive information.
summary.tldr: Cond-DP uses public feature structure to accelerate private regression without additional privacy cost.

title: Private Learning with Public Feature Conditioning

abstract: In RL post-training of LLM agents, calls to external tools take several seconds or even minutes, leaving allocated GPUs idle and inflating post-training time and cost. While many tool invocations repeat across parallel rollouts and could in principle be cached, naively caching their outputs for reuse is incorrect since tool outputs depend on the environment state induced by prior agent interactions. We present TVCACHE, a stateful tool-value cache for LLM agent post-training. TVCACHE maintains a tree of observed tool-call sequences and performs longest-prefix matching for cache lookups: a hit occurs only when the agent’s full tool history matches a previously executed sequence, guaranteeing identical environment state. On three diverse workloads—terminal-based tasks, SQL generation, and video understanding—TVCACHE achieves cache hit rates of up to 67% and reduces median tool call execution time by up to 6.9$\times$, with no degradation in post-training reward accumulation.

paragraphs: During reinforcement-learning post-training, language-model agents can spend seconds or minutes waiting for external tools while allocated GPUs sit idle. Repeated calls create an opportunity to reuse results, but the same call can produce different outputs after different prior interactions. A useful cache must therefore account for the environment state created by the agent’s history.

TVCACHE organizes observed tool-call sequences into a tree and uses longest-prefix matching to find reusable results. A cache hit requires the full tool history to match a previously executed sequence, which the framework uses to guarantee an identical environment state. This makes the sequence of interactions part of the lookup, rather than treating each tool invocation as an isolated request.

The authors evaluate the system on terminal tasks, SQL generation, and video understanding. They report cache hit rates up to 67% and reductions in median tool-call execution time of up to 6.9 times, without degrading reward accumulation during post-training. The results show how history-aware reuse can reduce a substantial waiting cost in agent training.
summary.tldr: TVCACHE reuses tool outputs only for matching interaction histories, reducing tool latency without degrading reward accumulation in the evaluated workloads.

title: Tvcache: A Tool-Value Cache for Post-Training LLM Agents

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning abilities, while smaller models ($\leq$ 3B parameters) significantly underperform on multi-step reasoning tasks. Based on empirical analyses of the Qwen-2.5 model family on math reasoning benchmarks, we find that more proficient reasoning is associated with fewer reasoning steps but higher information density per step, a property we term Dense Reasoning. Motivated by this observation, we propose DenseSteer, a training-free inference-time steering framework that enhances small-model reasoning by modulating internal representations toward dense reasoning patterns. Experiments show that our method yields consistent accuracy improvements without increasing token-level Negative Log-Likelihood, highlighting dense reasoning as an effective structural approach to mathematical problem solving.

paragraphs: Small language models often struggle with mathematical problems that require several reasoning steps. This paper examines the Qwen-2.5 family and finds an association between stronger reasoning and a particular structure: fewer steps, with more information carried by each step. The authors call this pattern dense reasoning, emphasizing the content of the steps rather than their sheer number.

DenseSteer turns that observation into an inference-time intervention for models with at most three billion parameters. It modifies internal representations to steer generation toward dense reasoning patterns. The framework requires no additional training, so its contribution is a way to influence how an existing small model reasons while it produces an answer.

Experiments report consistent accuracy improvements without an increase in token-level negative log-likelihood. Thus, the measured improvement in mathematical answers does not come with a deterioration in that token-level measure. The initial association alone does not establish that shorter reasoning is universally better; the intervention results support dense reasoning as a useful structural target for the small-model mathematical reasoning settings studied.
summary.tldr: DenseSteer improves small-model math accuracy by steering internal representations toward information-dense reasoning without additional training.

title: DenseSteer: Steering Small Language Models towards Dense Math Reasoning

abstract: The training of deep Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) has traditionally relied on Batch Normalization (BN), which stabilizes input currents and gradients during training. However, BN is not a universal solution. It is unsuitable for variable-length tasks and scenarios with reduced batch size, constraining the development of deep SNNs, where removing BN typically causes the training to fail to converge. This dependence stems not from a fundamental necessity of BN but from the current lack of reasonable initialization methods for SNNs. This paper addresses this core limitation by proposing SpikeInit, a novel initialization framework for SNNs. By modeling the response curve and gradient of spiking layers, SpikeInit initializes the weights and shape parameters of surrogate gradients to maintain stable firing rates during forward propagation and stable gradient magnitudes during backpropagation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that deep SNNs with SpikeInit can be trained stably without normalization and achieve superior performance compared to their normalized counterparts under identical settings. Furthermore, we demonstrate the scalability of SpikeInit by successfully training an ultra-deep, 1000-layer SNN without normalization. Our work provides a foundational step toward large-scale normalization-free SNN, liberating SNN design from the constraints of normalization.

The authors argue that this dependence reflects inadequate initialization rather than a fundamental requirement of spiking networks.

These choices target two connected goals: keeping firing rates stable as signals move forward and keeping gradient magnitudes stable as learning signals move backward.

The findings make initialization a concrete alternative for stabilizing deep spiking networks and support further development of architectures freed from the stated constraints of batch normalization.
summary.tldr: SpikeInit stabilizes firing rates and gradients through initialization, enabling normalization-free training of deep spiking networks, including a 1,000-layer model.

title: Training Deep Spiking Neural Networks without Normalization

abstract: Recent advancements in Reinforcement Learning (RL), particularly Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), have significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models. However, applying these problem-centric optimization methods to role-playing agents often leads to a loss of character fidelity and style collapse, as they prioritize context-specific utility over persona alignment. To address this, we propose Character-Centric Group Relative Policy Optimization (CRPO), a framework designed to realign RL objectives with the role-playing task. CRPO improves character distinctiveness through three mechanisms: decoupling task logic from stylistic rewards to resolve gradient conflicts, dynamically adapting optimization constraints based on character complexity, and utilizing generic responses as negative baselines to prevent the model from reverting to a common distribution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CRPO outperforms existing methods in consistency, emotion and others.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning methods that improve problem solving can create trouble for role-playing agents. Optimizing an answer for its immediate usefulness may weaken the character’s distinctive voice or persona. This paper treats that loss of fidelity as a mismatch between the training objective and what successful role-playing requires.

Character-Centric Group Relative Policy Optimization, or CRPO, changes the objective through three mechanisms. It separates task logic from stylistic rewards to reduce conflicts between their training signals. It adjusts optimization constraints to account for character complexity. It also uses generic responses as negative baselines, discouraging the model from drifting toward an undifferentiated style shared across characters.

Together, these mechanisms make character distinctiveness an explicit part of reinforcement learning. The reported experiments find improvements over existing methods in consistency, emotion, and other evaluated aspects. The result supports training role-aware reasoning with objectives that directly account for persona, so that better task performance can coexist with more faithful characterization.
summary.tldr: CRPO adapts reinforcement learning for role-playing by separating logic and style rewards, adjusting constraints, and discouraging generic responses.

title: CRPO: Character-centric Group Relative Policy Optimization for Role-aware Reasoning in Role-playing Agents

abstract: Generative priors in Image Super-Resolution (SR) often compromise faithful restoration, we attribute this limitation to a fundamental spectral misalignment between isotropic objectives and the intrinsic natural image manifold. While Direct Preference Optimization offers a path to alignment, its reliance on spectrally flat Gaussian noise fails to distinguish authentic high-frequency details from hallucinations. To bridge this geometric gap, we propose ASASR, a theoretically grounded framework that recasts the generative flow into a Sobolev-induced Riemannian geometry by explicitly coloring the noise transition kernel to mirror natural spectral decay. Driving this geometric alignment, we integrate a parametric adversary grounded in the Riesz Representation Theorem, which synthesizes targeted negative samples equivalent to worst-case Sobolev gradients to direct optimization along the tangent space of plausible structural failures. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that ASASR outperforms leading generative baselines, particularly in preserving spectral consistency and structural fidelity, offering a robust solution that effectively mitigates artifacts.

paragraphs: Generative image super-resolution can produce convincing detail that does not faithfully reflect the underlying image. This paper attributes that problem to a mismatch between training objectives that treat directions uniformly and the frequency structure of natural images. In particular, it argues that spectrally flat Gaussian noise in preference optimization does not adequately distinguish genuine fine detail from hallucinated detail.

The proposed ASASR framework changes the geometry of the generative process using a Sobolev construction. Its noise transition is explicitly colored so that its frequency profile follows natural spectral decay. This makes frequency structure part of the optimization itself. A learned adversary then constructs targeted negative examples corresponding to worst-case Sobolev gradients, directing training toward plausible ways that image structure can fail.

Evaluations report improvements over leading generative baselines, especially in spectral consistency and structural fidelity, together with reduced artifacts. The significance is the connection between how training noise is shaped and what restoration errors the model learns to distinguish. The approach aims to make generated detail more faithful by combining frequency-aware geometry with deliberately challenging structural examples.
summary.tldr: ASASR reshapes training noise and constructs adversarial structural errors to improve the fidelity of generative image super-resolution.

title: Coloring the Noise: Adversarial Sobolev Alignment for Faithful Image Super Resolution

abstract: Progressive Learning (PL) reduces pre-training computational overhead by gradually increasing model scale. While prior work has extensively explored depth expansion, width expansion remains significantly understudied, with the few existing methods limited to the early stages of training. However, expanding width during the mid-stage is essential for maximizing computational savings, yet it remains a formidable challenge due to severe training instabilities. Empirically, we show that naive initialization at this stage disrupts activation statistics, triggering loss spikes, while copy-based initialization introduces gradient symmetry that hinders feature diversity. To address these issues, we propose SPARKLING (balancing Signal Preservation And symmetRy breaKing for width-progressive LearnING), a novel framework for mid-stage width expansion. Our method achieves signal preservation via RMS-scale consistency, stabilizing activation statistics during expansion. Symmetry breaking is ensured through asymmetric optimizer state reset and asymmetric learning rate re-warmup. Extensive experiments on dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models demonstrate that, across multiple width axes and optimizer families, SPARKLING consistently outperforms training from scratch and reduces training cost by up to 35% under $2\times$ width expansion.

This paper focuses on increasing width partway through training, where instability makes expansion difficult. The authors find that naive initialization disrupts activation statistics and causes loss spikes, while copying existing components creates gradient symmetry that restricts feature diversity.

SPARKLING addresses these two problems separately. RMS-scale consistency preserves the scale of signals during expansion, stabilizing activation statistics. Asymmetric resets of optimizer state and asymmetric learning-rate re-warmup break the symmetry that would otherwise make copied components learn too similarly.

summary.tldr: SPARKLING stabilizes mid-training width expansion while encouraging feature diversity, reducing training cost by up to 35% under doubled width.

title: SPARKLING: Balancing Signal Preservation and Symmetry Breaking for Width-Progressive Learning

abstract: As LLM-powered agents have been used for high-stakes decision-making, such as clinical diagnosis, it becomes critical to develop reliable verification of their decisions to facilitate trustworthy deployment. Yet, existing verifiers usually underperform owing to a lack of domain knowledge and limited calibration. To address this, we establish GLEAN, an agent verification framework with GuideLine-grounded Evidence AccumulatioN that compiles expert-curated protocols into trajectory-informed, well-calibrated correctness signals. GLEAN evaluates the step-wise alignment with domain guidelines and aggregates multi-guideline ratings into surrogate features, which are accumulated along the trajectory and calibrated into correctness probabilities using Bayesian logistic regression. Moreover, the estimated uncertainty triggers active verification, which selectively collects additional evidence for uncertain cases via expanding guideline coverage and performing differential checks. We empirically validate GLEAN with agentic clinical diagnosis across three diseases from the MIMIC-IV dataset, surpassing the best baseline by 12% in AUROC and 50% in Brier score reduction, which confirms the effectiveness in both discrimination and calibration. In addition, the expert study with clinicians recognizes GLEAN’s utility in practice.

paragraphs: GLEAN verifies decisions made by language-model agents using expert-curated guidelines. Its motivation is that a verifier needs both relevant domain knowledge and confidence estimates that reflect actual correctness. The framework examines an agent’s sequence of decisions, allowing its assessment to incorporate how the agent reached an answer.

At each step, GLEAN rates alignment with multiple guidelines and combines those ratings into features. Evidence accumulates across the trajectory, and Bayesian logistic regression converts it into a calibrated probability of correctness. When uncertainty remains high, the framework actively seeks more evidence by expanding guideline coverage and performing differential checks. Verification effort is therefore directed toward cases where the existing assessment is less settled.

In clinical-diagnosis experiments covering three diseases in MIMIC-IV, GLEAN surpasses the best baseline by 12% in AUROC and reduces Brier score by 50%. These results indicate improvements in distinguishing correct from incorrect decisions and in the accuracy of confidence estimates. A clinician study also recognizes the framework’s practical utility.
summary.tldr: GLEAN accumulates guideline-based evidence and selectively investigates uncertain cases to produce better-calibrated assessments of agent decisions.

title: GLEAN: Guideline-Grounded Evidence Accumulation for High-Stakes Agent Verification

abstract: Grounding Large Language Models (LLMs) in Knowledge Graphs (KGs) has shown significant promise for complex Question Answering (QA) tasks. Since LLMs’ limited context window cannot accommodate the sheer volume of large-scale KGs, existing work usually utilizes agents to reason on real-world KGs, which follows reasoning paths derived from the queries step by step. However, the mismatch between query-derived paths and the KG’s structure, stemming from users’ lack of schema knowledge, usually leads the agents into dead ends. To address this problem, in this paper, we propose Backjump-on-Graph (BoG), a novel framework that empowers LLMs to retrospectively explore alternative reasoning paths at dead ends. We first propose to formalize each reasoning step with four atomic operations to create a structural scaffold that allows LLMs to revert to historical status. Next, we fine-tune the LLM with synthetic data containing the above atomic operations to instill basic backjump abilities. Finally, we leverage reinforcement learning and propose a hybrid reward function, which penalizes redundant transitions and promotes correct answers, to optimize the timing and landing nodes of backjumping. Extensive experiments on several KGQA benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our BoG method.

Backjump-on-Graph gives agents a structured way to revisit earlier states and try alternative routes. The framework expresses reasoning steps through four atomic operations, creating a scaffold for recovering historical states. It trains the agent to choose both when to jump back and which earlier node to return to. Experiments on several knowledge-graph question-answering benchmarks demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The approach makes recovery from unsuccessful exploration an explicit learned capability, addressing the mismatch between question-derived plans and available graph paths.
summary.tldr: Backjump-on-Graph trains language-model agents to recover from knowledge-graph dead ends by revisiting earlier nodes and exploring alternative paths.

title: Backjump-on-Graph: Empowering Large Language Models with Reinforced Retrospective Exploration for Agentic Knowledge Graph Reasoning

abstract: Flow Matching enables simulation-free training of generative models on Riemannian manifolds, yet sampling typically still relies on numerically integrating a probability-flow ODE. We propose Riemannian MeanFlow (RMF), extending MeanFlow to manifold-valued generation where velocities lie in location-dependent tangent spaces. RMF defines an average-velocity field via parallel transport and derives a Riemannian MeanFlow identity that links average and instantaneous velocities for intrinsic supervision. We make this identity practical in a log-map tangent representation, avoiding trajectory simulation and heavy geometric computations. For stable optimization, we decompose the RMF objective into two terms and apply conflict-aware multi-task learning to mitigate gradient interference. RMF also supports conditional generation via classifier-free guidance. Experiments on spheres, tori, SO(3), and SE(3) demonstrate competitive one-step sampling with improved quality–efficiency trade-offs and substantially reduced sampling cost.

paragraphs: Flow matching can train generative models on curved spaces without simulating trajectories during training, yet generating samples typically still requires numerical integration. Riemannian MeanFlow targets one-step generation on these spaces. The geometric challenge is that velocity vectors belong to tangent spaces that depend on location, complicating the definition of an average velocity.

RMF uses parallel transport to define an average-velocity field and derives an identity relating average and instantaneous velocities. A log-map tangent representation makes that identity practical for supervision while avoiding trajectory simulation and heavy geometric calculations. This supplies the geometric machinery needed to extend MeanFlow beyond ordinary flat-space generation.

For more stable optimization, the method divides its objective into two terms and applies conflict-aware multi-task learning to reduce interference between their gradients. It also supports conditional generation through classifier-free guidance. Experiments on spheres, tori, SO(3), and SE(3) demonstrate competitive one-step sampling, improved quality–efficiency trade-offs, and substantially lower sampling cost, supporting the approach across the evaluated manifold geometries.
summary.tldr: Riemannian MeanFlow adapts average-velocity learning to curved spaces for competitive one-step generation with reduced sampling cost.

title: Riemannian MeanFlow for One-Step Generation on Manifolds

abstract: Neural scene representations achieve high-fidelity rendering by encoding 3D scenes as continuous functions, but their latent spaces are typically implicit and globally entangled, making localized editing and physically grounded manipulation difficult. While several works introduce explicit control structures or point-based latent representations to improve editability, these approaches often suffer from limited locality, sensitivity to deformations, or visual artifacts. In this paper, we introduce Affine-Equivariant Kernel Space Encoding (EKS), a spatial encoding for neural radiance fields that provides localized, deformation-aware feature representations. Instead of querying latent features directly at discrete points or grid vertices, our encoding aggregates features through a field of anisotropic Gaussian kernels, each defining a localized region of influence. This kernel-based formulation enables stable feature interpolation under spatial transformations while preserving continuity and high reconstruction quality. To preserve detail without sacrificing editability, we further propose a training-time feature distillation mechanism that transfers information from multi-resolution hash grid encodings into the kernel field, yielding a compact and fully grid-free representation at inference. This enables intuitive, localized scene editing directly via Gaussian kernels without retraining, while maintaining high-quality rendering.

paragraphs: Neural radiance fields can render detailed scenes, but their internal representations often entangle information across space. This makes changing one region difficult without affecting others or introducing artifacts. The paper introduces Affine-Equivariant Kernel Space Encoding, or EKS, to make scene features more local and better behaved when the scene is spatially transformed.

Instead of reading features directly from individual points or grid corners, EKS combines them through anisotropic Gaussian kernels. Each kernel defines a localized region of influence whose shape can vary by direction. This provides a continuous feature field and supports stable interpolation under transformations. The kernels also become explicit controls through which a user can make localized scene edits.

To retain fine detail, training transfers information from a multi-resolution hash grid into the kernel representation through feature distillation. The resulting inference representation is compact and no longer requires that grid. The paper reports that this design supports localized editing through the Gaussian kernels without retraining, while maintaining high reconstruction and rendering quality.
summary.tldr: EKS uses localized Gaussian kernels and training-time feature distillation to support detailed NeRF editing without retraining.

title: Affine-Equivariant Kernel Space Encoding for NeRF Editing

abstract: Vector Quantization (VQ) has been widely used in visual and audio representation due to its effectiveness in compressing high-dimensional signals. However, existing VQ methods often rely on large and unstructured codebooks, which leads to inefficient code utilization and frequent codebook collapse. In this paper, we propose IChing Vector Quantization (IVQ), a lightweight and structured VQ framework inspired by IChing. IVQ introduces binary hierarchical composition and geometric symmetry relations into the codebook design, enabling a compact set of structured codes to represent the latent space while maintaining high utilization without codebook collapse. Experimental results show that IVQ achieves superior quality with significantly smaller codebooks and consistently higher utilization rates compared to several VQ variants in audio representation. Auxiliary experiments on visual reconstruction and cross-modal generation further validate the universality and robustness of IVQ. Codes are released at https://github.com/chouliuzuo/IVQ.

paragraphs: Vector quantization compresses visual or audio representations using a collection of discrete codes. Large, unstructured codebooks can be used inefficiently, with some codes receiving little use and codebook collapse reducing the effective representation. IVQ addresses this problem by building organization into the codebook itself, drawing inspiration from IChing.

The design combines binary hierarchical composition with geometric symmetry relationships. This gives a compact collection of codes a structured way to represent the latent space. The intended benefit is to maintain broad code use without collapse while reducing the size of the codebook needed for useful representations.

In audio experiments, IVQ achieves better quality with substantially smaller codebooks and consistently higher utilization than several vector-quantization variants. Additional experiments on visual reconstruction and cross-modal generation support its applicability beyond audio. These results make the codebook’s internal organization central to the contribution: a smaller structured vocabulary can represent signals effectively when its available codes are used more fully.
summary.tldr: IVQ organizes discrete codes through binary hierarchy and symmetry, reporting better audio quality with smaller, more fully used codebooks.

title: IVQ: Structured and Lightweight Vector Quantization via Binary Hierarchical Composition Inspired by $\textitIChing$

abstract: This position paper argues that current benchmarking practice in 12-lead ECG representation learning must be fixed to ensure progress is reliable and aligned with clinically meaningful objectives. The field has largely converged on three public multi-label benchmarks (PTB-XL, CPSC2018, CSN) dominated by arrhythmia and waveform-morphology labels, even though the ECG is known to encode substantially broader clinical information. We argue that downstream evaluation should expand to include an assessment of structural heart disease and patient-level forecasting, in addition to other evolving ECG-related endpoints, as relevant clinical targets. Next, we outline evaluation best practices for multi-label, imbalanced settings, and show that when they are applied, the literature’s current conclusion about which representations perform best is altered. Furthermore, we demonstrate the surprising result that a randomly initialized encoder with linear evaluation matches state-of-the-art pre-training on many tasks. This motivates the use of a random encoder as a reasonable baseline model. We substantiate our observations with an empirical evaluation of five representative ECG pre-training approaches across six evaluation settings: the three standard benchmarks, a structural disease dataset, hemodynamic inference, and patient forecasting.

paragraphs: This paper argues that evaluating learned representations of 12-lead electrocardiograms requires broader clinical targets and stronger evaluation practices. Three public benchmarks dominate the field, emphasizing rhythm abnormalities and waveform features. The authors contend that this scope overlooks other clinical information encoded in ECGs, including information relevant to structural heart disease and patient forecasting.

They evaluate five representative pretraining approaches in six settings: the three standard benchmarks, structural disease, hemodynamic inference, and patient forecasting. They also outline practices for evaluating tasks where multiple labels can apply and some labels are much rarer than others. Applying these practices changes the prevailing conclusion about which representations perform best.

A particularly striking finding is that a randomly initialized encoder, assessed through linear evaluation, matches leading pretrained approaches on many tasks. The authors therefore recommend including a random encoder as a reasonable baseline. This result makes the contribution of pretraining itself more important to establish, while its stated scope remains many tasks rather than every setting. Together, the findings support revising both what ECG benchmarks measure and how competing approaches are compared.
summary.tldr: Broader clinical targets and better evaluation practices change ECG representation comparisons, with random encoders matching leading pretraining on many tasks.

title: Position: Evaluation of ECG Representations Must Be Fixed

abstract: AI-driven automation threatens to erode government tax bases, lower living standards, and disempower citizens—risks that mirror the 40-year stagnation of wages during the first industrial revolution. While AI safety research has focused primarily on capability risks, comparatively little work has studied how to mitigate the economic risks of AI. This position paper argues that technical governance researchers should prioritize the study of token taxes: usage-based surcharges on model inference applied at the point of sale. We situate token taxes within previous proposals for robot taxes and identify two key advantages: they are enforceable through existing compute governance infrastructure, and they capture value where AI is used rather than where models are hosted. We then present a research roadmap. For enforcement, we outline a staged audit pipeline—black-box token verification, norm-based tax rates, and white-box audits—and identify open technical problems at each stage. For impact, we highlight the need for economic modeling of cost pass-through and deadweight loss. Finally, we discuss why FLOP taxes may be preferable, token taxes could stifle innovation, and how to prevent AI superpowers from vetoing such measures.

paragraphs: This position paper calls for research on token taxes as a response to AI automation’s economic risks. These taxes would add usage-based surcharges to model inference at the point of sale. The authors motivate the proposal through potential erosion of government revenues, lower living standards, and reduced citizen power.

The paper places token taxes within earlier proposals to tax robots and identifies two advantages: possible enforcement through existing compute-governance infrastructure and collection of value where AI is used rather than where models are hosted. It proposes a staged enforcement research agenda involving black-box token verification, norm-based rates, and white-box audits, with technical questions remaining at each stage.

They discuss whether taxes based on computation could be preferable, whether token taxes might inhibit innovation, and how powerful AI actors could obstruct adoption. The result is a research roadmap for evaluating feasibility and consequences, with the policy’s potential benefits weighed against explicit tradeoffs.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes a technical and economic research agenda for usage-based AI taxes, including enforcement, cost pass-through, and innovation tradeoffs.

title: Position: Token Taxes Can Mitigate AI’s Economic Risks

abstract: Whether deep vision models recognize objects primarily by shape or texture remains a central and unresolved question in computer vision. Early studies report a strong texture bias in convolutional neural networks (CNNs), while other work reports shape-biased representations. We argue that much of this apparent discrepancy reflects methodological confounds and a conflation of local contour sensitivity with genuine global shape understanding. Using minimal, tightly controlled stimuli, we directly compare cue-conflict and cue-suppression paradigms within a unified experimental framework. We show that standard CNNs consistently prioritize texture over global shape when cues compete, even when shape information is explicitly available. Evidence for shape bias typically reflects reliance on local fragments rather than invariant, relational representations of object structure. Our findings support the view that texture bias is fundamentally rooted in architectural inductive biases rather than data or optimization alone. This gap has direct consequences for robustness, safety, and generalization, and motivates the development of architectures that explicitly support global integration and relational reasoning, moving beyond incremental data-driven fixes. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/alikayyam/shape_vs_texture.

paragraphs: Studies disagree about whether convolutional neural networks primarily recognize texture or shape. This paper argues that some of the disagreement comes from experimental confounds and from treating sensitivity to small contour fragments as evidence of understanding an object’s overall structure. Distinguishing those abilities changes how claims of shape recognition should be interpreted.

The authors use minimal, tightly controlled stimuli to compare experiments where cues compete with experiments where cues are suppressed. Within this shared framework, standard CNNs consistently favor texture over global shape when the cues conflict, even with shape information available. Apparent shape bias typically reflects dependence on local fragments rather than stable representations of relationships across the whole object.

The findings support the authors’ view that architectural tendencies are a fundamental source of texture bias, beyond data and optimization alone. They motivate architectures designed for global integration and relational reasoning. The paper connects this representational gap to robustness, safety, and generalization, arguing that incremental changes to training data do not adequately address the underlying problem.
summary.tldr: Controlled experiments support the view that standard CNNs favor texture over global shape, motivating architectural changes.

title: Position: CNNs Don’t See Shape — And That Won’t Change Without New Architectures

abstract: Physiological waveforms (e.g., ECG, PPG, EEG) encode clinically meaningful information in fine-grained morphology, precise timing, and cross-channel dynamics, yet most machine learning systems still treat them as generic time series and optimize end-to-end prediction. In this position paper, we argue for verifiable physiological waveform reasoning: extracting localized, measurable signal evidence from raw signals, interpreting that evidence into physiological semantics, and supporting clinically grounded decisions. Waveform reasoning is challenging due to acquisition heterogeneity, signal fidelity, complex semantics and cross-channel coupled dynamics. We analyze why existing model families remain insufficient: physiological foundation models learn strong perceptual representations but remain weak at verifiable reasoning, while LLM-based adaptations have limited waveform understanding. To bridge this gap, we advocate verifiable, closed-loop systems that unify waveform semantics with language intelligence. Concretely, we propose a dual-process architecture that System 1 aligns physiological waveforms with language, and System 2 provides agentic reasoning via a Plan–Act–Verify loop, together enabling verifiable physiological waveform reasoning. We further propose evaluations beyond accuracy, emphasizing traceability, replayability, counterfactual robustness, and calibrated abstention.

paragraphs: Physiological signals carry information in precise shapes, timing, and relationships across channels. The paper argues that treating these signals as generic sequences for prediction leaves an important clinical reasoning objective underdeveloped. It proposes a process that identifies measurable evidence in particular signal regions, interprets its physiological meaning, and uses that interpretation to support clinically grounded decisions.

The authors identify complementary weaknesses in existing approaches. Physiological foundation models can learn strong perceptual representations but have limited verifiable reasoning, while adaptations built around language models have limited waveform understanding. Differences in acquisition, signal quality, complex meanings, and coupled channels make joining these capabilities challenging.

Their proposed architecture has two processes: one aligns waveform information with language, and another performs agentic reasoning through a Plan–Act–Verify loop. This is a proposal for a closed-loop system connecting interpretation with verification. The accompanying evaluation agenda goes beyond accuracy to include evidence traceability, replayability, robustness to counterfactual changes, and calibrated decisions to abstain.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes combining waveform understanding with agentic verification to support physiological reasoning grounded in measurable signal evidence.

abstract: Sampling is a popular way of scaling up machine learning algorithms to large datasets. The question often is how many samples are needed. Adaptive stopping algorithms monitor the performance in an online fashion and make it possible to stop early, sparing valuable computation time. We concentrate on the setting where probabilistic guarantees are desired and demonstrate how recently-introduced empirical Bernstein bounds can be used to design stopping rules that are efficient. We provide upper bounds on the sample complexity of the new rules as well as empirical results on model selection and boosting in the filtering setting.

paragraphs: Sampling can reduce the work required by machine learning algorithms on large datasets, but it leaves an important decision: how many samples are enough? This paper studies adaptive stopping, where an algorithm monitors information as samples arrive and decides when it can stop. Early stopping can spare computation that further sampling would otherwise consume.

The authors focus on settings that require probabilistic guarantees. They show how empirical Bernstein bounds can be used to construct efficient stopping rules, connecting the stopping decision to a formal statistical guarantee. The aim is to make sampling adaptive while preserving the assurance required by the task.

The paper provides upper bounds on the sample complexity of the new rules and reports empirical results for model selection and boosting in a filtering setting. These contributions address both how much sampling the rules can require and how they behave in applications. Their significance is a principled way to determine when additional sampling is unnecessary under the desired probabilistic criteria.
summary.tldr: Empirical Bernstein bounds yield adaptive sampling rules with probabilistic guarantees and upper bounds on sample requirements.

title: Empirical Bernstein stopping

abstract: This paper explores online learning approaches for detecting malicious Web sites (those involved in criminal scams) using lexical and host-based features of the associated URLs. We show that this application is particularly appropriate for online algorithms as the size of the training data is larger than can be efficiently processed in batch and because the distribution of features that typify malicious URLs is changing continuously. Using a real-time system we developed for gathering URL features, combined with a real-time source of labeled URLs from a large Web mail provider, we demonstrate that recently-developed online algorithms can be as accurate as batch techniques, achieving classification accuracies up to 99% over a balanced data set.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify malicious websites from features associated with their URLs. It uses lexical information about the URL itself alongside host-based information. The application presents two challenges: training data can exceed what batch methods process efficiently, and the features associated with malicious URLs change continually.

The authors investigate online learning, which updates a model as data arrives. This approach fits a setting where both the volume of examples and the evolving distribution matter. To evaluate it, they develop a real-time system for gathering URL features and combine that system with a real-time stream of labeled URLs supplied by a large webmail provider.

The experiments show that the online algorithms studied can match the accuracy of batch techniques, with classification accuracy reaching up to 99% on a balanced dataset. The balanced-data qualification is part of the reported result. The finding supports online learning as a practical way to handle this large, changing classification problem without necessarily sacrificing the accuracy achieved by batch training.
summary.tldr: Online learning detects malicious URLs as accurately as batch methods in the reported experiments, reaching up to 99% accuracy on balanced data.

title: Identifying suspicious URLs: an application of large-scale online learning

abstract: We analyze a family of probability distributions that are characterized by an embedded combinatorial structure. This family includes models having arbitrary treewidth and arbitrary sized factors. Unlike general models with such freedom, where the �most probable explanation� (MPE) problem is inapproximable, the combinatorial structure within our model, in particular the indirect use of submodularity, leads to several MPE algorithms that all have approximation guarantees.
originalAbstract: We analyze a family of probability distributions that are characterized by an embedded combinatorial structure. This family includes models having arbitrary treewidth and arbitrary sized factors. Unlike general models with such freedom, where the �most probable explanation� (MPE) problem is inapproximable, the combinatorial structure within our model, in particular the indirect use of submodularity, leads to several MPE algorithms that all have approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: The most probable explanation problem asks for the most likely configuration under a probability model. The paper studies this inference problem for a family of distributions containing a particular combinatorial structure. The family permits arbitrary treewidth and factors of arbitrary size, allowing models with broad and potentially complicated interactions.

Such freedom normally presents a serious obstacle: for general models with these properties, the abstract describes the most probable explanation problem as inapproximable. The authors identify additional structure within their chosen family that changes the situation. In particular, submodularity enters indirectly and supplies the basis for algorithms with approximation guarantees.

The paper develops several such algorithms, each accompanied by a guarantee on approximation. The significance is that useful guarantees can come from the internal organization of a model even when its treewidth and factor sizes are unrestricted. The result applies to the structured family under study; arbitrary treewidth alone does not make a general probability model amenable to these methods.
summary.tldr: Embedded combinatorial structure enables guaranteed approximate inference in a model family with arbitrary treewidth and factor sizes.

title: Approximation Bounds for Inference using Cooperative Cuts

abstract: Choosing a subgraph that can concisely represent a large real-world graph is useful in many scenarios. The usual strategy employed is to sample nodes so that the induced subgraph matches the original graph�s degree distribution, clustering coefficient, etc., but no attempt is made to preserve fine-grained relationships between nodes, which are vital for applications like clustering, classification, and ranking. In this work, we model such relationships via the notion of Personalized PageRank Value (PPV). We show that induced subgraphs output by current sampling methods do not preserve PPVs, and propose algorithms for creating PPV-preserving subgraphs on any given subset of graph nodes. Experiments on three large real-world graphs show that the subgraphs created by our method improve upon induced subgraphs in terms of preserving PPVs, clustering accuracy, and maintaining basic graph properties.

paragraphs: A small subgraph can provide a compact representation of a much larger network. Common sampling strategies try to preserve broad properties such as degree distributions and clustering coefficients. This paper argues that those summaries leave out fine-grained relationships between individual nodes, which matter for tasks including clustering, classification, and ranking.

The authors represent these relationships using Personalized PageRank Values, or PPVs. They show that induced subgraphs produced by current sampling methods do not preserve those values. Their proposed algorithms instead construct PPV-preserving subgraphs for any specified subset of nodes, making the relationships among retained nodes an explicit target of construction.

Experiments on three large real-world graphs compare the proposed subgraphs with induced subgraphs. The new methods perform better at preserving PPVs, improving clustering accuracy, and maintaining basic graph properties. The findings support evaluating a compact graph through the node-level relationships it retains as well as its overall statistical resemblance to the original network.
summary.tldr: Constructing subgraphs to preserve Personalized PageRank relationships improves relationship preservation and clustering accuracy in experiments on large graphs.

title: Preserving Personalized Pagerank in Subgraphs

abstract: We propose a new learning method for heterogeneous domain adaptation (HDA), in which the data from the source domain and the target domain are represented by heterogeneous features with different dimensions. Using two different projection matrices, we first transform the data from two domains into a common subspace in order to measure the similarity between the data from two domains. We then propose two new feature mapping functions to augment the transformed data with their original features and zeros. The existing learning methods (e.g., SVM and SVR) can be readily incorporated with our newly proposed augmented feature representations to effectively utilize the data from both domains for HDA. Using the hinge loss function in SVM as an example, we introduce the detailed objective function in our method called Heterogeneous Feature Augmentation (HFA) for a linear case and also describe its kernelization in order to efficiently cope with the data with very high dimensions. Moreover, we also develop an alternating optimization algorithm to effectively solve the nontrivial optimization problem in our HFA method. Comprehensive experiments on two benchmark datasets clearly demonstrate that our HFA outperforms the existing HDA methods.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation becomes harder when source and target data use different feature representations, including different numbers of dimensions. Directly comparing those vectors is then problematic. This paper proposes Heterogeneous Feature Augmentation, or HFA, to make information from both domains usable within a shared learning method.

Two projection matrices map the domains into a common subspace where their examples can be compared. The method then augments each transformed representation with its original features and zeros. This combines a shared representation with information specific to each domain, producing features that existing methods such as support vector classification and regression can use.

The authors develop a linear objective using the SVM hinge loss, describe a kernelized version for very high-dimensional data, and provide an alternating optimization algorithm for the resulting problem. Experiments on two benchmark datasets show HFA outperforming existing heterogeneous domain-adaptation methods. The results support combining cross-domain comparability with retained original features as an effective approach in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: HFA combines shared projections with original domain-specific features to learn across domains with different feature spaces.

title: Learning with Augmented Features for Heterogeneous Domain Adaptation
